So who are the most important non-quarterbacks for each NFC team? Let's check out what Dubin had to say for three different teams in the conference:
If you want to see the other 13 MVPs in the NFC, Dubin has them here .
With the start of NFL season less than one month away, it seems like the Rams are getting all they hype and although it's well deserved, there are plenty of other good teams out there, even if we aren't talking about them as much as we should.
With that in mind, Zach Pereles decided to take a look at five teams that we're not talking about enough.
1. Seahawks. At +1100, the Seahawks are tied for the longest odds to win the Super Bowl by any reigning champ in the last eight seasons. With the exception of them being on "Hard Knocks," they're not getting much buzz. That's a mistake. Last year wasn't just some lucky run. The Seahawks went 14-3, winning not only the competitive NFC West, but earning the No. 1 seed in the NFC. Their three losses were by a combined nine points. They bulldozed two of their three playoff opponents, including the Patriots in the Super Bowl.
2. Packers . It seems like it's said every year, but perhaps this is actually the year the offense becomes one of the league's best. Jordan Love has three talented, young receivers: Christian Watson and Jayden Reed both got extensions this offseason, and Matthew Golden is a strong second-year breakout candidate.  Parsons is anticipating an early- or mid-season return. Green Bay made several additions on defense during the offseason -- including coordinator Jonathan Gannon -- and has a relatively friendly early-season schedule, when they'll be without Parsons.
3. Broncos . They have longer odds than the Lions and the same odds as the Bengals to win the Super Bowl. Neither team even made the postseason last year. The Broncos were likely a freak injury to Bo Nix away from the Super Bowl. The Broncos are behind not only the Chiefs but also the Chargers in the AFC West odds. Even Denver's 9.5 win total seems low; it won 14 games last year and 10 the year before, when Nix was a rookie.
Zach has two more teams on his list and you can check out who else is being disrespected here .
It's been a busy few days around the NFL, and since it's nearly impossible to keep track of everything, I put together a quick roundup for you.
author: John Breech

title: Eric Bieniemy returns to practice for the first time since his wife's shooting, says it's 'great to be back'
summary: The couple's son was arrested and charged with the shooting
full_text:
Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy is back at practice for the first time since his wife, Mia Bieniemy, was shot in their Virginia home on July 26 . The couple's 27-year-old son, Elijah Zion Bieniemy, was arrested and charged with malicious wounding, use of a firearm in the commission of a felony and discharge of a firearm inside a dwelling, according to the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office.
Eric said it was "great to be back" as he waved to onlookers at the Missouri Western State University field.
Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy back at practice Monday, getting a hug from voice of the Chiefs Mitch Holthus. pic.twitter.com/xKmSjsUQtu
During his time away, Eric has kept in contact with head coach Andy Reid and the rest of the team. The offensive coordinator has watched live streams of practice during his absence.
"Yeah, first off, prayers to him and his family and Ms. Bieniemy, and she's doing better now," quarterback Patrick Mahomes said on Saturday . "So it's always great to hear the news from him about her, and it's been good to talk to him. He's been Zooming in. He's been live-streaming. I mean, he's still EB. It's not like he's not EB."
"He's calling you at the end of the night and talking to you ... throughout the day and all the plays and stuff like that. And so we'll be excited to get him back, but at the same time, we want him to take as much time as he needs to be with his family. But when he does come back, he'll be the most excited guy on the football field," the QB continued.
Elijah's court appearances are delayed due to a pending mental health evaluation.
After being their running backs coach from 2017-2017, Eric was the Chiefs' offensive coordinator from 2018-22, helping lead one of the strongest offenses in the NFL at the time to two Super Bowl wins. He was the Washington Commanders assistant head coach and offensive coordinator in 2023 and was UCLA's assistant head coach and offensive coordinator in 2024.
Eric spent last season as the Chicago Bears' running backs coach and returned to the Chiefs this offseason as their OC, Matt Nagy left for the New York Giants .
author: Shanna McCarriston

title: Terrion Arnold visiting with Seahawks and Saints amid legal troubles, per report
summary: Arnold reportedly has an arraignment hearing on felony charges this week
full_text:
Former Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold is fielding interest from several NFL teams despite the fact that he's facing eight felony charges of kidnapping and armed robbery. ESPN reports that Arnold will visit the New Orleans Saints after spending time with the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks . He has also visited with the Houston Texans .
The 23-year-old cornerback was arrested on felony charges in June, which ultimately led to his release from the Lions. Arnold faces the possibility of life in prison if convicted, and Fox Sports reports he has an arraignment hearing set for this week in Tampa, Florida, on Aug. 13.
Arnold scored a major legal victory last month when Chief Judge Christopher C. Sabella denied the state's request to keep the former first-round pick in custody until trial. He is allowed to travel for work, which apparently includes visits with teams, but otherwise must remain at home in Florida.
Arnold's agent, Nicole Lynn, revealed in a previous court hearing that four teams had reached out to Arnold. She also claimed there was a "very good likelihood" her client is signed in the next 45 days, according to the Detroit Free Press . Lynn testified that the Indianapolis Colts , New York Jets , Seahawks and Texans expressed interest in Arnold.
A part of these team visits is about vetting Arnold and getting more information about the situation he finds himself in. Despite the circumstances, it seems possible Arnold could indeed sign with a team in the near future. In 24 games played over two seasons with the Lions, Arnold recorded 91 tackles, 18 passes defended and one interception.
Arnold was arrested in June on four counts of kidnapping and four counts of armed robbery.
Back in February, Arnold and some of his friends were robbed during a stay in Largo, Florida. Multiple items were allegedly stolen , including $100,000 in cash and an $80,000 necklace. Police were called, and the group reported more than $250,000 in property losses.
This group then allegedly decided to take matters into their own hands, and gathered three men they believed were responsible for robbing them. The three men, who were actually apparently innocent of robbing Arnold and his friends, were allegedly jumped, held at gunpoint and had personal property taken. Arnold was not present for the assault, but police say he watched what happened via a live stream. Investigators now claim that Arnold was the primary conspirator.
A total of six suspects were arrested before Arnold: Five in February, and one in March. Arnold has denied being involved in the robbery. His attorneys released this statement back in June:
"Terrion Arnold categorically denies any involvement in the matters underlying the allegations made against him and maintains his innocence. There is no credible evidence linking Mr. Arnold to these allegations. Instead, the government appears to be relying on testimony from multiple convicted felons who have admitted their own involvement and may have substantial incentives to shift blame in an effort to lessen their sentences. Mr. Arnold looks forward to his day in court and is confident that the judicial process will lead to his ultimate vindication."
author: Jordan Dajani

title: Apparently, $2.1 billion doesn't buy a clear view: Bills fans discover major problem with new stadium
summary: Several fans say they were told railings wouldn't obstruct their views before purchasing seats
full_text:
Apparently, $2.1 billion doesn't buy what it used to. The Buffalo Bills held the first big event at their new stadium over the weekend, and although the new building received a lot of praise, there was also one massive complaint from fans.
However, before we get to that, let's take a look at a few things everyone liked about the new stadium: The concourses are bigger, there are better sight lines and there's even a massive folding table built into the stadium, which might be the coolest feature any new stadium has ever added.
This is the most Buffalo thing ever. 😂 pic.twitter.com/u2OSBA9uTi
Now that we got the good stuff out of the way, it's time to look at the biggest complaint about the new stadium. The Bills hosted nearly 52,000 fans for the team's "Blue and Red" practice on Saturday, and hundreds of fans in the building had an obstructed view of the field.
Whoever designed the new Bills stadium should wasn't very keen to detail. Imagine paying tens of thousands on PSLs and season tickets and walk into a view like this... pic.twitter.com/mGhzbCaMVs
That seems like a small design flaw.
As you can see, the biggest problem is that several hundred seats have views of the field obstructed by a railing. The fan below might have a bigger complaint than anyone.
They “assured” us we wouldn’t have an obstruction. pic.twitter.com/PqB7N2Sasw
Fans who bought seats at the new stadium had the chance to take a virtual tour before making their purchases, and that appears to be another part of the problem. When the fan above went on her virtual tour, the team showed her a seat with almost no obstruction, which is far from reality.
We asked if there was going to be an obstruction multiple times because it was a concern.  We were told that the image was just a rendering and there would be no obstruction. pic.twitter.com/6uUiHwJR2w
That's not a great look for a stadium that used $850 million in taxpayer funds to get built.
Another fan near that same section dealt with pretty much the exact same problem: During the virtual tour, they were told there wouldn't be any obstructions, only to find the exact opposite once they got to their seat.
Couldnt disagree with you more mike. We were pretty adamant about the obstructed views during our stadium experience.  We were told it wouldnt be an issue. This is what we were shown, and this is the end result. This is not acceptable. pic.twitter.com/RHj3qh2ink
A Bills fan in a nearby section had the same issue. The fan below was assured that the railing wouldn't obstruct their view.
They couldn’t show us the view from our exact seats, so they showed us a few seats down. This is the pic of that. We asked them if the railings in the pic were going to obstruct our view and they were adamant that the renderings weren’t to scale and it wouldn’t be a problem🤷‍♀️ pic.twitter.com/GUszwvq8O2
However, when they got to their seat on Saturday, this is what they saw.
This is our view in 418. We were told that the railing that was obstructing the view in the virtual tour wasn’t going to be a problem in real life. Well it is. pic.twitter.com/865Lu05pKU
I wouldn't want to be paying full price for that.
An obstructed view will sometimes happen when you sit in the front row of the upper section of a stadium, but in Buffalo, it's not just the front row. One fan shared a picture showing how badly his third-row seat was obstructed in the 400 level.
@mikewickett here ya go Mike I’m in the car with your caller Ryan telling you about the view being obstructed in the 400 section row 3 pic.twitter.com/7y108VvQmy
In this fan's section, that means at least three rows have an obstructed view.
The Bills are at least somewhat aware of the situation, and we know that because they didn't sell every obstructed-view seat. One photo that went viral from the stadium on Saturday showed a badly obstructed view, but the Bills didn't sell this seat, so in this situation, the team made the right decision.
I believe to have found what might well be the worst seat in the house. pic.twitter.com/2ywzoZplRT
As for the other obstructed seats, hundreds of fans appear to be impacted. The Bills can't really get rid of a railing or remove a staircase, so those fans are likely stuck with their obstructed views. Bills chief operating officer Pete Guelli told Pro Football Talk that the team will look at the situation on a "case-by-case basis."
If the team promised a seat without an obstructed view and didn't deliver, it should probably give impacted fans a discount on their tickets because you really shouldn't have to pay full price if you can't see the entire field.
author: John Breech

title: Which player will be the non-quarterback MVP for each NFC team in 2026?
summary: We know the importance of an NFL quarterback in the success of their team, but here are other NFC MVP candidates who could make a major impact in 2026
full_text:
Even in a modern NFL that is changing, quarterback play is still the single biggest determining factor in team success. For the most part, teams go as far as their quarterback can take them, and no further than that. That's just the way the league works.
It can be said, therefore, that the quarterback is the "most valuable player" on each team, no matter how you determine value. But of course, that doesn't mean there aren't other players who are incredibly valuable, and who play a significant role in determining the team's ultimate success during a given season.
We're here today to identify those players. These are the non-quarterback MVPs for each NFC team for the 2026 season.
If all goes according to plan for the Cowboys this year, their defense will show significant improvement. Williams is the key to making that happen, wrecking games from the interior of the defensive line. In Christian Parker's Vic Fangio-style defense, the penetrating defensive tackle has a huge role to play, and Williams is one of the best two-way interior linemen in the league, making him well-suited to success here.
Carter didn't have the flashy sack numbers that defensive linemate Brian Burns did last season, but Carter actually generated pressure at a higher rate, recording a sack, hit or hurry on 14.0% of his pass-rush snaps compared with 12.1% for Burns. If he can do a better job of converting pressures into sacks this season than he did a year ago, he has a chance to emerge as one of the top edge rushers in the NFL .
This one is pretty simple. Just look at the on-off splits (120-62-1 vs. 18-27) for the Eagles offense when Johnson is in the lineup over the last several years and you'll see how important he is. The offense basically falls apart whenever he's out of the lineup. Philly drafted an eventual successor this year in Markel Bell , but he's unlikely to uphold Johnson's standard as a rookie switching sides of the line. Johnson might be the most important player on the team, even including Jalen Hurts .
The Commanders spent a boatload of money and draft capital this offseason to transform their defense, but their biggest investment was in Styles, an absurdly athletic linebacker who makes plays all over the field. They need him to do a little bit of everything in Dan Quinn's defense, from ranging sideline to sideline to blitzing to covering backs and tight ends. This was one of the worst defenses in the NFL last season, so Styles certainly has his work cut out for him.
Loveland showed during his rookie season that he was well worth the No. 10 pick in the draft. He finished the year with 58 catches for 713 yards and six touchdowns, and he exploded down the stretch and in the playoffs. (In his final four games of the year, he caught 28 passes for 378 yards and two scores.) With DJ Moore no longer in town, he figures to be the focus of the passing attack for Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams , and he has the skill set to be a star at the position.
After a down year in 2025, the Lions reshaped their offensive line this offseason, and the makeover included shifting Sewell from the right side of the line to the left. He has been one of the best tackles in football for years, but now he'll arguably be playing an even more valuable role on Jared Goff's blind side. How he fares in his transition from one side of the line to the other will go a long way toward determining how this new-look line fares in 2026.
Parsons is going to miss a non-insignificant portion of the season, but he is so good and so key to what the Packers are going to want to do defensively that we can't help but pick him here. There are very few pass rushers in the NFL who can do what Parsons does when he's at his best, and if he returns to the field at anything close to his best coming back from his torn ACL, he's going to be the best player on this team by a significant margin, and provide a huge lift to the defense over the second half of the year.
Jefferson is coming off the worst year of his career, having averaged only 61.6 receiving yards per game after topping 87.5 in each of his first five NFL seasons. That was with J.J. McCarthy at quarterback, though, and with Kyler Murray under center he should be back to his usual self. Jefferson wins inside and out, down the field and in both the short and intermediate zones. He both opens things up for everyone else and dominates when the ball is thrown his way. He'll be back to proving he's a top-three wideout this season.
Robinson finished last season with 1,478 rushing yards and seven touchdowns, and he led the NFL with 2,298 yards from scrimmage. He just signed a monster contract and he is again going to be the centerpiece of the Atlanta offense. With major question marks at quarterback, the Falcons are going to depend on him to carry the load. If he's not the team's MVP, something has probably gone very wrong in Atlanta.
The Panthers are surely hoping that Phillips is their MVP after handing him a four-year, $120 million contract this offseason. When healthy, Phillips has been very good both rushing the passer and stopping the run, and he's heading into his physical prime at 27 years old. Carolina desperately needs someone to get after the quarterback after struggling to do so for the last several seasons, and Phillips is the guy the Panthers are counting on to do it at a high level.
Like Phillips, Young is heading into his prime years at 27 years old. He's also coming off the best season of his career, having picked up 10 sacks, 11 tackles for loss and 15 quarterback hits in just 12 games. He ranked sixth in the NFL with an 18.2% pressure rate, according to TruMedia, picking up a sack, hit or hurry at a higher rate than everyone except Will Anderson Jr. , Nik Bonitto , Parsons, Phillips and Josh Hines-Allen .
Wirfs missed five games last year due to injury, but still performed well enough to make the Pro Bowl. During his career, the Bucs have experienced a huge drop-off in EPA per play with Wirfs off the field (-0.02) compared to when he's been on (0.04). That's the equivalent of going from the ninth-best offense during that time to the 22nd best. If he's around to protect Baker Mayfield all year, the Tampa offense will be substantially better for it. If he's not, the Bucs could struggle to get things going.
McBride is the sun around which the Cardinals ' offense orbits. He has racked up at least 111 catches for 1,146 yards in each of the last two seasons, making the Pro Bowl each time and being named a first-team All-Pro last year. Arizona needs him to carry the load for the passing game so that Marvin Harrison Jr . and Michael Wilson can do their thing on the outside, and so that Jeremiyah Love has room to operate in the run game. If McBride plays to his potential, he's going to have another monster year.
The best defensive player in football now calls Los Angeles home. He may soon team with Aaron Donald along the defensive line, but even if he does, Garrett's ability to generate pressure and stop the run from the edge will be the key to the defense. There's a reason the Rams targeted him and paid such a premium to land him; he's a true game-wrecker unlike anyone else in the league.
There may not be a single non-quarterback whose team experiences a bigger drop-off at his position when he's out of the lineup than Williams. San Francisco has averaged 0.07 EPA per play with Williams on the field since 2020, and dropped off to just south of 0.00 when he's been on the sideline. The 49ers don't have much depth at tackle and are already dealing with injuries at the skill positions. They desperately need Williams to stay upright all year.
We could have gone with any number of players for Seattle. Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Leonard Williams would have been excellent candidates, for example. But Murphy is a rising star who broke out last season with seven sacks from the interior of the defensive line and is one of the keys to Mike Macdonald's explosive defense.…
author: Jared Dubin

title: Bears' Luther Burden III sidelined with groin injury: Here's when breakout candidate could return
summary: Chicago hopes its potential No. 1 receiver will return by the regular season opener
full_text:
The Chicago Bears experienced a scary moment during Saturday's practice when second-year wideout Luther Burden III and cornerback Tyrique Stevenson suffered injuries after a one-on-one rep in the red zone. Stevenson felt good enough to return to practice, while Burden did not. He was spotted walking gingerly toward the locker room with trainers.
CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz reports that Burden suffered a groin injury and is expected to miss about a month. The Bears hope he can return for the Sept. 13 season opener against the Carolina Panthers .
With DJ Moore in Buffalo, Burden is expected to headline Caleb Williams ' receiving corps along with Rome Odunze . With Burden sidelined, Zavion Thomas and Jahdae Walker should be in line to receive more reps.
Burden missing the entire preseason is not ideal, but it could have been much worse. Chicago has high hopes for its former No. 39 overall pick this year, and head coach Ben Johnson said earlier this offseason that he's "buying stock" in him.
"Just how he's approached his offseason, it's been electric," Johnson said. "He showed up yesterday, he had numerous explosive plays. I loved how in Phase 2 he was finishing every single rep that he took, and that really translated over to yesterday as well. So, he's in a really good spot. He's still developing and growing his route tree ...
"He's been extremely coachable, so I'm really happy with him."
In his first NFL season, Burden caught 47 passes for 652 yards and two touchdowns in 15 games played. He missed two games with a concussion and an ankle issue. Burden ranked third among wide receivers in yards per route run with 2.71 (min. 200 routes), trailing only Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Puka Nacua . According to CBS Sports Research, those 2.71 yards per route run were the most by a rookie wide receiver in the past 10 seasons.
The CBS Sports Fantasy Football team ranks Burden as WR27, projecting he will catch 73 passes for 1,057 yards and six touchdowns in 2026.
author: Jordan Dajani

full_text:
It feels like a bit of a make-or-break season in Houston for quarterback C.J. Stroud , as he has clearly regressed from his 2023 NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year campaign. Stroud wants to be in the $50 million per year quarterback club and is eligible for an extension, but the Texans don't appear in a major rush and have already slapped the fifth-year option on the former No. 2 overall pick.
Since I'm a glass half-full guy, first the good news: DeMeco Ryans and Stroud are only the second head coach/quarterback duo ever with a playoff win in each of their first three seasons in the league, after John Harbuagh and Joe Flacco in Baltimore. I believe the Texans will repeat as AFC South champions, and they are +110 favorites if you want to try futures betting on any of the best betting apps . Stroud was only sacked 23 times last year, but the Texans opted to remake the offensive line anyway, signing free agents in Braden Smith and Wyatt Teller and taking Georgia Tech guard Keylan Rutledge with their first-round pick at No. 26 overall. But perhaps the biggest help for Stroud comes in the form of wideout Tank Dell . This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here .

title: Five NFL teams we're not talking about enough: Seahawks under the radar again? Packers take next step?
summary: The headline-grabbing teams aren't the only ones worth paying attention to
full_text:
In mid-February, one team wins the Super Bowl and becomes a champion. And then, seemingly within a few days, everyone moves on. Within a month, we start declaring "offseason champions." This team hired a new, highly sought-after coach? Offseason champion. This team filled major holes in free agency? Offseason champion. This team crushed the draft (even though we've never seen a single player play a single down in the NFL )? Offseason champion.
Sometimes the teams that are the quietest, though, are the ones making the greatest strides toward becoming an actual football champion. And that's the goal, right? Last year, the Seahawks were the perfect example. They traded away Geno Smith and signed Sam Darnold , a move most felt lukewarm (at best) about. They traded away DK Metcalf and released Tyler Lockett , their biggest-name offensive stars of late. Their "big" outside signings were Cooper Kupp and DeMarcus Lawrence , and their biggest retention was Ernest Jones .
Offseason champions? Hardly. Only four of our 15 staffers picked Seattle to even make the playoffs last year .
So how can we course correct this year? How can we find great values? Here are five teams that haven't made a ton of noise this offseason but could make plenty when the results actually matter.
At +1100, the Seahawks are tied for the longest odds to win the Super Bowl by any reigning champ in the last eight seasons. It's not that hard to see why. The Seahawks lost Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III in free agency and saw several other key contributors walk, too. They also lost offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak to the Raiders ' coaching job.
But, with the exception of them being on "Hard Knocks," they're not getting much buzz. That's a mistake. Last year wasn't just some lucky run. The Seahawks went 14-3, winning not only the competitive NFC West, but earning the No. 1 seed in the NFC. Their three losses were by a combined nine points. They bulldozed two of their three playoff opponents, including the Patriots in the Super Bowl. DVOA, a metric that adjusts for opponent strength, says the 2025 Seahawks were the third-best Super Bowl champion ever .
There's too much being made about the uncertainty -- at offensive coordinator, at running back, etc. It's not as if Kubiak had been overly successful before coming to Seattle; Mike Macdonald deserves the benefit of the doubt when it comes to his hires. And while Seattle will miss Walker's explosiveness, Seattle only ranked 28th in rushing success rate last year.
Macdonald is terrific. He was No. 2 in our coach rankings and unanimous No. 1 in our defensive play caller rankings . The defense should once again be excellent. Devon Witherspoon is a top-five cornerback, the interior defensive line duo of Leonard Williams and Byron Murphy II is the best in the NFL, and Jones was an All-Pro last year. Safety Nick Emmanwori is an emerging star. The Seahawks are just fine not generating a lot of headlines while generating a lot of wins.
On Dec. 7, the Packers were 9-3-1 and had won four straight games entering a showdown with the Broncos . Green Bay ranked in the top five in several defensive categories, including yards per play, yards per pass attempt and explosive play rate.
Then things fell apart. Leading in the third quarter, Micah Parsons tore his ACL. Green Bay lost that game and its next three regular-season games, and then they blew a 21-3 lead against the Bears in the wild card game. The defense completely fell apart without Parsons (and, it should be noted, several other key players), and the offense never quite reached the heights it sometimes looked like it could.
It seems like it's said every year, but perhaps this is actually the year the offense becomes one of the league's best. Jordan Love has three talented, young receivers: Christian Watson and Jayden Reed both got extensions this offseason, and Matthew Golden is a strong second-year breakout candidate.
Parsons is anticipating an early- or mid-season return . Green Bay made several additions on defense during the offseason -- including coordinator Jonathan Gannon -- and has a relatively friendly early-season schedule, when they'll be without Parsons.
The Broncos' elation of a divisional round win over the Bills quickly turned to stunned heartbreak when, moments after the game, news broke that Bo Nix had fractured his ankle. One week later, with backup Jarrett Stidham under center, they lost 10-7 to the Patriots.
It's impossible to definitively say the Broncos would have won with Nix, but given how their defense dominated ... you get the picture. Now? They have longer odds than the Lions and the same odds as the Bengals to win the Super Bowl. Neither team even made the postseason last year. The Broncos were likely a freak injury away from the Super Bowl. The Broncos are behind not only the Chiefs but also the Chargers in the AFC West odds. Even Denver's 9.5 win total seems low; it won 14 games last year and 10 the year before, when Nix was a rookie.
The Broncos' passing attack should be significantly more dynamic with Jaylen Waddle in tow. He creates explosives down the field and with the ball in his hands, a perfect complement to the bigger-bodied Courtland Sutton . The excellent offensive line returns, and J.K. Dobbins is back and healthy, leading a running back room that has plenty of depth. The defense returns basically everyone except defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers . Denver should be a shoo-in playoff team at worst.
In the course of handing out offseason winners, there are also offseason losers, and it's easy to make the case that the Jaguars were one of them. Jacksonville lost its top running back ( Travis Etienne ) and its All-Pro linebacker ( Devin Lloyd ), made only minor additions and used its only top-80 pick on Nate Boerkircher , who projects as a rotational blocking tight end.
But what about the internal development? Trevor Lawrence caught fire down the stretch of last season as Jacksonville won eight straight games before losing a close one to the Bills in the playoffs. He could simply continue to play at a high level, now in Year 2 of Liam Coen's offense. Coen has proved he's among the game's best offensive minds. The wide receivers -- Brian Thomas Jr. , Jakobi Meyers , Parker Washington and at times Travis Hunter -- provide a nice mix of complementary skills. Bhayshul Tuten and free agent Chris Rodriguez Jr . could be a nice 1-2 running back punch.
If Hunter can be a bigger contributor defensively, that would be huge, too. Jacksonville's defense was a top-10 unit by most measures last year.
Here's one team well outside the projected playoff picture to be bullish on. The Saints added Etienne to boost a sluggish rushing attack, signed guard David Edwards to fortify an offensive line that features two young, talented tackles and drafted Jordyn Tyson No. 8 overall to pair with Chris Olave .
New Orleans won four of its final five games, with Tyler Shough looking better and better after taking over as starter midseason. Chase Young quietly posted a resurgent year with 10 sacks in just 12 games and an 18.1% pressure rate, seventh in the NFL (min. 200 pass-rush snaps). There's young talent in the secondary. The Bryan Bresee injury hurts, but this is an intriguing option in the oft-underwhelming NFC South.
author: Zachary Pereles

title: Have Giants, Saints finally found franchise QBs? History points to Year 2 leaps for Jaxson Dart, Tyler Shough
summary: Dart and Shough don't have to become Eli Manning or Drew Brees, but their rookie seasons suggest they could finally end two long QB searches
full_text:
The Giants have spent the better part of a decade looking for Eli Manning's replacement. The Saints have taken nearly as long trying to find life after Hall of Famer Drew Brees . Different cities, different organizations, same question: did they finally get their guy?
New York cycled through names like Daniel Jones , Tommy DeVito and Russell Wilson before handing the offense to Jaxson Dart . In New Orleans, the list included Teddy Bridgewater , Jameis Winston , Derek Carr and Spencer Rattler before turning to Tyler Shough . Every move started with guarded optimism and ended with the search continuing.
This time feels different.
Not because Dart and Shough are guaranteed to become franchise quarterbacks, but because their rookie seasons in 2025 resembled those of quarterbacks who historically took major steps forward in their sophomore campaigns. Giants and Saints fans have heard such promises before. This time, there are reasons to believe.
Quarterbacks don't usually break out because they throw for 4,000 yards as rookies. They break out because they already show the traits that consistently translate -- efficiency comes before production and limiting mistakes comes before stardom. The breakout usually arrives later, a function of everything else coming together.
To see how Year 2 often unfolds, I looked at every quarterback since 2010 who started at least eight games as a rookie and tracked what happened in his second season.
The quarterbacks who break out in Year 2 don't all get there the same way. But history shows a few recurring paths.
Elite rookie became an even better Year 2 quarterback.
Coaching change unlocked his talent.
Offensive coaching change disrupted his development.
Supporting cast and offensive environment deteriorated.
Knee injury fundamentally altered his trajectory.
The lesson isn't that every quarterback falls into one of these distinct categories. It's that context matters as much as talent.
Herbert built on an outstanding rookie season. Lawrence took off once Jacksonville got the coach right. Prescott regressed when the offense around him regressed ( Ezekiel Elliott was suspended, the offensive line was banged up). Mac Jones lost momentum after an offensive overhaul that included losing coordinator Josh McDaniels. And Griffin's trajectory changed because of injury late in his rookie season. Development is rarely linear, and it's almost never isolated from what's happening around the quarterback.
So where does that leave this year's class? If there's one quarterback I'd bet on to make a Year 2 leap, it's Dart. What surprised me most was how consistent the results were. Whether I looked at historical comparisons or projections, they kept pointing back to the Giants quarterback.
The Giants didn't spend Dart's rookie season trying to hide him. Once he became the starter, Brian Daboll asked him to run the offense, push the ball downfield and consistently make big-boy NFL throws. As the season progressed, Dart looked increasingly comfortable doing exactly that. And while it didn't always work, the results were encouraging.
Dart's rookie numbers were modest: 2,272 passing yards, 15 touchdowns and a 91.7 passer rating across 12 starts. The more encouraging story lived beneath those numbers. Dart consistently challenged defenses downfield while protecting the football -- just five interceptions on 339 attempts -- even after Malik Nabers was lost for the season in Dart's first NFL start.
By November, Daboll wasn't calling games like he was trying to protect a rookie. He was calling them like he expected Dart to make NFL throws. (And, yes, also like he was trying to save his job. Both things can be true.) Dart rewarded that trust. The game never felt too big, and that's a common thread for many successful Year 2 quarterbacks.
Dart's closest rookie profiles produced a variety of successful Year 2 seasons. Bo Nix's statistical output most closely resembles Dart's projected production, while Russell Wilson and Marcus Mariota represent more efficient versions of that same developmental path.
The point isn't that Dart will become Wilson or Mariota; it's that his closest historical comps generally built on their rookie seasons instead of plateauing or regressing.
These aren't projections carved in stone; they're a range of likely outcomes based on how quarterbacks with Dart's rookie profile have historically developed. The takeaway is simpler: quarterbacks who looked like Dart as rookies usually became legitimate NFL starters, not placeholders. That's the standard in New York -- finding a quarterback good enough to stop searching.
If there's one quarterback I think we (and "we" is doing a lot of work here -- I mostly mean "me") may have underestimated, it's Shough. His rookie season hinted at something the box scores couldn't fully capture.
Dart has the higher ceiling, but Shough may have the higher floor. The NFL saw an older, often-injured quarterback coming out of college, and that's why he lasted until the second round. But his rookie season suggested something more interesting: a quarterback who already played the position with surprising efficiency. He completed 67.6% of his passes, averaged 7.3 yards per attempt and posted a 91.3 passer rating over nine starts for a Saints offense that never quite established a consistent identity around him.
Continuity matters, too, with the second-year quarterback returning alongside his second-year coach. There is no learning a new offense. Instead, Shough can grow within the one he already knows.
The names tell an interesting story. Carr, Dalton and Bridgewater: two second-round picks and a late first-rounder, all multi-season starters. Not an All-Pro among them (there are eight Pro Bowls), but all proved they could win in the league. Carr and Dalton started for nearly a decade. Bridgewater was on his way before a devastating knee injury changed his career. Even Minshew carved out multiple productive seasons despite being a Day 3 pick.
As for Shough, his historical comps aren't built around superstardom -- their superpower is stability.
New Orleans doesn't need an MVP. It needs a quarterback it can stop replacing every offseason. For a franchise that has most recently cycled through Carr, Rattler and Haener, stability would be a revelation. Shough does not need to become Brees. He just needs to become the quarterback the Saints stop trying to replace.
The focus here is on Dart and Shough because they're the quarterbacks the historical analysis kept pointing back to. That doesn't mean Cam Ward and Shedeur Sanders won't become good NFL starters. It just means their rookie seasons produced much wider ranges of possible Year 2 outcomes.
Ward belongs in the conversation because he was the No. 1 overall pick and started all 17 games as a rookie. Sanders belongs because he could very well open 2026 as Cleveland's starter. Neither, however, produced the same combination of historical matches and Year 2 projections that made Dart and Shough stand out.
Ward's rookie season looked different from Dart's and Shough's: he threw for 3,169 yards and finished with an 80.2 rating that undersold how much the Titans offense asked of him. The closest Year 2 path is Lawrence: improvement without automatic stardom. Lawrence's second season was cleaner and more productive, but it did not instantly turn Jacksonville into a juggernaut.
Sanders is the opposite. In eight starts, Sanders threw seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions, flashing enough ability to keep Cleveland curious -- and enough volatility to keep everyone guessing. He has the widest range of outcomes in Year 2 because he showed flashes that make you think there's more there. He was also more inconsistent than Dart, Shough and Ward.
Sure, Sanders could turn into a functional starter, but he could also remain a high-variance player. Neither outcome would be shocking.

title: Falcons add RB Trey Sermon
summary: Atlanta’s adding another veteran option to their running back group, signing Marietta native Trey Sermon to a one-year deal. Just because you have Bijan Robinson doesn’t mean you can’t worry about your depth. Sermon was a third round pick for the 49ers in 2021 and followed a familiar trajectory for a 49ers reserve runner, dealing […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - AUGUST 21: Trey Sermon #27 of the Pittsburgh Steelers escapes a tackle from Jon Rhattigan #49 of the Carolina Panthers during the second half of an NFL Preseason 2025 game at Bank of America Stadium on August 21, 2025 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Atlanta’s adding another veteran option to their running back group, signing Marietta native Trey Sermon to a one-year deal . Just because you have Bijan Robinson doesn’t mean you can’t worry about your depth. Sermon was a third round pick for the 49ers in 2021 and followed a familiar trajectory for a 49ers reserve runner, dealing with injuries and ultimately falling out of favor as the team quickly cycled through options. Sermon will join the Falcons hoping to battle Nate Carter, Cash Jones, and Tyler Goodson for the team’s third back role behind Bijan and Brian Robinson. With Bijan unlikely to play much during preseason and Brian pretty locked in to his role, expect all four backs to get plenty of run in the first week of preseason and (if they all stick around) over the coming weeks as well. He wound up on the Eagles in his second season, spent two years with the Colts, and signed with the Steelers last season and now has 505 yards and three touchdowns on the ground to go with 22 receptions for 138 yards. With a good line—and the Falcons should once again have one—Sermon’s physicality and speed can make him a fun reserve back, especially because he can catch the ball and block when called upon. To this point in his NFL career, the production has been underwhelming and he’s struggled to find a home, but there is no locked-in third back in Atlanta and he should get a fair shot to show the role is his. With Cash Jones providing a lot of utility as a receiver and special teamer in camp, Carter having that intriguing breakaway speed, and Goodson doing a bit of everything well, though, Sermon will have to be sharp to get that chance. Give him a warm welcome, and we may see him as soon as Friday night.
author: Dave Choate

title: Biggest takeaways from the first week of Falcons training camp
summary: The first week of Falcons training camp is behind us. It was an eventful seven practices, with a lot of good and, sadly, one very serious injury. Ultimately, I came away from Flowery Branch feeling pretty good about the direction of the team despite a different approach than I’m used to at training camp. It’s […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Atlanta, Falcons, USA; Atlanta Falcons wide receivers huddle during training camp at IBM Performance Field. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The first week of Falcons training camp is behind us. It was an eventful seven practices, with a lot of good and, sadly, one very serious injury. Ultimately, I came away from Flowery Branch feeling pretty good about the direction of the team despite a different approach than I’m used to at training camp. It’s clear that Kevin Stefanski runs things differently than Raheem Morris and even Arthur Smith. How that will impact the regular season remains to be seen. All that being said, I put together my overall takeaways from the first week of Falcons training camp in a show format. I’ll also have my written notes down below for those who prefer that. If you’ve got time, give both a click to help us out. Check out the video, podcast, and notes below! Watch the show below or on YouTube You can also listen to all of our video shows in an audio-only podcast format, available on all your favorite podcast platforms or by using the player below. The podcast typically posts a few hours after the live show records. Biggest takeaways from Falcons training camp One thing to note off the top is that Stefanski’s training camp practices are run differently than those of Raheem Morris or Arthur Smith. For starters, they’ve typically been about half as long as I’m accustomed to. Morris and Smith typically practiced for the full two hour block every single day, while Stefanski practices between 60-90 minutes most days. Some days were closer to the full two hours, but especially early in camp, practices were shorter and lighter. That being said, when the pads came on, Stefanski actually allowed full contact tackling. This is not something that we saw from Morris. The players seemed very happy about this, with several mentioning how different this approach was from the previous regime. While we haven’t seen the preseason games yet, Stefanski mentioned that he’s likely to play starters in both the first and third games, and that there’s going to be a lot more emphasis on the preseason in general. That’s a major departure from Morris, who refused to play any starters in preseason. Again, we don’t know how this will play out and translate into the regular season. The team already suffered one major season-ending injury in practice, and risking starters in preseason action remains a controversial decision. It’s also one that’s been embraced by a number of the top teams in the league, so perhaps there is some correlation. We’ll see how this plays out over the next month. The quarterback competition between Penix and Tua is real Michael Penix Jr. hasn’t been cleared for full contact, and there’s no telling exactly when that will happen. That being said, Penix doesn’t appear to have any limitations, physically speaking. While he’s not participating in full team 11-on-11 work, he’s taking a similar allotment of snaps to Tua Tagovailoa and the other quarterbacks in 7-on-7. Penix is healthier than most outsiders assume based on reporting. Watching him in camp, it looks like he could be cleared any day—and his lack of clearance is probably more precautionary than anything. Penix himself said as much, saying he feels great, is getting a little bit better every day, and also could theoretically be cleared “any day”. The last step for him is final clearance from his doctor, which doesn’t have a specific timeline at this point. My guess is if all goes well, the hope will be to get Penix cleared for at least the third preseason game. In order for Penix to have a shot to start Week 1, I think he’d need to be getting full team work by at least that time. All that being said, Tua Tagovailoa has looked good in training camp. He’s been very efficient overall and typically superior to Penix in the red zone, although Penix has continuously wowed with his deep ball and aggressiveness on deeper targets. It’s difficult to compare the two because Penix’s snaps are more or less on a timer (with a simulated pass rush) versus Tua’s being an actual offensive line versus defensive line situation. Sometimes Tua gets more time as a result, sometimes a lot less. Obviously, Tua’s 11-on-11 snaps are more representative of an actual game environment. That’s why it’s important for Penix to get some full team reps, sooner than later. At this point, he’s done a great job of keeping up with Tua based on the eye test. But without full team reps to make a direct comparison, the team may be forced to go with Tua for the early part of the season, simply because he’s been able to practice with the full team and Penix has not. It’s also important to note that the QB competition isn’t going to end with the Week 1 starter being named. This is likely to be an ongoing battle, no matter who wins the job to open the season. Even if Tua is given the job initially, he’ll have to play well to keep the team from going to Penix, and vice versa. There’s no loyalty to either player from the coaching staff or front office at this stage. The most impressive player of camp? WR Zachariah Branch This shouldn’t surprise anyone, but the most impressive player of the first week of Falcons training camp is rookie wide receiver Zachariah Branch. The electric athlete wowed early with his 1-on-1 prowess, then continued his dominance into team drills and fully padded practices. His route running is far more advanced than what he showed on tape at Georgia, and his hands have arguably been the best of any receiver at camp. That’s not to say he’s been flawless, but for a third-round rookie to be the story of camp? Far beyond even my most optimistic expectations. The Falcons passing game will change significantly in 2026 Much was made in the offseason about Atlanta likely running their offense out of 12 (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR) personnel, given the lack of receiving talent on the roster and Stefanski’s preferences for the tight end position. I doubt Stefanski’s preferences have changed—the tight end position will be heavily targeted, I have no doubt—but the outlook of the team’s receiving talent most certainly has. Jahan Dotson has looked like a solid WR2, playing both outside and in the slot and generally looking like an efficient option. I doubt he’ll be a major head-turner on a weekly basis, but Dotson is exactly the type of reliable and versatile chain-mover that the Falcons offense lacked in 2025. At slot receiver, Olamide Zaccheaus has acquitted himself well and generally looked like a solid WR3 option. I think he could provide similar value to what Atlanta got out of Ray-Ray McCloud in years past. But the biggest change is how quickly Zachariah Branch has rocketed up the depth chart, and he may force his way into the starting lineup by the time Week 1 arrives. Branch provides an explosive element to the passing game that Atlanta otherwise lacks. He’s an elite separator who can stress the defense vertically and horizontally, and is probably the Falcons best yards-after-catch weapon outside of Bijan Robinson. Branch offers Atlanta a quick game target who can turn a screen or a jet sweep into a big play, while also flashing deep speed to test an opponent’s coverage. Zaccheaus is a more polished player at this stage, but Branch is a lot more electric. We’re also going to see the middle of the field targeted much more frequently under Stefanski and Tommy Rees. Drags, digs, crossers, smash concepts, slants, we saw it all in the first seven days of training camp. There’s a clear emphasis on getting these quarterbacks and receivers used to running middle of the field concepts. That’s a big departure from Zac Robinson’s passing game, which seemed to deliberately exclude some of those concepts. Another major departure from Robinson’s pass concepts is that every single skill position player is a potential target. For Atlanta, that means a lot more targets to…

title: Falcons roster 2026: Jawaan Taylor activated off PUP list
summary: In excellent news, the Falcons announced Monday afternoon that they have activated Jawaan Taylor to return off the PUP list. The Falcons also have signed defensive end Cameron Sample, and in corresponding moves, Atlanta has waived long snapper Philip Florenzo and waived/injured offensive lineman Jack Nelson. Outside of the quarterback spot, RT is one of […]
full_text: Feb 3, 2025; New Orleans, LA, USA; Kansas City Chiefs offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor (74) during Super Bowl LIX Opening Night at Ceasars Superdome. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con In excellent news, the Falcons announced Monday afternoon that they have activated Jawaan Taylor to return off the PUP list. The Falcons also have signed defensive end Cameron Sample, and in corresponding moves, Atlanta has waived long snapper Philip Florenzo and waived/injured offensive lineman Jack Nelson. Outside of the quarterback spot, RT is one of the biggest questions on the roster right now — and Taylor’s activation from PUP helps. After Kaleb McGary’s surprise retirement this offseason, Taylor is hoped to be the answer at right tackle, and now that he’s cleared to practice, we’ll get to see how realistic that hope is. The Cameron Sample signing gives the Falcons some depth with run-stopping prowess. There is no 1 for 1 replacement for second-year defender Jalon Walker, or for James Pearce Jr. if he misses significant time (I expect at least six games, and I expect we will get a suspension confirmed before roster cuts). But Sample, a Snellville, Ga. native, does have some upside, including 26 quarterback hits, eight tackles for loss, and seven sacks for the Bengals over the past four seasons. No offense to Florenzo and Nelson, but no big shock on those waivers. We’ll see how they work Taylor into practice the next couple of days, and I expect we’ll get to see both Taylor (unless they’re still taking precautions with the injury that landed him on PUP) and Sample in preseason action this weekend.

title: Ravens rookies Vega Ioane, Ja’Kobi Lane look NFL-ready at training camp
summary: It was another hot one at The Castle on Saturday, and the humid weather eventually culminated in a lightning storm that forced practice inside for the final part of the day, but the practice put in by the Ravens showed a lot of promise and a few things to work on as they enter their […]
full_text: OWINGS MILLS, MARYLAND - JULY 29: Vega Ioane #71 of the Baltimore Ravens participates in a drill on the first day of training camp at Under Armour Performance Center Baltimore Ravens on July 29, 2026 in Owings Mills, Maryland. (Photo by Jamie Sabau/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was another hot one at The Castle on Saturday, and the humid weather eventually culminated in a lightning storm that forced practice inside for the final part of the day, but the practice put in by the Ravens showed a lot of promise and a few things to work on as they enter their final ramp-up before preseason ball next week. The major story of the day came during 7-on-7 drills when Zay Flowers, fresh off inking a new contract earlier in the week, collided with safety Jaylinn Hawkins and stayed down on the field. Flowers got up and then went back down to the turf, and you could feel the concern wash over the crowd. He eventually made his way behind the offensive players and had a trainer assist him in stretching, then got up and limped off the field to make his way inside. At first, it looked like an injury to his left knee, but head coach Jesse Minter confirmed that the injury was a quad contusion and that Zay is considered day-to-day. Head coach Jesse Minter says WR Zay Flowers has a quad contusion and will be day to day. — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) August 8, 2026 It was a refreshingly quick turnaround to injury reports we’ve received in the past, and I’m very glad to hear it doesn’t appear to be serious. I’d imagine that they operate with an abundance of caution for the remainder of the preseason and keep Zay sidelined to preserve his health. The Ravens were already likely to favor their rookie pass-catchers in the preseason anyway, and no member of that group has done more to make a name for themselves than Ja’Kobi Lane. Another @cantGuardJak1 highlight for the people pic.twitter.com/dQrWhfuHGJ — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) August 8, 2026 Lane once again put in a strong practice, hauling in multiple contested catches and making it look easy. He was able to beat Keyon Martin along the sideline for the snag you see in the video above, and he made a nice grab over the shoulder on a deep shot as he was shadowed by Nate Wiggins. Coach Minter praised Lane for his “businesslike approach” to learning so far and acknowledged that the upbeat and carefree personality he’s shown on the field somewhat masks how serious he is about his preparation. On the defensive side of the ball, if I had to pick a guy that impressed me most on the day, I’d lean toward T.J. Tampa. Tampa’s game has shown a ton of growth since joining the Ravens two years ago, and I was very impressed with how quickly he’s adjusted to playing the ball rather than playing the man. His physicality was one of the strongest parts of his game coming out of Iowa State, but he’s shown a more polished game this offseason, especially in one-on-ones. He laid out for a nice pass breakup as he undercut Tez Walker, and Coach Minter praised Tampa’s “knack for… being around the ball.” The majority of what we saw elsewhere was about what you’d expect for this point in the offseason: a major emphasis on timing, placement and getting the small details right. The O-line had three flags for false start (by my count), but they were also able to get set effectively and draw Kyle Hamilton offsides on one play. In position drills, you could see the focus from Coach Ledford on guys getting effective leverage and the right pad level on blocks as they started their stances beneath a metal frame that encouraged them to drive up and out rather than straight up into their blocks. I saw Ledford having lots of individual conversations with guys as well, which inspires a lot of confidence in his attention to detail, particularly with the young guys in that group. While Vega Ioane qualifies as one of the young guys, you’d never know it watching him. He looks as pro-ready as I’ve seen from a lineman in a long time, and his ability to keep his feet moving and drive his defender backward was a thing of beauty. Here are a number of other notes from Saturday’s practice: During media availability, both Marlon Humphrey and Justice Hill made mention of accountability with the new coaching staff and how much it’s helped them improve their preparation. Humphrey mentioned Minter’s expertise with the secondary unit, even joking that Minter had basically said he’d played like “trash” last season before pointing out ways to improve, and Hill noted that Coach Faulkner’s emphasis on new and creative drills in pass protection helped the running back room play a more complete game. UDFA linebacker Dominic DeLuca put together another good practice and had a pass breakup on Elijah Sarratt. Rookie tight end Josh Cuevas drew some oohs and ahs from the crowd during one-on-ones as he shook Keondre Jackson with a nice stutter-step move. It was the kind of move you don’t really expect to see a tight end hit, and I like seeing him show some swagger and confidence trying things out. Jaylinn Hawkins ran a lot of reps against the first-team offense today, and while his success was a mixed bag, it certainly signals confidence from the coaches about his ability to be a regular member of the starting secondary. Even with the false starts, the offense looked very smooth for this part of the offseason when dialing up pre-snap motion, formation shifts and audibles at the line. I’ll be interested in seeing how smooth it looks in live-game action next week.

full_text: Last week we asked Buffalo Rumblings readers how they were feeling about the Buffalo Bills after the start of training camp this summer . As everyone who follows the NFL well knows, a generous helping of salt is necessary when weighing in about the sport at this point of the calendar. That said, all anyone has to go on right now are training camp practices, press conferences/media appearances, and the myriad commentary by reporters. It’s natural then that they serve as the only concrete ways to meaningfully consume the new-look Bills ahead of preseason football (which itself may not reveal much to observers). So, how did Rumblers respond in regards to Buffalo’s new brass and the few nuggets of practice centered around a reformulated team looking to break an AFC Championship impasse? For the majority of our readers, hope springs eternal. Leading the way with 56% of the vote are those Rumblers who said they’re “cautiously optimistic” about the Bills at this point in the summer. There’s a lot to be excited about — especially on defense given the scheme switch. Plus, president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane has given quarterback Josh Allen a new top wide receiver option in DJ Moore. Don’t forget about running back James Cook III when considering the offense’s role this season. The reigning NFL rushing yards leader appears ready to run it back. That could have played into the percentage of Rumblers (30%) who said they’re “super excited” about Buffalo in August. Much further down the polls were the 12% of voters who “haven’t seen enough yet,” and the 2% of folks who remain “cautiously pessimistic.” Perhaps that 2% of voters really doesn’t like the new alternate uniforms ? Think you’ve got what it takes to make a play with the Buffalo Bills in 2026? Head over to FanDuel Sportsbook now to put it to the test !

title: New Highmark Stadium is fun for Skarekrows of all sizes
summary: The Buffalo Bills opened their new stadium in style, with over 50,000 fans attending the annual “Return of the Red and Blue” practice. That’s right, over 50k for a practice. Among those attending were my sister that I frequently mooch off of, our football friend (of Mando helm fame), my two daughters, and myself. I […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills opened their new stadium in style, with over 50,000 fans attending the annual “Return of the Red and Blue” practice. That’s right, over 50k for a practice. Among those attending were my sister that I frequently mooch off of, our football friend (of Mando helm fame), my two daughters, and myself. I also needed to know if it passed the muster of one other entity, so I snuck in a guest. If you promise not to tell anyone, I’ll show what the stadium looks like through his eyes. Entering the stadium I did a write up on the Highmark Trail , noting how much fun stuff is outside the fence line of the stadium and that remains true. The family circle (the area surrounding the bison statues) was fully open and packed as expected. At the old stadium, getting through the fence was both security and ticketing. Now it’s just security, with many fan activities set up inside the fence line, but not quite in the building yet. But enough for now, let’s take a peek through the eyes or my special guest. Meet ‘Lil Krow! I’ll talk more about his origin story in a minute, but first, here’s a shot of the approach to the stadium, his attempt to ride the bison, and his first time on a football field. As mentioned, the bisons are open to the public at all times and are the signature feature of the Highmark Trail and Family circle. The little field is inside the fence. Along with that were giveaways from various sponsors (like Wegmans) and foundations ( like Doug Flutie’s autism foundation ). There was a place for caricatures, mini golf on the mini field, a person-sized bobblehead of Josh Allen, places for food and Bills shopping. Here’s the important note I believe for fans. This required you go through security but you did NOT need a ticket yet. In other words, fan can participate in a lot of the pregame stuff even if they’re not going to the game. In that final picture, that sign is on the glass looking into the stadium itself. We had still not yet shown anyone a ticket. Now for a little detour. ‘Lil Krow’s Origin Story Not that long ago I went to a jersey singing put on by Thurman Thomas and his wife, The Ghost. It was part of their marketing campaign for their venture into near field tech. They gave us some samples of their work. I made one of the chips they game me into a mini avatar of myself. If you see me at a Bills game this year, come say “hi” to me, Regular Krow; and ask to tap your phone to ‘Lil Krow to see the near field tech in person and get a sneak peak at all things Skarekrow. Right now, anyone lucky enough to tap ‘Lil Krow can get a spoiler on what dangerous thing I’m building for my Mando armor. Anyway, ‘Lik Krow had to make a special stop… Thank you to Thurman Thomas, The Ghost, and VeriLink for making ‘Lil Krow possible. Let’s continue his quest. Watching the game While there are many things to discuss with the new stadium, arguably the most important thing is seeing the game. The ticketing is right at the building now. I can’t vouch for every entrance, but for the one we entered into, as soon as your ticket is scanned, here’s your view. You can see much of the bowl and the scoreboard. And maybe another 30 feet and you’re looking at the field. There are access stairs, escalators, and elevators all over. Getting between levels was easy with enough access points where we took stairs that felt like we were alone. Again, there were 50,000 people and everyone was walking around. I know there’s views from all over, so for context the pictures in the seat were from the very back of the 300 level. I absolutely loved the view. I was able to see the entire field easily. The verticality of the seats made for great sightlines. Despite the steepness of it all, the walkway and seat design made it easy to stand up and let other fans by as they meandered to and fro. We got to test the new partial roof too as a pop up storm dumped a ton of rain in short time. A lot of people in the 100s took shelter in the concourses, and there’s a pic in there showing the view from there if you needed to pull back. Where I was we got a tiny sprinkle blow in when the wind shifted just right. Speaking of wind, compared to how it used to be the air is very still in the stadium. That’ll be great in winter, but if you’re going to a summertime game, don’t count on a cool breeze to help you out. I know Chris covered a lot of it, but I’ll give my two cents on some things too. The seats were comfortable, the sound system seems like an upgrade, the scoreboards and visuals are fantastic, and did you notice the closed captioning by the scoreboard? Watching a practice was pretty sick and watching a game here is going to be insane. Luckily, thanks to mooching off my sister, I won’t have to wait long. The extras I noted on social media that part of the human condition is to experience change as loss. I’ll miss the old stadium, but was simple awestruck at how many cool things the new stadium features. I come from a little town that’s packed with artwork, and my favorite aspect of the new Highmark is how there’s something on display everywhere you look. Please note; we walked around for about an hour and still missed a ton. Here’s some of what we caught. There’s so much detail in everything, if you get a chance to go, stop and take it all in. I only tried an order of wings for food, and the quality was quite good. The chicken was cooked very well and the sauce (mumbo) was flavorful. I could get 20 wings locally for the amount I spent on just five, but I don’t know if the prices are much worse than the old joint sadly. Speaking of details, check out the paper in the box. Despite being a giant enclosed building, walking around in many areas feels open. Shockingly so at time. It was a bit hazy in the one direction, but check out what you can scope in the distance. There’s one thing that I struggled to decide on whether to put it here or in the game section. I landed on putting it here. There was live music playing as we entered the stadium. There’s a place called the “Charge Bar” which dominates one end zone. It looks like this… In addiction to the slick looking charge stripe you might notice that’s where the band is. When we went to Cleveland to watch the game last year, I was a bit jealous that they had areas to highlight various things like live music. Old Highmark had former players lead the charge from a corner of the field, and that was fine, but something about the Cleveland experience felt more dynamic. I don’t think I need to feel jealous any more. Until next time… I’ll be back very soon, as my sister gifted me her tickets to the Panthers preseason game. Maybe I’ll do a follow up and let you know how things look from the charge bar area, where her seats are. Until then though, it’s farewell from Regular and ‘Lil Krow… Epilogue There were some naysayers about various things and I decided to poke fun at that. I noticed a small amount of exposed steel cable behind the seats and posted it on Twitter as a joke like a sarcastic “The Bills can’t do anything right.” For the record, what I’m about to show you is completely normal. This is the equivalent of a tiny bit of a plastic tag stuck in new clothes. It’ll come out when you wash it if you don’t notice it and fix it first. I did not intend for this to be the post of the night. Why the heck did this blow up? Anyway, I’ll let this stand as a reminder that there are many imperfections I’m sure. That said, a lot of people are missing the great things while they fixate on what might be the sewing needle fingers of the Other Mother as she creeps out to give you button eyes.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: cornerback Dee Alford
summary: The Buffalo Bills deployed Taron Johnson and Cam Lewis as their primary slot corners for most of this decade. Johnson, for his part, had earned a starting role as early as his rookie year in 2018, though he didn’t become a full-time starter until the following season. Lewis worked his way onto Buffalo’s roster as […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 13: Dee Alford #20 of the Atlanta Falcons tackles Josh Palmer #5 of the Buffalo Bills during the second quarter at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 13, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills deployed Taron Johnson and Cam Lewis as their primary slot corners for most of this decade. Johnson, for his part, had earned a starting role as early as his rookie year in 2018, though he didn’t become a full-time starter until the following season. Lewis worked his way onto Buffalo’s roster as a scrappy undrafted rookie who became a valuable, versatile member of the defensive secondary. Now, with Johnson and Lewis both gone, it’s time for some new blood at the slot corner spot. The Bills have a clear plan for what they intend to do with that position, as they spent somewhat big free agent dollars on a veteran to fill the role. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss that newly-signed veteran. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Dee Alford Number: 23 Position: CB Height/Weight: 5’11” 180 lbs. Age: 28 (29 on 11/5/2026) Experience/Draft: 5; signed a reserve/futures contract as a free agent with the Atlanta Falcons on 1/10/2022 College: Tusculum Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 3/12/2026 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Alford’s three-year contract with Buffalo is worth a total of $15.75 million, of which $10.12 million is guaranteed. Alford’s cap hit for the 2026 season is $3.23 million. Buffalo would carry a dead cap charge of $7.875 million if they were to release him. 2025 Recap: Alford had his best professional season in 2025, setting career-highs in interceptions (3) and pass breakups (13) while playing in 16 games. He had 67 tackles, two sacks, six tackles for loss, and one forced fumble while playing 57% of Atlanta’s defensive snaps. He was the team leader in pass breakups, and only rookie safety Xavier Watts had more interceptions on Atlanta’s roster than Alford did. Alford was particularly good in Atlanta’s 24-14 victory over Buffalo in Week Six. According to Pro Football Reference , he had six tackles, a sack, three pass breakups, and an interception in the game; quarterback Josh Allen was just 3-for-6 for 25 yards when targeting Alford in that game. Overall, Alford allowed 67.1% of the passes thrown his way to be completed, allowing four touchdowns and holding opposing quarterbacks to an 89.2 QB rating when targeting him. Alford allowed 571 passing yards on 79 targets. For comparison’s sake, Buffalo’s top nickel corner last season, Taron Johnson, allowed 63.6% of the passes thrown his way to be completed for 363 yards an two touchdowns. Opposing quarterbacks had a 94.7 QB rating on 55 targets in Johnson’s 13 games. Positional outlook: Alford is one of six players listed at cornerback on Buffalo’s current roster. Christian Benford, Maxwell Hairston, Davison Igbinosun, D.J. Miller, and Toriano Pride Jr. are the others. Jordan Hancock is listed at defensive back, but he plays both nickel corner and safety. Te’Cory Couch, Kani Walker, and Jordan Dunbar are all listed at defensive back, but they primarily play corner, as well. 2026 Offseason: Alford has been the top option in the slot thus far at training camp and in practice. He was shaken up during practice on August 7, but he was able to participate in the team’s first practice at Highmark Stadium, so he’s healthy at the moment, as well. 2026 Season outlook: Alford was one of the first free agents signed by the Bills back in March, so it’s clear that the team and new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard view him as an important piece of what they plan to do. The guarantees on his contract signify his hold on a roster spot, as it would cost the Bills twice as much to release him this season than it would merely for them to keep him on the team. So, it’s not a question of whether Alford is on the team, but a question of whether he can continue the string of solid play he showed last year with Atlanta. Alford has had an interesting career, as he played in the Canadian Football League for a season after college and before joining the Falcons. Alford was a member of the Winnipeg Blue Bombers in 2021 after sitting out the 2020 season due to COVID-19. He was a starting corner on that Winnipeg squad, and while he did not record an interception, he did make 48 tackles for the CFL’s top-ranked defense, and he did help Winnipeg win its second-consecutive Grey Cup at the end of the 2021 season. Alford’s raw numbers are good, and while the advanced metrics show a player who can be beaten (and we’ve seen that in some one-on-one drills in training camp , as well), he’s a scrappy player who isn’t afraid to mix it up with much larger players. He’s also the player who injured Bills’ wideout Joshua Palmer on a hip-drop tackle last season, so I do wonder if he’s bought Palmer lunch at some point this summer (I’m only half-kidding). I expect that Alford will be Buffalo’s primary nickel corner this year, and while there may be some packages where the Bills use three safeties, I think those will come at the expense of a linebacker, not a corner. Alford is best suited for play in the slot, and he should be a fine replacement for Taron Johnson, who has long been a staple of the Bills’ defense. If Alford can continue to progress, then this could be a steal of a signing for Buffalo.

Defensive Backs (10) * Christian Benford Maxwell Hairston Dee Alford Davison Igbinosun Cole Bishop CJ Gardner-Johnson Jordan Hancock Damar Hamlin Jalon Kilgore Sam Franklin Jr. The only change here that represents any semblance of surpise would be Hamlin over Geno Stone. Franklin Jr. even had practices with the first-team group during CJGJ’s short injury absence, and he’s an animal as a gunner on the punt team. Also, don’t be surprised if Kilgore is on the field in sub packages as a rookie. If it weren’t for the sensational camp from KEO, the former South Carolina safety would be drawing all the headlines as the most impressive Bills rookie in Rochester. And no Kani Walker… yet. title: Fan confidence has plenty of room to grow in 2026
summary: Last week, we asked fans of the Carolina Panthers if they were confident in the current direction of the team. The survey closed before the Hall of Fame game kicked off last Thursday and thus reflects the state of the fanbase prior to the Panthers becoming the first undefeated team of 2026. Two thirds of […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - JULY 23: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers passes the ball during the Carolina Panthers Training Camp at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on July 23, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, we asked fans of the Carolina Panthers if they were confident in the current direction of the team. The survey closed before the Hall of Fame game kicked off last Thursday and thus reflects the state of the fanbase prior to the Panthers becoming the first undefeated team of 2026. Two thirds of Panthers fans are confident that Carolina is heading in the right direction. The Panthers, if you recall, are currently coming off of their first division title and their first playoff berth in a decade. They are returning the majority of their starters from last season and have made several personnel moves this offseason that should help the team take the next step forward. Those moves include signing Jaelan Phillips and Devin Lloyd, as well as drafting Monroe Freeling. So why are a third of Panthers fans still hesitant about their favorite team’s future? I think there are two reasons. First, that decade between playoff games was a rough time to be a Panthers fan. Matt Rhule, Frank Reich, and the first two years of Bryce Young’s career were wildly inconsistent at best. Often, they were just downright atrocious. A lot of us are firmly planted in “I’ll believe it when I see it” mode when it comes to Carolina’s potential success. Some of us might not even believe until we see them repeat a good season. And, no, I don’t think winning the NFC South with a losing record counts as a first good season. I love it, but it doesn’t count. Second, Young’s inconsistent performances across his first two to three seasons have not inspired a lot of confidence. Between his offensive line, running backs, and wide receivers, Young is now in charge of operating what may be one of the most talented offenses the Panthers have ever fielded. There are no more excuses. He has two years on his contract to earn the confidence of the team’s leadership. But fans, who already have one foot out of the door, won’t give him that long. From their perspective, the season opener this year against the Chicago Bears will be the most important game of Young’s career. A strong performance by Young and a win will go a long way towards lifting the overall confidence of Panthers fans. Any degree of struggle and a loss will make earning back the trust of some fans nearly impossible. Checkout FanDuel , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation.
