title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 34 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change […]
full_text: 18 Nov 2001: Carolina Panthers Wesley Walls #85 celebrates a fourth-quarter touchdown during their game against the San Francisco 49ers at Ericsson Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. San Francisco won game 25-22 in overtime. DIGITAL IMAGE Mandatory Credit: Erik Perel/ALLSPORT | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #34. Wesley Walls Panthers stats: 98 games, 324 receptions, 3,902 yards, 44 touchdowns; 5 Pro Bowls, 3 All-Pro Second Team Career stats: 196 games, 450 receptions, 5,291 yards, 54 touchdowns ; 5 Pro Bowls, 3 All-Pro Second Team If you looked up the term “late bloomer” in the NFL dictionary, the image of Wesley Walls would appear somewhere next to Steve Young. Walls played his college ball at Ole Miss and became a second round pick by the San Francisco 49ers in 1989. He spent his first five seasons with the 49ers and had a very unremarkable career with them while backing up Pro Bowl tight end Brent Jones. Wall missed the entire 1992 season due to injury, but in the four seasons in which he was healthy for the 49ers he amassed just 11 receptions for 67 yards and one touchdown. That’s not the level of production teams look for in second round picks after five years in the league. He went to the New Orleans Saints in 1994 and spent two productive seasons there with a total of 95 receptions, 1,100 yards, and eight touchdowns. In 1996 the Panthers brought him to Carolina for what would become a fantastic seven-year run in Charlotte that included five Pro Bowl seasons and three All-Pro Second Team nods. In his first season with the Panthers — his age-30 season, by the way — Walls made his first Pro Bowl after reeling in 61 receptions for 713 yards and 10 touchdowns for the 12-4 upstart Panthers. He would put up similar numbers in each of the next three campaigns to follow, and he made the Pro Bowl in each of those four seasons. His best year came in 1999 with career highs of 63 receptions, 822 yards, and 12 touchdowns. Over seven seasons with the Panthers he hauled in 324 receptions, 3,902 yards, 44 touchdowns with five Pro Bowls and three All-Pro Second Team nods. After leaving the Panthers following the 2002 season he played one year for the Green Bay Packers before calling it a career. Wesley Walls was a late bloomer by NFL standards, and we were fortunate as Panthers fans to go on that remarkable journey with him.

Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Right now, he’s DE4, so he’d better show something. UDFA defensive tackle Jayden Loving is nearly as athletic as van den Berg, so I’ll have my eye on him too. title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: Caleb Williams
summary: Alright, let’s lock into a contract extension that I think most Bears fans are curious about: Caleb Williams. We’ve been looking at several key veterans across the Bears roster and whether the Bears, in the next 12 months, should extend them (Cash), cut them (Slash), or wait a year and make a determination (Slash). This […]
full_text: LAKE FOREST, ILLINOIS - JULY 29: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears speaks to the media during Chicago Bears Training Camp at Halas Hall on July 29, 2026 in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images Alright, let’s lock into a contract extension that I think most Bears fans are curious about: Caleb Williams. We’ve been looking at several key veterans across the Bears roster and whether the Bears, in the next 12 months, should extend them (Cash), cut them (Slash), or wait a year and make a determination (Slash). This one is easy; it’s the details that are trickier. Caleb Williams: Cash There’s no reason to spend a lot of time discussing why Caleb should be extended. He has the late-game heroics, the generational talent, the relationship with Ben Johnson, the huge leap from year one to year two, he’s only getting better and we’ve seen the players (NFL Network’s Top 100) ranked him as the 10th best QB, Jeremy Fowler’s poll ranked him as the 10th best QB, and Mike Sando’s QB Tiers ranked him as the 11th best QB. After two seasons, Caleb Williams has cracked the top 10 QBs in the NFL by everyone across the league. He has a chance to be pushing to be a top 5 QB by the end of this season. He will easily be the best QB in Bears history when it’s all said and done (Sorry, Sid Luckman, your 80-year reign at the top is over). You don’t mess around when you have a talent like Caleb Williams. You pay him. So what kind of contract are we looking at for Caleb? It’s going to be expensive. This is going to be the largest contract the Bears have ever given out, and it’s not even going to be close. In fact, I will go out on a limb and say that this contract will double the largest contract the Bears have ever handed out (which the honor now belongs to Darnell Wright). When you look at the highest-paid QBs in the NFL, there is a collection of QBs that are making $55 million per season (Joe Burrow, Josh Allen, Jordan Love, Trevor Lawrence, Matthew Stafford). That’s where the negotiation begins. There’s no chance that Caleb would accept less than $55 million per season, and I think he’s going to clear that. There are only two QBs that make above that $55 million threshold. Dak Prescott, who makes $60 million per season, and Patrick Mahomes, who sits at $64 million per season. It should be noted that both Prescott and Mahomes are on their third contract and not their second contract, which obviously is a little different than the position where Caleb will be negotiating from. I also think it’s worth noting that I think Caleb is going to drive a hard bargain. I think down the line, we may see Caleb taking discounts so the Bears can sign more players, but I think for contract number two, Caleb is going to be looking to break the bank. I think he’s going to ask to be the highest-paid QB in the NFL. I don’t think he necessarily will get it. But I think, if the Bears start at $55 million per season, I think Caleb and Carl Williams counter with $65 million per season. Now I think when we are trying to settle on a final AAV, it will also depend on how many years Caleb is willing to go. The Bears will want a 5-year deal so they can lock him in at this price longer; Caleb will want a 4-year deal so he can re-negotiate the deal sooner with a bigger salary cap and more money available. I think (no inside info, just a hunch) that the Bears and Caleb would be agreeable to a 5-year deal if the Bears are willing to go north of the Dak Prescott deal. I have a hard time seeing the Bears are going to go North of Patrick Mahomes; after all, it is PATRICK MAHOMES. So I think it’s reasonable that a deal somewhere in the range of 5 years at $62 million per season for a total of $310 million would make sense. That would give Caleb the second-highest-paid annual average salary and the third-highest total value contract in the NFL. But that isn’t all that needs to be discussed; we also need to discuss guarantees. That’s where the Bears are going to have to get a little creative. There’s a difference between fully guaranteed and total guarantees. Fully guaranteed is the money the player receives no matter what. Total guarantees include guarantees that kick in during the deal. For example, the Bears could guarantee three full years of a 5-year deal and do a deal that if he’s on the roster for day 1 of the league year in his second year under that contract, that the fourth year becomes fully guaranteed. What does playing with that money do? Well, any guaranteed money needs to go in escrow. Now, I have heard that’s something that the NFL doesn’t police carefully. It’s not like we hear stories of NFL teams failing to make payroll, so most agents and players don’t push to make sure that happens. But it wouldn’t shock me if that’s something Carl and Caleb push for. If the Bears split up the guarantees as I suggested above, they aren’t on the hook to put the total guarantees in escrow, only the full guarantees. That would allow George McCaskey to split up those funds over 2 or 3 different occasions to help soften the blow of taking a huge amount of cash and putting it aside. With the guarantees, it’s hard to imagine the Williamses accepting less than about 3 years of the contract fully guaranteed, with a fourth year kicking in at some point during the contract. Other than the disastrous Deshaun Watson contract, the QB with the most fully guaranteed is Josh Allen at $147 million (his total guarantees are at $250 million). So I think that’s the number Caleb eclipses. I think he lands somewhere around $155 million fully guaranteed, while having his total guarantees up around $240 million (currently, Allen is tops with $250 million in totals, while Dak Prescott is 2nd at $231 million). What does that contract work out to? If I had to guess now, the Bears and Caleb Williams will agree to a contract somewhere around 5 years, $310 million, with $155 million fully guaranteed and total guarantees around $240 million. It would be a massive contract that would alter how the Bears operate moving forward. George McCaskey is going to have to put on his big boy pants and take a seat at the table. It’s time to step up and operate like the owner of a multi-billion-dollar organization.

title: Bears sign WR Ray-Ray McCloud III, waive WR Kyron Hudson
summary: The Bears have signed veteran wide receiver Ray-Ray McCloud III, the team announced on Monday. As a corresponding move, they have waived undrafted rookie wide receiver Kyron Hudson with an injury designation. McCloud, who turns 30 in October, is entering his ninth season in the NFL. He’s played in 100 games across stints with six […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - SEPTEMBER 28: Atlanta wide receiver Ray-Ray McCloud (34) returns a kick during the NFL game between the Washington Commanders and the Atlanta Falcons on September 28th, 2025 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Bears have signed veteran wide receiver Ray-Ray McCloud III, the team announced on Monday. As a corresponding move, they have waived undrafted rookie wide receiver Kyron Hudson with an injury designation. McCloud, who turns 30 in October, is entering his ninth season in the NFL. He’s played in 100 games across stints with six teams, typically serving as a backup wide receiver and a primary return specialist. He most notably led the NFL with 367 punt return yards as a member of the Steelers in 2021. As a receiver, his most productive year came in 2024, during which he tallied 62 catches for 686 yards and a touchdown for the Falcons. In said 2024 season, McCloud ranked No. 68 among 90 qualified wide receivers in PFN WR Impact Scoring . His time in Atlanta came to a bizarre end, as he was sent home midway through the 2025 season for an “excused absence” before he was outright released late in October. He signed with the Giants’ practice squad soon after and made appearances in two regular season games. At 5’9” and 190 pounds, McCloud began his NFL career playing primarily in the slot. However, in each of his last four seasons, he’s taken a higher percentage of his offensive snaps out wide. His signing comes in the wake of Hudson suffering an injury that saw him taken out of Saturday’s practice. Starting wideout Luther Burden III also suffered a groin injury on that day of practice, though he’s anticipated to return to the Bears for their regular season opener against the Panthers.

title: Bears Injury Updates for Ozzy Trapilo, Zavion Thomas, and Luther Burden III
summary: I was not expecting to see a noteworthy Sunday night Chicago Bears news drop, but in his recent training camp notebook at Sports Illustrated, Albert Breer gave the first update we’ve had all year on left tackle Ozzy Trapilo. “It looks like Ozzy Trapilo, who started six regular-season games at left tackle, then tore his […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - DECEMBER 14: Ozzy Trapilo #75 of the Chicago Bears guards Myles Garrett #95 of the Cleveland Browns during the second half on December 14, 2025 at Soldier Field in Chicago Illinois. (Photo by Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images I was not expecting to see a noteworthy Sunday night Chicago Bears news drop, but in his recent training camp notebook at Sports Illustrated , Albert Breer gave the first update we’ve had all year on left tackle Ozzy Trapilo. “It looks like Ozzy Trapilo, who started six regular-season games at left tackle, then tore his patellar tendon in the wild-card round, might be back sooner than expected.” Initial reports on the injury were bleak, with some believing he may miss the entire season, so “sooner than expected” would be great. Breer also had positive stuff to say about Caleb Williams, Colston Loveland, and Darnell Wright, and he painted a much prettier picture of Chicago’s defensive line than most have. Speedy rookie wideout Zavion Thomas left yesterday’s practice with a knee injury, and ESPN’s Courtney Cronin received some positive news about him. “I’m told he’s dealing with soreness in his knee and is likely day-to-day in his recovery,” Cronin shared . “He shouldn’t be out long.” Those preseason and joint practice reps are valuable for young players, so hopefully Thomas is back soon. And finally, we shared the initial report on Luther Burden III last night, and now ESPN’s Adam Schefter has shared what his sources are telling him about the injury. “Chicago WR Luther Burden III is expected to miss the preseason due to the strained groin injury he suffered Saturday, but the Bears believe he should be back for the team’s regular-season opener vs. the Panthers, per sources.” Which is pretty much what was reported last night, but considering Burden’s importance to the offense, and how good he looked all offseason, I could see the Bears being extra cautious with his return. The Bears are practicing at Stevenson High School today, and we’ll share a camp report on that later this afternoon.

title: Ja’Marr Chase is chasing an NFL single-season touchdown record
summary: Ja’Marr Chase has become one of the NFL’s premier receivers ever since getting drafted to the Cincinnati Bengals and reunited with Joe Burrow. He is up there with the top names in the sport as fellow LSU teammate Justin Jefferson also sits atop the leaderboard for top wide-outs in the league. However, Chase has his […]
full_text: Ja’Marr Chase has become one of the NFL’s premier receivers ever since getting drafted to the Cincinnati Bengals and reunited with Joe Burrow. He is up there with the top names in the sport as fellow LSU teammate Justin Jefferson also sits atop the leaderboard for top wide-outs in the league. However, Chase has his eye on setting an NFL record instead of just becoming the clear-cut top WR1 in the league. In a recent sit-down after a training camp practice, Chase made it known he is targeting the NFL single-season record of 23 receiving touchdowns set by Randy Moss in 2007. Ja’Marr Chase isn’t worried about topping JSN or Justin Jefferson for WR yardage crown anymore But there’s 1 last individual goal Chase needs: 23 TDs, to break NFL single season record. pic.twitter.com/ldeP5D9NRE — Cameron Wolfe (@CameronWolfe) August 9, 2026 If Chase could make this happen, not only would he be seen as the clear-cut No. 1 receiver in the NFL, but the Bengals would likely also be having a great season in the Queen City. With the connection that Burrow and Chase have, though, it seems more likely this could eventually happen than it didn’t. Let’s hope it does. We have needed something major to cheer for the last few seasons, and this would be a win-win all around.
author: Ethan DeWitt

(Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals have some questions at cornerback. While DJ Turner II appears to be a breakout star, the other primary boundary cornerback, Dax Hill has been sidelined with hamstring tightness. In training camp, that is the perfect opportunity for a player lower on the depth chart to prove themselves. With Hill sidelined, DJ Ivey and rookie Tacario Davis have had a chance for extended opportunities to show coaches what they can do. Going against two of the best receivers in the NFL in Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins is not only good practice work for them, but a chance to show defensive coordinator Al Golden what they can do against the best of the best. As of now, it appears Ivey is doing the most with the opportunity. Bengals News: 1 Bengals training camp bright spot won’t surprise fans “Ivey has made the most of his time running with the first team, with a pass breakup on a deep post from Burrow to Higgins on Tuesday, then in perfect position to break up another deep ball for Higgins on Thursday. He hasn’t been picked on consistently or caught out of step.” Ivey has appeared in 36 games since becoming a seventh-round pick in 2023. If camp is any indication, he could be in line for an even bigger role this season. Bengals Veteran Emerges as Preseason Trade Candidate “Slaton is currently listed as one of the backup defensive tackles on the Bengals’ depth chart, but he could soon be lapped by players like Landon Robinson and Kris Jenkins. Slaton is on an expiring contract, and it would save the Bengals nearly $7 million by making a move.” Suddenly, the defensive tackle room has become crowded. After two big offseason additions paired with two premium draft picks in recent years, could Slaton be the odd man out? New experienced, vocal leaders are setting a tone for the Bengals defense “Adding high-level talent who have done it before, you’ve seen it on the tape and seen it in their careers,” coach Zac Taylor said. “You add to that the humans they are and the leaders they are. Not only did we add a lot of really talented players, they’re really good in the locker room and aren’t afraid to lead and help everyone else get to the next level.” There is a different feeling around the Bengals’ defense this offseason and with the players they brought in, it seems that championship experience was a big reason why. The Black Cloud Hanging Over Zac Taylor and the Bengals Entering 2026 Zac Taylor spoke candidly about the failures of the last three seasons and the impact it has had on him. Heading in to a season where he could be coaching for his job, it appears he is ready to attack 2026 with some tenacity. title: 7 takeaways from Cincinnati Bengals’ first depth chart of the 2026 season
summary: We made it. The Cincinnati Bengals play football this week vs. the Detroit Lions. It’s only Preseason Week 1, but the starters are playing, and we’ve gone so long without football that most of us would take anything we can get at this point. Since the Bengals play their first game against someone other than themselves this […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals linebacker Joe Giles-Harriswide (43) tackles wide receiver Mitch Tinsley (82) while running plays during training camp, Friday, Aug. 7, 2026, at Paycor Stadium in Downtown Cincinnati. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co We made it. The Cincinnati Bengals play football this week vs. the Detroit Lions. It’s only Preseason Week 1, but the starters are playing, and we’ve gone so long without football that most of us would take anything we can get at this point. Since the Bengals play their first game against someone other than themselves this week, the team has released their first iteration of the 2026 depth chart . There aren’t really any eye-popping surprises, but there are some interesting little tidbits of information that can be found by reading between the lines. Andrei Iosivas is WR3 and Colbie Young is WR6 This should be no surprise. Iosivas is a talented receiver, and of the guys on the roster outside of Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, he has done the most damage on the field in the regular season. Behind Chase is Mitch Tinsley, who broke into the league last season; behind Iosivas is Charlie Jones (who is also on top of the depth chart as a return specialist), and behind Higgins is Young. Cashius Howell moving on up Despite being a rookie who needs to earn his keep, second-round pick Cashius Howell has already taken the second-string DE spot behind Boye Mafe, overtaking Isaiah Foskey, someone who’s flashed some potential and that Al Golden is very familiar with from their Notre Dame days. Howell has reportedly been a “ monster ” in training camp and could be primed for a major role this year, perhaps as the first edge player off the bench. Drew Sample is TE1 The Bengals’ tight end situation is going to be very fluid. Who is on the field will depend on the situation the offense is in. Mike Gesicki is going to be the primary pass catcher from the position, but he’s more of a slot receiver than tight end. This shows that Sample is separated from the other tight ends on the roster, which includes Tanner Hudson, Erick All Jr., and Jack Endries. Samaje Perine cemented as RB2 Chase Brown is RB1. That’s no surprise, but Perine will get plenty of playing time. He’s alone as RB2 while Tahj Brooks and several others are together at RB3. Perine, who will be 31 in September, is still a major part of this offense. Depth on the defensive line The defensive line has gone from a weakness of the Bengals to (hopefully) a strength. They added Dexter Lawrence and Jonathan Allen, who are on top of the depth chart at defensive tackle. BJ Hill and TJ Slaton, last year’s starters, are backups on the depth chart. Josh Newton in the doghouse The Bengals didn’t do a lot of work at the cornerback position in the offseason outside of signing free agent Ja’Sir Taylor and drafting Tacario Davis in the draft. Josh Newton, who was a backup last year, has dropped far and is now a third-stringer. This tracks, based on what we’ve heard out of camp. Jalen Davis and DJ Ivey at nickel Davis starting in the slot should be no surprise. He’s been working in the slot for the Bengals since 2020, and was Mike Hilton’s backup. Ivey being the backup slot corner might be a surprise to some, though. He was a seventh-round pick in 2023 and may have found his spot on the roster. What were your initial thoughts when you saw the depth chart? Sound off! 2026 Cincinnati Bengals Depth Chart

title: Joe Burrow is excited to get Erick All Jr. back
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have largely cycled through tight ends in the Burrow era, finally keeping one for several years with Mike Gesicki after he signed an extension following a successful 2024 season in stripes. However, even with Gesicki playing well, the Bengals have missed having a do-it-all tight end who can go out and catch […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals have largely cycled through tight ends in the Burrow era, finally keeping one for several years with Mike Gesicki after he signed an extension following a successful 2024 season in stripes. However, even with Gesicki playing well, the Bengals have missed having a do-it-all tight end who can go out and catch the ball just as well as he can stay in and block. Based on recent quotes, it seems like Joe Burrow is also excited to get Erick All Jr. back out there on the field. “It’s great to have him back,” Burrow said following a recent practice. “Obviously, he had a lot going on with his knee, but you wouldn’t know it by looking at him. He looks fit, fast, explosive. He’ll play a big role for us this year.” As with the other tight ends on the Bengals roster, Hudson and Gesicki are essentially big receivers who rarely stay in to block, and Sample and Grandy are essentially extra linemen who largely stay in to block and rarely are primary targets on pass plays. A couple of years ago, the Bengals attempted to remedy this by drafting All in the fourth round out of Iowa. Early in the season, it seemed as if he was really transforming the offense, as it was much less predictable what the Bengals would do with him on the field. The new offensive dream died early on in 2024, though, as the reason Erick All fell in the draft struck again and he suffered an injury that not only knocked him out of the rest of 2024, but all of 2025 too. Now, All is back, and if healthy, he can change the Bengals offense into an entirely different beast. The Bengals didn’t put all their eggs in the All basket, however; they drafted Jack Endries in the 2026 NFL Draft, who, like All, may have the potential to play as both a blocker and receiver. The Bengals offense has been great under Burrow even without a do-it-all tight end, but having someone like that can only help the team, so hopefully All can stay healthy this year and going forward.

title: Browns QB decision might be about the future after all, just not in the way many thought
summary: The Cleveland Browns might be inching closer to a decision in their quarterback competition, despite both Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders struggling throughout OTAs and training camp. It got to the point that some started to wonder if Dillon Gabriel would enter the starter conversation. Saturday’s practice process, where HC Todd Monken said one thing […]
full_text: Cleveland Browns quarterbacks Shedeur Sanders and Deshaun Watson take part in a drill on the first day of minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus of the Cleveland Browns in Berea, Ohio on June 9, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cleveland Browns might be inching closer to a decision in their quarterback competition , despite both Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders struggling throughout OTAs and training camp . It got to the point that some started to wonder if Dillon Gabriel would enter the starter conversation . Saturday’s practice process, where HC Todd Monken said one thing before practice about Sanders taking first-team reps and then gave all of them to Watson , while our reporting is such that the change happened before Monken’s statements to us in the media . Many believed that the Browns future would lead Sanders to getting the job , but GM Andrew Berry and Monken both said that winning and production in 2026 would decide who was the starting quarterback. Throughout training camp, Monken has also made it clear that cadence and the presnap process are vital for the starting quarterback. Given that Berry and Monken (despite just being hired) could be on the hot seat if the 2026 season goes poorly, it makes sense that the decision-makers want to compete this season rather than focus solely on the future. If the future was the only variable, Sanders would have the starting position almost no matter what happened in training camp. It is, however, possible that the future is a part of why Watson seems to have taken control of the QB competition. Cleveland’s offense is full of young players: RB Quinshon Judkins TE Harold Fannin Jr. LT Spencer Fano WR KC Concepcion WR Denzel Boston WR Isaiah Bond Helping that core of players develop, along with being more competitive in 2026, could be the reason the veteran Watson, who has been better but not great at presnap activities, is the likely choice. For the Browns young guys to continue to develop, getting the process right is key. If the quarterback is unable to get the plays in, make the right audibles, slide the protections, and get the play off in time, that young group could learn bad habits, struggle to focus on their own details, and see their development set back. Should Sanders be the starting quarterback in Cleveland? In a vacuum, probably. He’s young, cheap, and has some upside. If Sanders was the only focus, starting him at QB would make sense. If Sanders’ struggles (Watson has his own after the snap) limit the growth of those six players listed above, the choice also becomes clear in the other direction. It seems like what Monken has prioritized as vital (presnap process) is not only leading to Watson’s role as the Browns starter but also could be a way to focus on the future with the other key positions on offense. While the quarterback position is important, Cleveland’s young core developing on offense is equally or more important in the 2026 season. Maybe Berry and Monken are focused on the now (winning) and not yet (developing for the future), which could soon lead to Watson being announced as the Browns starting quarterback in 2026. title: Revisiting Deshaun Watson’s contract insurance for Browns: Very different totals reported
summary: The Cleveland Browns are set to receive millions towards their salary cap due to the long history of injuries with quarterback Deshaun Watson; at least that was the report that we covered back in early July. The credits, reportedly, will be spread out over several seasons and will cease in 2029. The source of the […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - MAY 27: Deshaun Watson #4 of the Cleveland Browns walks off the field after the Cleveland Browns OTA Offseason Workouts at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on May 27, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Cleveland Browns are set to receive millions towards their salary cap due to the long history of injuries with quarterback Deshaun Watson; at least that was the report that we covered back in early July . The credits, reportedly, will be spread out over several seasons and will cease in 2029. The source of the salary cap credits is an offshoot of Watson’s restructured deal last year, which included an insurance policy. Now, with it seeming more and more likely that Watson could be named the starter over Shedeur Sanders , we look back on Florio’s original report and a couple of widely differing reports that have come out since we originally covered the information . Mike Florio of Pro Football Talk took Watson’s restructured deal from 2025 and spent some time with it. Florio has a law degree from West Virginia University, so things such as this are right up his alley. Florio then began to wonder himself. We aren’t sure if there is a specific answer, but it has to be significant, right? Cleveland had an insurance policy that potentially would pay millions if Watson had a torn Achilles tendon, and some time was lost. In this case, the entire year. So, Florio decided to do the legwork and find a number and construct the query. The item was placed on his honey-do list. Florio digs What was the bottom-line, definitive savings for the Browns, if any? The answer could be given in a cash number or perhaps in cap space. After all, Watson inked a five-year, fully guaranteed contract, and 2026 is his final year of the deal, although there are cap breakdowns all the way until 2030. Certainly, the insurance premiums the Browns took out on Watson were a hefty monthly payment. But it paid off. It began with the March 2023 restructured deal, which included an “Insurance Addendum.” This add-on allowed Cleveland to purchase almost $92 million covering the 2023 through 2025 NFL seasons for any injury to Watson. The amount of coverage then varied as the seasons fell off the calendar: Over $58 million for 2024 and 2025, and just over $33 million for 2025. The cap breakdowns show a return of his signing bonus for each year paid by the insurance policy. Watson had a shoulder injury in 2023 and a torn Achilles tendon in 2024, which he re-tore later, which spilled into the majority of 2025. The Browns had a 21-day window for his return, but the coaching staff declined to play him since the season was basically lost. In all, Watson missed 38 games over the three seasons, all under the insurance policy. The Deshaun Watson numbers via Florio Credits by year after the restructured 2023 agreement: 2023: $8.79 million Here are the credits by year after the restructured 2024 contract: 2024: $8.79 million 2025: $8.79 million 2026: $8.791 million 2027: $8.755 million 2028: $8.755 million The 2025 restructured deal, adds other credits: 2025: $7.983 million 2026: $7.992 million 2027: $8.018 million 2028: $7.983 million 2029: $7.983 million Watson also restructured his contract again in March of 2026. That adds one more credit: 2026: $4.951 million Wow, that is a lot of money. Right? Not so fast. Jason from Over the Cap quickly pushed back on Florio’s reporting: You are not interpreting the numbers correctly. The numbers are what remains of the cap value from the original bonuses. The $8.79M reflects revaluing the bonus after the refund is received, its not the refund itself. Teams also receive credits in their adjustments for prior… — Jason_OTC (@Jason_OTC) July 6, 2026 Then, Jack Duffin of The OBR, our most trusted source for Browns salary cap information, followed that up with his own numbers, which ended up being far less than what Florio reported but he noted he didn’t have the full information, as an insurance policy is not a part of records available through the NFLPA: If you did 62% of insurance split ( DBN note: Duffin did a great job reverse engineering other cap credits the Browns got to come to this number ) across 17 games, then earned after 6 consecutive games missed. It is closer but the second is roughly double this amount: 2023 – $1,013,990 2024 – $2,534,974 2025 – $17,762,087 From Florio’s number of almost $90 million, it seems more likely that the team will receive around 60% of that amount ($54 million) as salary cap relief over the next few seasons, despite the entire amount being returned to owner Jimmy Haslam via the insurance policy. Still a lot of money added to the salary cap but spread out over six seasons, starting a couple of years ago, it isn’t the boon we originally covered if Duffin and OTC are correct. Until we get to those future seasons and reporting is out, we will still be left with the uncertainty.
author: Jared Mueller

(Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images For a while now, NFL teams have internally debated the topic of playing time in preseason games, while fans have been doing it externally. Who should play and how much? Injury is always the big concern when this topic comes up. Some teams have decided not to play any of their stars, opting on the side of caution. Other teams have coaches that like to get their players some playing time just to get a feel for things again. Usually rookies get some playing time since they have never participated in NFL football before, and it would be good if they knew what they were going against by the time Week 1 rolled around. But what about a rookie who people think is going to be a star? This isn’t like sitting Dak Prescott or CeeDee Lamb etc. Should the Cowboys play Caleb Downs in the first preseason game? title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 34
summary: It is Day 34 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: Hall of Fame quarterback Troy Aikman of the Dallas Cowboys sets up to pass during the Cowboys 34-10 victory over the Philadelphia Eagles in the 1992 NFC Divisional Playoff Game on January 10, 1993 at Texas Stadium in Irving, Texas. (Photo by Joseph Patronite/Getty Images) It is Day 34 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Welcome in for Day 34 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit the afternoon the young 1992 Cowboys proved their regular-season rise would translate to January. Dallas had won a franchise-record 13 regular-season games, but Philadelphia arrived with a veteran defense, an explosive quarterback and no interest in treating the Cowboys like an established contender. Sunday, January 10, 1993 — 12:30 p.m. ET Texas Stadium, Irving, Texas Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 34, Philadelphia Eagles 10 Dallas had completed a 13-3 regular season, won the NFC East and earned the conference’s second seed behind the 14-2 San Francisco 49ers. Philadelphia entered as an 11-5 wild-card team and arrived with confidence after scoring 26 fourth-quarter points in a 36-20 comeback victory over New Orleans. The Eagles were experienced, dangerous and built around a defense that had caused Dallas considerable problems during the Cowboys’ rise. The rivalry had become one of the league’s most bitter. Philadelphia had embarrassed Dallas 31-7 on Monday Night Football in October, handing the Cowboys their first loss after a 3-0 start. Dallas responded with a 20-10 win at Texas Stadium four weeks later, but the playoff meeting offered the only result that would settle which team had truly gained control of the division. For Troy Aikman and the Cowboys’ emerging core, this was also an opportunity to prove they were no longer the inexperienced team that could be overwhelmed by Philadelphia’s aggression. The Eagles controlled the opening possession and took a 3-0 lead on a Roger Ruzek field goal, but Dallas responded immediately. Kelvin Martin’s 39-yard kickoff return gave the Cowboys excellent field position, and Aikman completed the drive with a one-yard touchdown pass to Derek Tennell. Tennell had joined the team only days earlier, yet his touchdown gave Dallas a 7-3 advantage and the early lead. The game remained tight until the final minute of the first half. Aikman connected with Alvin Harper for 41 yards before finding Jay Novacek for a six-yard touchdown. On the following kickoff, rookie safety Darren Woodson forced Vai Sikahema to fumble, allowing Lin Elliott to add a field goal as time expired. Dallas scored 10 points in the final 47 seconds and entered halftime leading 17-3. The Cowboys put the game away after the break. Emmitt Smith finished a strong opening drive with a 23-yard touchdown run, and Elliott later added a 43-yard field goal. Dallas controlled the third quarter from start to finish, outgaining Philadelphia 176 yards to minus-16 yards and extending its lead to 27-3. Dallas’ defense made life miserable for Randall Cunningham. Russell Maryland and Tony Tolbert recorded two sacks apiece, while Jim Jeffcoat added another. Philadelphia managed only 178 total yards and converted just one of its 12 third-down attempts. The Eagles could not run the ball consistently, protect Cunningham or keep their defense off the field. Dallas finished with 346 total yards, 22 first downs and more than 35 minutes of possession. The Cowboys converted seven of 12 third downs and scored 34 unanswered points after Philadelphia’s opening field goal. Against a defense that had embarrassed them three months earlier, Dallas looked stronger, deeper and far more composed. This game belongs on the countdown because it marked the moment Dallas stopped looking like an emerging contender and began looking like the best team in football. The Cowboys absorbed Philadelphia’s early pressure, dominated the line of scrimmage and turned a bitter rivalry game into a 24-point playoff victory. #Cowboys vs #Eagles 1993 Divisional Round Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 34, Philadelphia Eagles 10 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/vOhNfgzbU9 — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) August 10, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game Tennell’s one-yard reception was the only touchdown catch of his NFL career. He had joined Dallas as a free agent only days before the game and had previously been Aikman’s teammate at UCLA. title: How new players are doing at Cowboys training camp
summary: Where do things stand with the Dallas Cowboys new additions this year? Now that we’re at the halfway point of training camp and with the first preseason game about to get underway against the Seattle Seahawks, we thought this would be a great time to share which new players are currently shining and others who […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 3: Cobie Durant #2 of the Dallas Cowboys walks onto the field during training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields on August 3, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Where do things stand with the Dallas Cowboys new additions this year? Now that we’re at the halfway point of training camp and with the first preseason game about to get underway against the Seattle Seahawks, we thought this would be a great time to share which new players are currently shining and others who still have something to prove. So far, early returns are better than expected. Veteran additions The jury is still out on safeties Jalen Thompson (hip) and P.J. Locke (knee) after missing time with injuries, but thankfully both are currently working their way back into the lineup. Both are expected to be key contributors on the back end of Dallas’ secondary and should start proving themselves now that they’re healthy. Outside of them, the Cowboys vet additions have mostly performed better than expected, some even shining. DT Otito Ogbonnia Ogbonnia has been one of the more impressive free agent additions for the Cowboys. If he’s not blowing up plays, he’s batting down passes at the line of scrimmage. He’s an underrated signing that could pay huge dividends this year as an upgrade along the interior of Dallas’ defensive line. QB Sam Howell Howell has had his moments throughout training camp, but hasn’t proven to be a clear upgrade over last year’s backup, Joe Milton. Both are competing to be the QB2 this season, but right now it’s Milton running with the second team. That could change for Howell with a strong showing in preseason. CB Cobie Durant An argument could be made Durant has been the defensive star of training camp for the Cowboys. He’s been an absolute menace in coverage and if he isn’t breaking up passes, he’s coming away with the INT. He’s probably Dallas’ best outside addition and a steal on a one-year, $4 million contract. CB Derion Kendrick Kendrick has yet to break out form the crowd at training camp. He’s been playing primarily out of the slot, but has shown he can play outside as well. That kind of position flex could end up earning him a roster spot. He’s definitely someone to keep an eye on from here on out. OLB Rashan Gary (trade) Gary is quietly having impressive training camp. Not only has he been praised for his leadership ability, getting named to the Cowboys Leadership Council, but he’s been showing up in practice as well, especially as run defender. Playing inside and out, he’s an upgrade for Dallas’ DL. LB Dee Winters (trade) Winters may not be receiving the same kind of attention as DeMarvion Overshown or Jaishawn Barham, but he’s been showing up in practices both the run defender and in pass coverage. He’s currently the Cowboys most experienced LB and could wear the green dot at times this year. Rookie additions Early returns on the Dallas Cowboys rookie additions have been better than expected. Nearly half of them have have flashed from time to time. Consistency will be key for all of them, but so far it looks as if several of them could play key roles this year, even starting roles. DB Caleb Downs Downs is the real deal and has been better than advertised, and that’s saying something. No matter how much the Cowboys throw at him, he’s absorbed and performed above expectations. He might already be their best defensive player and could be the best rookie in the league this year. OLB Malachi Lawrence Lawrence has been praised for the steady progress he’s made throughout training camp by the Cowboys coaching staff. He splashed his first-round talent from time to time in practice, but is still considered a work in progress making the jump from a small school to the NFL. LB Jaishawn Barham Barham is unfortunately dealing with a groin injury that isn’t considered to be serious, but prior to that was blowing things up in practice. Whether it was in run defense or in pass coverage he’s exceeding everyone’s expectations, so much so he’s pushing for a starting job. CB Devin Moore Moore is currently dealing with a groin injury, but prior to that had a solid training camp for a rookie. He looks like a future project for the team with potential. Playing in some preseason games would be ideal to judge his game day composure. DT LT Overton Overton’s name wasn’t hardly mentioned early on in training camp, but he’s been coming on as of late as someone to keep an eye on. If he can continue to string some good practices together and show up in preseason, he could earn a role for himself this year. WR Anthony Smith While he’s having a pretty quiet training camp, Smith’s deep threat ability and special teams value makes him someone to keep an eye on in preseason. He’s currently in contention for Dallas’ fifth and probably final WR roster spot, along with several others. TE Michael Trigg Even though he joined the Cowboys as an undrafted free agent, Trigg has been one of their most impressive rookies so far. With Jake Ferguson and Brevyn Spann-Ford roster spots secured, he could push Luke Schoonmaker off the roster and win the TE3 job. Camden Brown Brown is another undrafted player having a strong showing so far in training camp with the Cowboys, even working with the second-team offense recently. He’s made several impressive athletic TD catches, putting himself in the WR mix for a roster spot.
author: Brian Martin

title: The most obvious Cowboys trade candidate
summary: The Dallas Cowboys will take the field on Saturday against the Seattle Seahawks. With a condensed preseason schedule of only three games, there isn’t much playing time for players at the bottom of the roster to get meaningful snaps in live action. With the intent to trim the roster from 90 to 53 players, the […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 4: Luke Schoonmaker #86 of the Dallas Cowboys in an offensive stance during training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields on August 4, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys will take the field on Saturday against the Seattle Seahawks. With a condensed preseason schedule of only three games, there isn’t much playing time for players at the bottom of the roster to get meaningful snaps in live action. With the intent to trim the roster from 90 to 53 players, the Cowboys will have to place a substantial amount of talent on waivers and risk losing them for nothing. It’s not to say the Cowboys have a surplus of premier options on the 90-man roster, but essentially if they have to part with the talent they have, a trade for a player or more plausibly, future assets aren’t a crazy idea. Before anyone tries to reignite the embers on trading George Pickens, nope. It’s not going to happen. The Cowboys look like they are trying to field a team capable of contending for a deep playoff run, and trading Pickens for a team ready to win now is counterintuitive. The team looks content to worry about his contract when the time comes, and so does Pickens, it would seem. So who else? What other player is the most reasonable option for Dallas to trade? Luke Schoonmaker When looking at the Cowboys roster as a whole, its glaring how obvious of a trade candidate Luke Schoonmaker becomes. Schoonmaker was taken way too high for the team’s ambitions, and even at the time, fans knew spending a second-round pick on a tight end where Dak Prescott could get the most out of nearly any tight end wasn’t a good idea. Schoonmaker hasn’t provided the team enough return on investment and should be on the outs with the team. In the time since Schoonmaker was drafted, Jake Ferguson has stepped up and taken control of the #1 tight end spot and earned a sizable payday, ensuring there’s no chance Schoonmaker surpasses him. Brevyn Spann-Ford has entered the picture. He is much better at blocking and has started to flash some upside as a pass catcher. With Schoonmaker and Spann-Ford both in contract years, Spann-Ford seems the most reasonable to extend. Brevyn Spann-Ford sold the hell out of this route for the TD. #Cowboys pic.twitter.com/8TE4AI7sn6 — Patrik [No C] Walker (@VoiceOfTheStar) August 8, 2026 It doesn’t stop there either. Undrafted tight end Michael Trigg has been making plays at training camp, and it’s hard not to notice his skills as a pass catcher. With his athleticism, he’s sure to catch the eye of 31 other teams during the preseason, especially with the Cowboys playing in an isolated window on Saturday night. The season-ending injury to Princeton Fant didn’t provide Schoonmaker with breathing room for long, as Dallas added Zack Kuntz off waivers shortly after Fant’s injury. Envision how the Cowboys see the position: Ferguson as the tight end one of the group, Brevyn Spann-Ford as the number two option, Trigg as the athletic project. Don’t be surprised to see the Cowboys move Schoonmaker for a day-three pick. Michael Trigg sliding grab to end practice pic.twitter.com/TZSxj0PXZU — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) August 6, 2026 Sure, there’s other names some could consider, but none make as much sense as Schoonmaker. The Cowboys appear to have a deep room at cornerback, but questions still surround DaRon Bland’s health, Shavon Revel’s confidence, and where Caleb Downs will spend most of his time. The secondary isn’t top heavy for the Cowboys and the team shouldn’t be as willing to part with their secondary or tertiary options on the depth chart. You can also make the same argument for inside linebacker as well. With that said, who are some players you think the team should trade?
author: LP Cruz

title: Dallas Cowboys 2026 Opponent Preview: Los Angeles Rams
summary: One of the next big offseason boxes to check for the Dallas Cowboys as they continue 2026 training camp in Oxnard, California is their upcoming joint practice with a fellow NFC, the Los Angeles Rams. This practice will happen on Tuesday the 11th. The Cowboys will also see the Rams this regular season, in Week […]
full_text: SEATTLE, CA - JANUARY 25: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) smiles while walking to the sidelines during the second quarter of the NFC championship game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026 in Seattle, CA. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) One of the next big offseason boxes to check for the Dallas Cowboys as they continue 2026 training camp in Oxnard, California is their upcoming joint practice with a fellow NFC, the Los Angeles Rams. This practice will happen on Tuesday the 11th. The Cowboys will also see the Rams this regular season, in Week 15 off their week 14 bye. This stretch has been circled by many Cowboys fans as the time where we may learn what this 2026 team is truly all about. If the Cowboys go into Thanksgiving still in contention for the division and playoffs at large, they’ll host the Eagles on Turkey Day followed by a Monday Night Football tilt at the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks, the bye, then the Rams. Certainly the Cowboys football-related part of the offseason has quickly come with a lot of hype for what’s going on at the training fields in Oxnard, but for the totality of the offseason, the hype machine award is a runaway win for the Rams. Sean McVay’s team has progressed inch by inch in the playoffs since 2023, losing in the Wild Card round in 2023, the Divisional round in 2024, and NFC Championship game last year. In their last two seasons, these playoff exits were to the teams that went on to win the Super Bowl, and in blowout fashion compared to the games the Rams gave both the Eagles and Seahawks on the road. Perhaps having the Lombardi trophy reside within their division after losing an epic 31-27 championship game at their rivals was the motivation for the Rams to do their signature Rams thing to get closer to another championship of their own, as they’ve used all avenues of player acquisition to become the absolute trendiest pick to win it all right now. Since we’ve only been covering mostly free agent moves, draft classes, and coaching changes in these previews, we’ll start here by going over the trades the Rams have made as a huge part of their roster build as well. The most notable player the Rams traded for is grabbing Myles Garrett away from the Browns in exchange for their own pass rush star Jared Verse, and giving up a first-, second-, and third-round pick in the next three drafts to Cleveland. The Garrett trade has also stirred up the potential for a reunion with Aaron Donald, who worked out at the team’s practice last Wednesday. Talk about a defensive line that can close out games for a team with a high-powered offense, and the Rams are assembling just that. The other Rams trade came back in March, getting cornerback Trent McDuffie from the Kansas City Chiefs. Rams Key Free Agent Signings/Departures * SIGNED IN FREE AGENCY CB Jaylen Watson LB Grant Stuard TE Tyler Higbee (Re-signed) Kam Curl (Re-signed) OL Justin Dedich (Re-signed) OL David Quessenberry (Re-signed) * DEPARTED IN FREE AGENCY WR Tutu Atwell CB Cobie Durant (DAL) CB Ahkello Witherspoon CB Roger McCreary The McDuffie trade for the Rams was just the start of a ton of reshuffling in the secondary for defensive coordinator Chris Shula. The Rams allowed 53 pass plays of at least 20 yards last season. Only the Bears allowed more and also made the playoffs along with the Rams, and the next closest playoff team was the Texans with 47. Adding Jaylen Watson (another former Chief) and McDuffie immediately gives the Rams a chance to get their cohesion back. Any cornerbacks that sustained a run of playing meaningful snaps in Steve Spagnuolo’s Kansas City defense have to bring experience, scheme flexibility, and the ability to hold up in man coverage, and that’s exactly what the Rams have now. This should bode them well specifically in their NFC West matchups against the Seahawks, 49ers, and Cardinals. Bringing back Kam Curl was also a positive move in the right direction for the Rams secondary at safety, where he’ll continue lining up next to Kam Kinchens. The Rams have plus speed at linebacker with Nate Landman and Byron Young, plus arguably the best finisher at defensive end in Garrett, making this a defense with a clear objective to get teams behind the sticks and fly around at all three levels. On offense, its the Rams that are the grandfathers of the heavy 13 personnel usage that other teams are now frantically trying to catch up to. Bringing back Tyler Higbee in free agency keeps the Rams depth at TE strong with Higbee, Colby Parkinson, Terrance Ferguson, and draft pick Max Klare – which brings us to the rest of the Rams draft class. Rams 2026 Draft Class Round 1, Pick 13: QB Ty Simpson Round 2, Pick 29 (61 Overall): TE Max Klare Round 3, Pick 29 (93 Overall): OT Keagen Trost Round 6, Pick 16 (197 Overall): WR CJ Daniels Round 7, Pick 16 (232 Overall): DT Tim Keenan III The Myles Garrett trade was the most recent catalyst to put the Rams firmly in Super Bowl contending status, so much so that it’s collectively made fans forget the puzzlement around their first-round pick. In a division that sent three teams to the playoffs, the Rams opted for a player that will help them down the road at quarterback, but no immediate help for either their starting QB Matthew Stafford or the defense. Tight end Max Klare is help for Stafford beyond the first round in the draft, as was WR CJ Daniels from Miami. Add in four of the five projected starters on the offensive line having starting experience from 2025 or before with this team, a RB tandem of Kyren Williams and Blake Corum, and a top three at WR of Davante Adams, Puka Nacua, and Jordan Whittington, and the justification isn’t hard to find for the Rams punting on immediate help with a first-round pick. What a move like that also does is raise the expectations for the Rams coaching staff to get the absolute most out of all the depth they have to work with, which brings us to our look at the new faces on LA’s sideline. Rams 2026 Coaching Staff * New to staff this season: Assistant Head Coach Kliff Kingsbury Special Teams Coordinator Bubba Ventrone Adding Kliff Kingsbury to a coaching staff led by Sean McVay feels borderline unfair, but that is the world the Rams are living in going into 2026. Cowboys fans can be happy Kingsbury isn’t paired up with their own former DC in Dan Quinn in the NFC East with the Commanders anymore, but still can’t avoid Kingsbury for at least one game in 2026. For this move to make the Rams offense even more diabolical, they’ll need a solid foundation up front to make sure Stafford is protected. Ryan Wendell will go into his fourth straight season as the team’s offensive line coach to provide this foundation, and Scott Huff is back for a second season as tight ends coach after coaching offensive line for the Seahawks previously. Ron Gould is also a returning experienced coach at running backs working with a veteran group out of the backfield. Pair this with the Rams defensive run game coordinator and DL coach Giff Smith being in that position since 2024, and the difference the Rams can make right at the point of attack on both sides of the ball could be their biggest strength all season. Even new special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone comes with assistant head coaching experience at this past stop with the Browns. This Rams team is built to win now through what they did on the trade market, in free agency, in a lesser sense the draft, and to tie it all together, Sean McVay’s impressive coaching staff. The Cowboys have won their last two regular season meetings against the Rams, on the road in 2022 and at home in 2023, but will face a very tough challenge looking to extend this streak to three games in 2026. In the short term, it will be very telling to see at the joint practice how Brian Schottenheimer calls plays against this retooled Rams defense, and likely more importantly, how Christian Parker and the defense…

title: Cowboys 53-man roster prediction through halfway point of training camp
summary: It’s difficult to believe the Dallas Cowboys have already hit the halfway point of training camp. A lot has happened since arriving in Oxnard, which has given us some clarity about the makeup of this year’s team. While there are few things that still need to be ironed out between now and the start of […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 4: Brian Schottenheimer of the Dallas Cowboys on the field during training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields on August 4, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s difficult to believe the Dallas Cowboys have already hit the halfway point of training camp. A lot has happened since arriving in Oxnard, which has given us some clarity about the makeup of this year’s team. While there are few things that still need to be ironed out between now and the start of the season, the roster is starting to take shape, so much so, we thought we’d attempt to predict Dallas’ final 53-and roster. Quarterback (2) Dak Prescott, Joe Milton Joe Milton and Sam Howell are still probably in a head-to-head battle to secure the QB2 spot with the Cowboys this year, but Milton seems to have a slight edge right now. He’s shown noticeable improvement on his touch passes and has the most upside of the two QBs. There’s a chance both could still make the roster, but Milton’s encouraging development would allow them to use that extra roster spot elsewhere. Running back (4) Javonte Williams, Jaydon Blue, Phil Mafah, Hunter Luepke The depth of behind Williams was once a concern prior to entering training camp, but no longer so. The RB position group is much deeper than expected and has been one of the bigger surprises for the Cowboys. Both second-year RBs Blue and Mafah have been impressive enough to probably secure a roster spot, but they aren’t going unchallenged. Israel Abanikanda has been impressive a well and we all know they love Malik Davis. Wide receiver (5) CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Ryan Flournoy, KaVontae Turpin, Anthony Smith With Lamb, Pickens, and Flournoy locked in his Dallas’ top three receivers and Turpin has the return specialist/gadget player, the fifth and final WR spot is currently up for grabs. We gave rookie Anthony Smith the nod here due to his ability to stretch the field as well as a special teams value. But, it’s one spot at this position that could change. Tight end (3) Jake Ferguson, Brevyn Spann-Ford, Michael Trigg Ferguson and Spann-Ford are the only TE roster locks for the Cowboys right now. Luke Schoonmaker could be pushed off the roster if Michael Trigg continues to shine throughout the rest of training camp and preseason. We predict that’s exactly what’s going to happen, making Schoonmaker a potential trade candidate. Offensive line (9) Tyler Guyton, Tyler Smith, Cooper Beebe, Tyler Booker, Terence Steele, TJ Bass, Nate Thomas, Drew Shelton, Ajani Cornelius Guyton, Smith, Beebee, Booker, and Steele are locked in to be Dallas’ starting five offensive line with Thomas and Bass serving as the primary backups. Shelton sticks around as a developmental prospect and Cornelius has a position flex to play G or OT. The one concern with this group is Beebe’s backup. Bass could be the solution, but Dallas could go a little deeper here with a more proven veteran. Defensive tackle (5) Quinnen Williams, Kenny Clark, Otito Ogbonnia, Jonathan Bullard, LT Overton Williams and Clark have been as advertised, giving Dallas a disruptive duo on the interior of their defensive line. Ogbonnia has been a pleasant surprise and has gained everyone’s attention as one of the standouts at training camp. Bullard and Overton round out the group for now, but their roster spots are less secured. Either can be replaced by an outside addition after roster cuts are made. Outside linebacker/Edge (6) Rashan Gary, Donovan Ezeiruaku, Malachi Lawrence, James Houston, Sam Williams, Marist Liufau If the Cowboys make the “substantive” trade Jerry Jones has hinted at, it will likely be at OLB. For now, we have Gary, Ezeiruaku, Lawrence, Houston, and Williams as roster locks with Liufau sticking around due to his special teams value and position flex to play both OLB and off-ball LB. Dallas seems to be highly motivated to upgrade the position further, that could change things substantially. Inside linebacker (5) DeMarvion Overshown, Dee Winters, Jaishawn Barham, Curtis Robinson, Shemar James Barham has been the talk of training camp and has been working with the starters along with Overshown and Winters. Robinson and James round out the group as solid backups and key special teams players. Keep an eye on Justin Barron though. He’s had a strong camp and could push a roster spot. An outside vet addition could be in play as well due to Overshown’s injury concerns and the lack of overall experience of the group. Cornerback (6) DaRon Bland, Cobie Durant, Shavon Revel, Caelen Carson, Devin Moore, Reddy Stewart Despite the initial concerns, CB has actually been one of the better position groups throughout training camp, so much so, tough decisions will need to be made here. Bland, Durant, and Revel, are roster locks right now with Carson and Moore close in the running. And due to past injury concerns at the position, we believe Dallas could go a little deeper here with Steward, who has been playing both CB and safety, getting the last spot. Safety (5) Caleb Downs , Malik Hooker, Jalen Thompson, P.J. Locke, Markquese Bell Downs, Hooker, Thompson, and Locke should be considered roster locks, but the last spot is less secure. Bell currently seems to have the edge on his competitors, however, Alijah Clark and Julius Wood are both playing well and could unseat him. Special teams (3) Brandon Aubrey, Bryan Anger, Trent Sieg Nothing to see here. There is no doubt these three are roster locks.

title: What to make of the progress of Shavon Revel Jr. so far
summary: The Dallas Cowboys entered training camp with plenty of defensive question marks, but none are quite as riveting as what’s going on at the cornerback position. With uncertainty across the depth chart, everyone is trying to guess how this group shakes out. DaRon Bland is out to prove his foot issues are firmly behind him, […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys entered training camp with plenty of defensive question marks, but none are quite as riveting as what’s going on at the cornerback position. With uncertainty across the depth chart, everyone is trying to guess how this group shakes out. DaRon Bland is out to prove his foot issues are firmly behind him, Cobie Durant wants to validate his free agent investment, and Shavon Revel Jr. is looking to take a huge leap in his second year. While veterans like Bland and Durant have looked sharp, the reviews on Revel have been a bit of a mixed bag. It is still early in the process, but his camp performance is starting to paint a picture of exactly what kind of player the team has for the upcoming season. The most encouraging piece of news is that his knee looks fantastic. It is a night-and-day difference from last year when he was seen wearing a massive knee brace that made his movements look incredibly stiff. Early last month, video clips surfaced of him moving with impressive fluidity . Now, getting overly excited about a football player running around on grass is usually not recommended, but for someone recovering from a knee injury, seeing him plant and cut without hesitation was a beautiful sight. All signs point to him finally being fully healthy. When the pads finally came on, the coaching staff immediately threw everything at him. He lined up repeatedly against the team’s star receivers, which is a brutal assignment for anyone. Both CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens gave him plenty of problems, but to his credit, he refused to give them breathing room. Last Monday turned into a true breakthrough day for him . Even when the star wideouts managed to haul in passes, he made them work for every bit of it. While that sticky coverage is exactly what you want to see, his hand placement still needs a lot of work. He constantly uses his hands to gauge space and far too often becomes too grabby with the jerseys. When he gets beat off the line of scrimmage, he panics, doesn’t trust his makeup speed, and starts tugging. He has already accumulated a heavy dose of flags in camp, and quite honestly, that penalty count could be even higher since several of his pass breakups have left receivers frustrated, frantically gesturing to the refs. On the bright side, his reaction time and closing burst in off coverage look great. He is making smart decisions and arriving at the target right when the ball gets there, which has led to some impressive pass breakups. He is doing a fine job of using his frame to get his inside hand around on slant routes to disrupt plays. Unfortunately, he still cannot resist using that trailing hand to hook the receiver around the waist. He has had quite a few close calls that possess serious yellow laundry potential. In his defense, many corners fall victim to interference calls when trying to survive against someone like Pickens. Another positive piece of news is that his confidence is riding high. He has complete trust in his body now, and his explosive movement proves it. He possesses all the necessary raw physical traits, so the current challenge is simply teaching him how to use them without making costly mistakes. With new defensive coordinator Christian Parker in his corner, a man known for polishing raw potential into All-Pro talent, his developmental odds look favorable. If the staff can clean up the technical flaws, he has a real chance to become a lockdown defender in this league. But for the immediate future, everyone needs to brace themselves for some predictable growing pains. With Bland and Durant looking more refined at the moment, it could mean that the second-year corner takes a back seat in the primary rotation early on. Of course, given how injuries inevitably rear their ugly heads during the season, he will get plenty of opportunities to prove himself. It might just be a bumpy ride initially, giving fans some major Anthony Brown flashbacks where you will likely see him jump a route for a big play on one series, only to surrender a deep shot or draw a costly penalty on the very next drive. The good news is that the upside is absolutely there to overshadow the deficiencies, making it a matter of when, not if, he puts it all together. In the grand scheme of the defense, the depth of the Cowboys’ cornerback room should allow him to continue to develop. If he can learn to trust his feet instead of his grip, he can take a positive step forward. The talent is there. And now that the knee is finally healthy, the trajectory is pointing straight up.
author: Dan Rogers

title: Cowboys news: Quinnen Williams’ rep at training camp sparks extension speculation
summary: Dallas has historically been slow to extend their top talent, with George Pickens being the most recent example. However, with Quinnen Williams’ representative showing up to Dallas’ training camp, it opens the door to the possibility of the Cowboys extending him earlier than expected. Also, undrafted free-agent signing Michael Trigg has the production to suggest […]
full_text: Dallas has historically been slow to extend their top talent, with George Pickens being the most recent example. However, with Quinnen Williams’ representative showing up to Dallas’ training camp, it opens the door to the possibility of the Cowboys extending him earlier than expected. Also, undrafted free-agent signing Michael Trigg has the production to suggest he could make the final 53-man roster. Plus, Pickens continues to impress at camp, and Dallas catches a stray shot during Brees’ Hall of Fame induction. Super agent Lynn, Quinnen Williams’ rep, visits Cowboys’ contract guy – Angel Torres, Cowboys Wire If the Cowboys want to get it done, they would be better served getting it done early. This is still speculative, but it is a good sign of progress towards retaining Quinnen Williams. While its not uncommon for agents to check in on their clients, Ft. Worth Star Telegram’s Nick Harris points out how notable it was to see Lynn spend the majority of her time at the session speaking with Adam Prasifka, Cowboys senior director of salary cap and contracts. While no official details have emerged, the timing is significant. Cowboys COO Stephen Jones told the media during the team’s introductory press conference that Williams was at the top of their list in regards to an extension. Cowboys Should Make Room for Michael Trigg in 26′ – Cody Warren, Inside The Star Trigg could be the undrafted player breakout of 2026. There is competition at the position among players, but don’t write off Trigg just yet. Trigg finished his career with 108 catches for 1,419 yards and 14 touchdowns. In his final season as a Baylor Bear, he showed why he was one of the best tight ends in the country when he had 50 receptions for 694 yards and six touchdowns . Those are good numbers for a tight end and the yards put him in the top 3 for tight ends in 2025. When those numbers are compared to the college stats of an underachieving tight end on the Dallas Cowboys roster, it should be a no-brainer who the team keeps. George Pickens is far and away Cowboys’ biggest offensive star in camp – Jess Haynie, The Landry Hat The success of George Pickens’ camp isn’t the surprising part; it’s the fact that he is still impressing despite Dallas’ reluctance to sign him long-term. Players respond to contract adversity in different ways, sometimes based on personality and sometimes due to circumstances. Dallas certainly had a different experience last year with Micah Parsons, who had no issue making a spectacle of the contract talks or “holding in” during camp. But given his illustrious four-year run with the Cowboys up to that point, Parsons had a more legitimate beef with the front office. Whereas Dallas arguably saved Pickens’ career from how things went in Pittsburgh, Parsons had carried the defense practically since his rookie year. Hall of Fame QB Drew Brees Shades Cowboys During Enshrinement Speech – Randy Gurzi, Sports Illustrated The Cowboys continue catching strays, even from players in other divisions. Granted, as far as strays go, this one was tame. Brees was sharing his appreciation for his former head coach Sean Payton and shaded the Cowboys in doing so. Brees said Payton wanted to soak in the celebration after beating Dallas, where Payton spent three seasons as an assistant coach. “I miss the three-hour flights home from Dallas to New Orleans after a big win, by the way, that’s supposed to be an hour flight. But Sean would have the pilot circle ten times so we could soak up the celebration,” Brees says. Spagnola: Connecting the Cowboys to Drew Brees’ career – Staff, DallasCowboys.com Hall of Fame weekend passes again, and Dallas does not have an inductee of their own. However, they can at least claim a piece of Drew Brees. First, former Cowboys Super Bowl winning offensive coordinator Norv Turner was the San Diego head coach in 2001 when the Chargers plucked Brees out of Purdue with the first pick in the second round of the NFL Draft. The next season and for three more after that with the Chargers, his head coach became Marty Schottenheimer, the father of Cowboys current head coach Brian Schottenheimer. And for those four seasons, young Brian Schottenheimer became his quarterbacks coach with the Chargers. Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 35 – Mike Poland, Blogging The Boys The season inches closer. So let’s revisit an iconic 1994 matchup between the Cowboys and a team they have been pestered by for years now. The matchup showcased two franchises at different stages of their development. Dallas, already the league’s dominant young team, sought to defend its title with Troy Aikman, Emmitt Smith, and Michael Irvin. Meanwhile, Green Bay, under the guidance of Mike Holmgren and Brett Favre, was beginning its return to relevance. Despite a Wild Card round victory over Detroit, securing their first postseason win in 11 years, the Packers faced a much steeper test at Texas Stadium. Daily discussion question: How much do you trust Shavon Revel Jr. right now?
