title: Giants’ defense doesn’t get much love in PFF player rankings
summary: The New York Giants’ defense enters 2026 with optimism, but with a lot to prove. Pro Football Focus illustrated how much in a recent look at the best 32 players at each position on defense. Only three Giants, defensive tackle D.J. Reader and edge defenders Abdul Carter and Brian Burns, were listed among the top […]
full_text: D.J. Reader | Getty Images The New York Giants’ defense enters 2026 with optimism, but with a lot to prove. Pro Football Focus illustrated how much in a recent look at the best 32 players at each position on defense. Only three Giants, defensive tackle D.J. Reader and edge defenders Abdul Carter and Brian Burns, were listed among the top 32 players at their respective positions. Reader was No. 26 among interior defensive linemen. PFF said : Reader’s play in Detroit didn’t reach the heights of what we saw from him with the Houston Texans and Cincinnati Bengals, but he was still solid. In his 10-year career, he has never had a season with a PFF pass-rush or run-defense grade lower than 60.0. He should be a solid player for a Giants team that traded away Dexter Lawrence. Lawrence was ranked No. 4, and Leonard Williams No. 5. On the edge, Carter was No. 16 and Burns No. 20 . That is interesting, considering 2025 production. Of Carter, PFF said: Relatively low sack production caused a strong rookie season from Carter to fly a little bit under the radar. His 84.5 PFF pass-rush grade was the 10th-best among edge defenders, while his 18 quarterback hits were tied for fifth-most at the position. Given what we know about pressure rate and sack rate, if he even just performs as he did as a rookie in 2026, that sack production will likely increase, and that’s not factoring in a probable step forward in his second year. Of Burns, PFF said: Burns set a career high with 29 combined sacks and hits last season, and has earned a PFF pass-rush grade above 70.0 in all seven of his years in the NFL. He hasn’t been able to consistently produce at an elite level as a pass-rusher, but has still been good enough to form a formidable duo with Carter heading into the 2026 campaign. At off-ball linebacker, Tremaine Edmunds. signed to a three-year, $36 million contract by the Giants this offseason, was left out of the top 32. A year from now, I would guess the top 32 list will include Arvell Reese. At cornerback, Paulson Adebo, who may now be facing competition to keep his starting job, was not among the top 32 players . At safety, Jevon Holland was bypassed . Giants fans won’t be thrilled that Xavier McKinney was No. 3 and Julian Love No. 17. Both of those players have been better after leaving the Giants.

full_text: John Harbaugh answering a question during training camp. | Getty Images The New York Giants will be back at Quest Diagnostics Training Center in East Rutherford, N.J. on Monday holding their first 10 training camp practices in West Virginia. Fans will not be allowed to attend the 1:30 p.m. practice. Big Blue View will not be in attendance. We will, though, have all of the news, highlights, and analysis as quickly as we can. Head coach John Harbaugh said Saturday that he was happy with the time spent in West Virginia. “I think we got a lot better. That’s probably what we got out of it. We improved tremendously. We’re much further along than we were when we started,” Harbaugh said. “I think we can look back and say that we’ve come a long way. “I mean, the competition is really tough in this league, and every team is doing the same thing. So, you’re in a race every single day to be at least the best you can be. And everybody’s trying to do the same thing in the NFL, so that’s why it’s so tough, but I thought our guys did a good job. I’m happy with where we’re at. It’s just a matter of keeping your head down and staying after it every day. Never taking a breath in terms of your mindset and determination to get better.” Injury news There are a few notworthy injuries to monitor: Cornerback Dru Phillips has missed a couple of practices with what has been called a “mild” knee sprain. Will he be back? Edge defender Brian Burns has been limited by an ankle injury. Center John Michael Schmitz missed Saturday’s practice after being hit in the head on Friday. Coach John Harbaugh was not sure on Saturday if Schmitz had been placed in the concussion protocol. We should learn more on Monday. Can Skattebo’s reps were limited the past couple of practices. How much will he work on Monday? Interesting development at cornerback Paulson Adebo is generally considered the Giants’ No. 1 cornerback. Adebo, though, has done some work during recent practices with the second team. Adebo did not have a great 2025 season, and with a new coaching staff it is a trend worth monitoring. Adebo said recently that he knows last season was “not good enough.” Are Harbaugh and defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson telling him what they have seen this summer isn’t good enough? Practice schedule this week The Giants open their preseason at MetLife Stadium on Saturday against the Minnesota Vikings. Here is this week’s practice schedule: Monday, August 10: 1:30 – 4 p.m. Tuesday, August 11: 1:30 – 4 p.m. Wednesday, August 12: 1:30 – 4 p.m. Thursday, August 11: 1:30 – 4 p.m.

title: NY Giants rookie report: Impactful Arvell Reese leading the way
summary: With two weeks of New York Giants training camp in the books, how are the team’s 2026 draft picks performing? Let’s take a look. Arvell Reese The No. 5 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft spent his time in West Virginia showing all of the reasons the Giants were thrilled to select him. He […]
full_text: Arvell Reese | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect With two weeks of New York Giants training camp in the books, how are the team’s 2026 draft picks performing? Let’s take a look. Arvell Reese The No. 5 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft spent his time in West Virginia showing all of the reasons the Giants were thrilled to select him. He made plays going forward against the run and as a blitzer. He made plays going backward in zone coverage, and playing man-to-man. He made plays going sideline to sideline. He occasionally lined up on the edge. In other words, he showed every skill the Giants were hoping to see. When we had an opportunity to speak with him near the end of the West Virginia stay, Reese wasn’t bragging. “Every day I come out here, there’s always something I’m looking to get better at,” Reese said. “As you watch the film, there’s always something to pick up on to get better at and correct the next day. So, yeah, that’s a day-in, day-out thing. Every day I’m looking to get one percent better at something.” Reese has shown a desire to earn respect from his teammates since the day he was drafted, and that is part of what endears him to veteran players. Head coach John Harbaugh loves Reese’s playmaking. What impresses him most, though, is how few assignment mistakes Reese, the team’s youngest player at 20 years of age, makes despite carrying a heavy plate of responsibilities. “You see the talent, obviously,” Harbaugh said. “I think he’s very sharp for a first-year guy. He gets things right pretty much all the time, makes very few mistakes. He’s a very serious-minded guy, and he’s very determined. I mean, he’s doing things well.” Reese was matter-of-fact when I asked him about Harbaugh’s comment. “That’s very important. That’s my job to do that. I get to do that, you feel me?,” Reese said. “So, it’s very important. I take a lot of pride in that, in knowing my stuff and making sure I’m doing everything right. Mistakes happen, but try to just limit those mistakes and not make the same mistake twice.” Francis ‘Sisi’ Mauigoa Remember Andrew Thomas’s rookie season? John Michael Schmitz’s? Evan Neal’s? None of them were good, and that is important context to keep in mind when you assess Mauigoa, the No. 10 overall pick. Harbaugh is not looking for Mauigoa to play like a Hall of Famer from Day 1. He is looking, at least initially, for functionality that does not hold the offense back. “It’s hard. It’s a tough position to play because there’s so much that goes into it. So, you probably have to be a little bit understanding because everything is new to those guys, and there’s so much nuance and detail to the position. So, the ability to function in a way that you can operate with, that’s probably where it starts,” Harbaugh said recently.“ I mean, they have to know where to go. The footwork’s got to be – fundamentals have to be sound enough that they just don’t get whipped right away, which can happen because it can ruin the play. So, they’ve got to have that certain level of competence out of the gates. That’s a must. “And really, very few guys – there’s very few offensive linemen, really, no matter where they get drafted, that can actually pull that off their rookie year. So, hopefully Sisi’s one of those guys. So far so good, but we’ll see.” Mauigoa has taken every snap of training camp as the starting right guard. It has certainly looked to the naked eye as though Mauigoa has been meeting or exceeding the bar Harbaugh has set. Veteran inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds has found himself hooked up regularly with Mauigo during 11-on-11 periods. “He’s a good player. Obviously he’s strong with his hands, has good foot movement, good footwork. Just attention to detail,” Edmunds said. “I think the guys that’s on the o-line are making him better as well. He’s learning from some of the older guys, but early impressions, he’s strong. He understands blocking schemes and where to be at. So, he’s doing a good job right now. “It’s still early for him though, training camp is a long way. So, I think each day that we come out here, once he starts playing in the games, that would be another test for him and he’ll continue to get better. But so far, I’ve definitely been liking what I’ve been seeing from him.” Nose tackle D.J. Reader has also had some battles with Mauigoa. “He’s very heavy-handed and he can move,” Reader said. “It’s good to be around some young, joyful energy. I’m getting up there in some years. He’s a kid, I know he’s going to make me bring it every day. He’s going to make me better for it, and he’s going to get better for it. “He can get some push on you. I tend to believe in myself being pretty strong. He does a good job, though, of bringing the power to you.” Colton Hood The cornerback competition is interesting. Hood, Paulson Adebo, Deonte Banks, and Greg Newsome are the top four cornerbacks. In some order. I just couldn’t tell you what that order is. All four have taken first-team reps. All four, including Adebo, have taken second-team reps. Hood is holding his own. There have been good moments: On Tuesday, he broke up a fade in the corner of the end zone to the since-released Beaux Collins. On Friday, he forced an incompletion in coverage against tight end Isaiah Likely. There have been bad moments, like Friday when Dalen Cambre caught a hitch route, spun, and left Hood grabbing at air as he ran down the field. “jJust like any rookie. They’re going to have their rookie turns and their rookie curves and everything like that, but he’s getting better and better each and every day, said veteran defensive back Ar’Darius Washington. ”He comes in. He works. He wants to get better. He wants to learn. He wants to talk.“ Hood knows there are things he still doesn’t know. “I’m learning a lot from the veterans,” Hood said near the end of last week. “Just getting up to speed with the playbook and everything. It’s been a good camp. I’ve learned a lot and I’m going to continue to learn.” At the end of mandatory minicamp, cornerbacks coach Addison Lynch said there were areas of his game where Hood needed to improve. Hood believes he is taking steps in the right direction. “I’m definitely recognizing formations better. I have a better understanding of the playbook and what the guys are doing around me,” Hood said. “I think those are the two biggest things that I had to work on.” Hood is trying not to focus on how the cornerback depth chart will play out. “I don’t really wonder about it. I’m just going to take it day-by-day,” Hood said. “Just keep going. And being the best version of myself. “When it’s time for me to go and be out there, I’m going to be out there and do what I need to do. I’m not really going to look at it, I’m just going to do what I’m told and do what I’m taught, and just do my job.” Malachi Fields The third-round pick has not been as productive this summer as he was in the spring. Of course, a big part of that is that Fields was limited during the past week by an undisclosed injury. When Fields has been able to practice, many of his reps have been with Jaxson Dart and the starting offense. Bobby Jamison-Travis If you are looking for a detailed breakdown of Jsmison-Travis’s performance, I can’t give you one. It is virtually impossible to get a clear look at nose tackle play from our vantage point. I do believe Jamison-Travis is making the roster. Let’s see what he does in the preseason games. J.C. Davis I was hoping to see Davis, the 192nd pick in the draft, show some positional flexibility this summer. To date, that has not happened. Davis has been the third-team left tackle throughout training camp, with undrafted free agent Ryan Schernecke on the right side. I don’t know how Davis makes the 53-man roster if left tackle is the only position he can play. Andrew Thomas is healthy, and Marcus Mbow is the swing tackle. Josh Ezeudu has been the second-team right tackle, and the Giants know he has experience at both left tackle and guard in an…

summary: The number two overall pick in the NFL Draft always enters the league with his fanbase expecting big things his rookie year. Jets fans are excited to have David Bailey. The hope is that he eventually turns into a transformational player for the defense and becomes a standout pass rusher. What are the expectations for […]
full_text: Jun 10, 2026; Florham Park, NY, USA; New York Jets edge David Bailey (31) warms up during minicamp at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center. Mandatory Credit: John Jones-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The number two overall pick in the NFL Draft always enters the league with his fanbase expecting big things his rookie year. Jets fans are excited to have David Bailey. The hope is that he eventually turns into a transformational player for the defense and becomes a standout pass rusher. What are the expectations for year one? We took a look in this week’s SB Nation Reacts poll. Our question was whether Bailey would hit double digit sacks in year one. I think it was a bit of a trick question because Bailey doesn’t necessarily need to have 10+ sacks in order for his rookie season to be considered a success. Of course he can’t put up like 2 sacks and expect fans to be happy, but a tally of 8-9 along with a high pressure rate would be an excellent sign for his future. Of course a player this talented might dominate the league from the second he steps on the field, but Jets fans only need to see him look the part. He can take the next step in year two. title: Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Darius Cooper is undeniable
summary: Today marked the ninth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES UP NEXT: The Eagles practice again tomorrow starting at 10:00 AM Eastern. We’ll hear from Vic Fangio prior to practice around 9:40 AM.
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Philadelphia, PA, USA; Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver Darius Cooper (80) in action during minicamp at Jefferson Health Training Complex. Mandatory Credit: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Today marked the ninth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed down at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES The Eagles were in full pads following Sunday’s rest day. Putting in a good week of work ahead of Saturday’s preseason game. Practice got a bit chippy at times. Most notably, Tyler Steen put Ty Robinson into the ground during an 11-on-11 rep and there was a big pile of linemen bodies on the ground with a lot of loud cursing going on. Steen also seemed to get annoyed with Uar Bernard at one point. Later, Saquon Barkley threw a shove at Andrew Mukuba after the end of a long run. Competitive intensity. EAGLES INJURY REPORT: BGN’s Alexis Chassen covered the Eagles’ injury news in more detail. I’ll just note here that neither DeVonta Smith nor Makai Lemon have returned to practice. Lemon seems to be on track to miss the Eagles’ first preseason game, which he probably would’ve played in if he was healthy. Cam Jurgens was back at practice after leaving early for the second day in a row on Saturday. Sounds like his exits were heat exhaustion-related more than anything else. The other big news item here is that Willie Lampkin left practice early to walk to the medical tent with a trainer. Something to monitor, hopefully not serious. Ditto for Johnny Wilson, who is newly missing practice. JALEN HURTS UPDATE: Hurts started practice stronger than he finished it. THE GOOD: Hurts had a well-timed connection with Hollywood Brown along the left sideline. Hurts hit Darius Cooper a number of times. More on that in a dedicated Cooper section below. Hurts found a crossing Elijah Moore open and hit him in stride for good YAC potential. After the play, Hurts and Moore did their own little celebration together. I think Hurts is going to want Moore on the roster. THE BAD: On the whole, Hurts has done a better job of not holding onto the ball for forever this summer. But he had a relatively higher number of “sacks” and throwaways today. During a situational period towards the end of practice, Hurts threw an interception to a diving Quinyon Mitchell on a target intended for Brown. Didn’t look like a good throw or decision. Mitchell got up and punted the ball in celebration. Hurts realistically failed to get the offense in the end zone late in another situational scenario. I use “realistically” here because he got a throw off to a leaping Moore in the end zone for a touchdown (good grab and nice effort to uncover while going up against Cooper DeJean) … but it took him over 10 seconds to make the throw. It felt like a real pass rush would’ve disallowed a score on that play. Nolan Smith made sure to vocalize as much with some colorful language after that rep. DAILY DARIUS COOPER IS AWESOME REMINDER: Cooper was impossible not to notice today; I kept writing his name down over and over. Not a joke: I think he might’ve set a new franchise record for most catches by an Eagles player during team drills in a single practice. It began with back-to-back good receptions in 7-on-7. His success carried over to 11-on-11, where he got open on an out route to beat Riq Woolen. He made an over-the-shoulder grab down the right sideline with both Michael Carter II and Zack Baun trailing. Cooper also made a good adjustment while going to the ground to catch an off-target throw from Hurts late in practice. Put simply: good things happen when the Eagles throw the ball to Cooper. He’s proven himself to be a reliable option who gets open and catches the ball. Based on merit, I don’t know how one can argue he’s not a top three receiver on this roster right now. And if Cooper hasn’t already outshined Dontayvion Wicks, who is currently considered to be WR2, he’s pretty close to doing so. And that’s not a slight to Wicks, who’s looked good. If I’m the Eagles, I wouldn’t play Cooper much — if at all — in the preseason. He should be a real part of the offense this season. Hurts clearly trusts him, as evidenced by the quarterback shouting him out without even being prompted to do so . Fred Johnson, not Markel Bell, rotated in at first-team right tackle today when Lane was resting. Bell previously had multiple days as the top option there. BACKUP QUARTERBACK BATTLE UPDATE: Today was Tanner McKee’s day to be first up at QB2. McKee had some good connections with down-the-depth-chart receivers Samari Toure and Erik Ezukanma. He also had an ugly throw fall short of Toure over the middle and was guilty of holding the ball to get “sacked” more than once. McKee was still better than Andy Dalton, who had his worst practice of the summer. The veteran signal caller had some passes broken up and went through a series where he looked totally out of sync with his targets. Dalton misfired on successive throws to Will Shipley in the flat before throwing behind Cooper over the middle … and then way overthrowing a wide open Quez Watkins deep downfield. The backup quarterback battle continues to be close. Interested to see how it evolves over the course of the preseason games. Let’s talk more about slow starts for Makai Lemon and Eli Stowers. With the likes of Cooper, Wicks, and Moore stepping up, maybe the Eagles won’t need Lemon to produce right away after all. Maybe he’ll get healthy soon and look awesome upon returning to practice. I don’t want to suggest that he can’t possibly have success as a rookie. But the missed time is genuinely concerning. It’s also difficult to merely give him the benefit of the doubt in the context of Howie Roseman’s struggles with drafting at this specific position. For all the greatness that Roseman — a future Hall of Famer — has accomplished, he’s drafted just two receivers that have earned a second contract with the Eagles since he rose to power in 2010: DeVonta Smith and Riley Cooper. DeVonta was a really obvious pick as the Heisman Trophy winner in 2021. As for Cooper … yikes. Just because Roseman’s other receiver picks didn’t pan out doesn’t mean Lemon is definitely doomed to a similar fate. I’m only suggesting that it’s reasonable to have some worries at this point in time. As for Stowers, PHLY’s EJ Smith saw a positive rep from him on a different field than I was watching (see embedded tweet below). I noticed a bad rep where he dropped the ball after being contacted from behind by Michael Carter II. This isn’t the first time in camp that Stowers failed to make a catch upon being met with some physicality. To a bigger point, I am wondering if Stowers will even be active for Week 1. He’s not a top two tight end right now since he’s clearly behind Goedert and Johnny Mundt (who had a nice grab for a short gain today). Is he definitely TE3? I asked other practice observers for their thoughts on this matter and they agreed that Stowers could be a healthy scratch … early on in the season, at least. PHLY’s Fran Duffy recently noted that Stowers was bullied in special teams drills by undrafted rookie Joshua Weru, who has stood out despite lacking previous American football experience. It’s not necessarily the end of the world if Stowers can’t majorly contribute as a rookie but it doesn’t seem ideal if the coaching staff doesn’t trust a second-round pick to suit up for game action. Of course, there’s still time before we get to that point. Eli Stowers just caught a touchdown pass on a vertical route during a team session between the second-team offense and the first-team defense. Looked like a busted coverage against the starters, but that’s his biggest play of training camp. #Eagles — EJ Smith (@EJSmith94) August 10, 2026 I missed most of the Eagles’ offensive line vs. defensive line 2-on-2 drills, which took place on a different field while I was viewing 7-on-7. Outsourcing…

title: Sean Mannion says the Eagles will still “lean into” the tush push
summary: The Eagles are working toward their first preseason game against the Ravens, and offensive coordinator Sean Mannion spoke to reporters over the weekend about the team’s expectations, and what they want to see from an operational standpoint and from the offense as a whole. Here’s some of what the OC had to say: On the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 01: Philadelphia Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion is shown during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on August 1st, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Eagles are working toward their first preseason game against the Ravens, and offensive coordinator Sean Mannion spoke to reporters over the weekend about the team’s expectations, and what they want to see from an operational standpoint and from the offense as a whole. Here’s some of what the OC had to say: On the tush push “It’s going to be a part of what we do. It’s been an extremely effective play here, and we’re going to lean into that. It’s something that this organization has executed at a high level. So along with many other elements to our offense, certainly it’s something that will be a part of it.“ On the “call-it” periods Mannion talked about how it’s a huge priority for him to get the plays in quickly to the QB to allow for the offense to get up to the line and assess the defense. “These call-it periods in practice have been huge for that, both for our operation by position groups on the field and then also as a staff, just to manage kind of the lines of communication that’ll take place on game day. It’s critical. We want to apply pressure to the defense at all times. Part of that, frankly, is how you break the huddle, approach the line of scrimmage, get lined up, begin your motions if there’s motions on that specific play. It’s a huge weapon and a huge part of our offense that we work on every day.” The OC later explained how massively helpful the call-it periods have been for him as a play-caller. Being able to go through the whole process as a staff, including things like managing substitutions, and doing so as close to a game setting as possible, will have them ready for Week 1. Mannion talked about his goals for the Eagles first preseason game in terms of play-calling, and he pointed to sharpening the process of the game day logistics. He explained that there are so many parts to the operation behind the scenes, so it’s about every person executing what they’ve mapped out. They’ll be working through all those logistics in real time throughout the rest of the preseason. On the WR group Mannion made sure to give the wide receiver credit for the time they are dedicating to their craft in training camp. He noted that the group as a whole will stay after practice to run routes with QB Jalen Hurts, or spend time on the jugs machine, and the whole WR room has embodied the commitment to improvement that the coaching staff has been emphasizing. The OC said it’s been exciting to watch guys like Elijah Moore and DeVonta Smith out in practice, and they want to build an offense around the strengths of their players. Makai Lemon “It’s been going well. It’s an unfortunate part of camp. Sometimes you lose a guy for a few days, but he’s been super engaged in the meetings. Out at walkthrough, he has a script, he’s following every play. He’s kind of mirroring the alignment of his position in the offense. He’s been making the most of a situation where you obviously want guys to be out there, but he’s been super engaged. I know he’s attacking his rehab to get back out.” Darius Cooper Mannion said that Darius Cooper has done a great job so far. He noted that the WR unfortunately missed time in the spring due to injury, but he’s done a lot of nice things now that he’s back out on the field. The team loves Cooper’s skillset, and are excited about the different attributes he brings to the group. Dontayvion Wicks “Wicks is a great worker. He’s got a ton of talent. He’s off to a really good start. One of the things I’d like to highlight about really our whole wide receiver group is these guys are blocking in the run game at a really high level. The effort they’re putting in — Wicks is certainly a huge part of that. As a group collectively, again, everybody is attacking each day, ready to get better.” On Saquon Barkley’s involvement “Saquon, he’s a tremendous player. Everything we do offensively ultimately is about how do we put all of our players in the best position to succeed. Obviously, Saquon’s a focal point of our offense, that goes without saying. We carry that mindset into everything we do schematically, what we’re repping at practice and all the different facets of that go hand in hand. As we build the run game, as we build what we’re going to do formationally, you want the play pass game, the keeper game to play off of that. All of these things need to marry with one another. We’re always trying to maximize our players’ skill sets. Saquon obviously chief among them, and then all the different things kind of spawn off of that.” Other notables Mannion talked about QB Cole Payton, and said that the rookie has done a really nice job so far. He pointed out that there were a couple of days when Payton needed to better protect the football, but overall the OC is happy with where the QB is in his development. He went on to say that Payton has made tremendous improvement in terms of timing, rhythm, and accuracy, and is doing everything he can with the limited reps he gets. As for the OC’s philosophy on trying new things in practice, he explained that they want treat every practice as if it was a game, and execution matters. So, he doesn’t subscribe to trying things, or using a different approach to practice than they would in a game. The team is days away from their first preseason game, and Mannion said he’s looking for execution and play style from the offense. They want to see the effort and physicality guys are playing with, and then operationally, they want to see a clean process from sideline to line of scrimmage. Mannion had good things to say about the offensive line depth — guys like Markel Bell and Drew Kendall. He said that the OL has been highlighted by a group of veterans who have played at a high level for a long time, but they are really excited about the young guys they have on roster, as well.

title: Eagles sign 3 players, including their former draft pick
summary: The Eagles are in their second week of training camp, and with injuries and evaluations, the roster is in constant fluctuation. The team made six moves on Monday, including signing all three players they had in for work outs over the weekend: DT David Blay, RB Ja’Quinden Jackson and OLB Tarron Jackson. To make room […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 21: Defensive end Tarron Jackson #75 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs a play during the fourth quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at FirstEnergy Stadium on August 21, 2022 in Cleveland, Ohio. The Eagles defeated the Browns 21-20. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles are in their second week of training camp, and with injuries and evaluations, the roster is in constant fluctuation. The team made six moves on Monday, including signing all three players they had in for work outs over the weekend : DT David Blay, RB Ja’Quinden Jackson and OLB Tarron Jackson . To make room on the roster, Philadelphia waived undrafted rookies OG Jaeden Roberts and TE Dae’Quan Wright , and also placed RB Elijah Mitchell on IR. Mitchell left Saturday’s training camp practice early, and by heading to IR ahead of the team’s final roster cuts, he’ll be unable to return for the 2026 season unless the Eagles release him with an injury settlement. DT David Blay The interior defensive lineman went undrafted out of Miami earlier this year, but ended up signing with the Patriots before he was ultimately waived a few days before landing with the Eagles. Howie Roseman loves a local guy, and Blay is a Levittown, PA native who started his collegiate career at West Chester University. The 6-foot-2, 292-pound DT then went to play two seasons at Louisiana Tech before his final transfer to Miami. RB Ja’Quinden Jackson The running back went undrafted out of Arkansas in 2025, but signed with the Jaguars and spent his rookie season on Jacksonville’s practice squad. Despite signing Jackson to a futures deal in January, the team waived him in May, and he’s been looking for a team ever since. As the Eagles start to consider work loads, having depth at running back will be important through the rest of training camp — especially considering the team lost Elijah Mitchell to injury. OLB Tarron Jackson The Eagles brought back Jackson, who was drafted in the sixth round by the team in 2021. The OLB played in Philadelphia through most of the 2024 season, except for a brief stint with the Panthers for three months late in the summer before returning to Philly. He signed with the 49ers in early-2025, but was placed on IR in July of that year after suffering a scary injury in training camp, per NFL.com . “Jackson collapsed on the field after he was blocked on a play late in practice and was on the ground for several minutes before being taken off on a stretcher and taken to the hospital in an ambulance. Coach Kyle Shanahan said Jackson was conscious, able to communicate and feel all his extremities.“ Jackson was activated off the team’s IR in February and must be ready to get back on the field.

title: One major outlet’s crazy preseason ranking of the Eagles
summary: Your Philadelphia Eagles are not the preseason favorites to represent the NFC in Super Bowl 61. That’s OK and totally understandable. Despite winning the Super Bowl two years ago, the ‘25 Birds confoundingly disappointing season as well as the seemingly complete overhaul of the offense may understandably affect how many will view this team’s chances. […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 07: Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni speaks with the press during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on August 7th, 2026 at the Jefferson Health Training Complex on August 7th, 2026 in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Your Philadelphia Eagles are not the preseason favorites to represent the NFC in Super Bowl 61. That’s OK and totally understandable. Despite winning the Super Bowl two years ago, the ‘25 Birds confoundingly disappointing season as well as the seemingly complete overhaul of the offense may understandably affect how many will view this team’s chances. The consensus preseason power rankings by national media generally seem to have the Eagles on the fringe of the top-10. The Ringer: No. 6 Fox Sports: No. 7 The Athletic: No. 9 Yahoo!: No. 9 ESPN’s NFL Power Index: No. 10 Now, I’ve always been a big supporter of independent thought and the avoidance of group think. But I think the good folks at USA Today may have veered off course just a wee bit with their outrageously negative preseason ranking of the 2026 Birds. In their latest rankings, they have the Birds at No. 19 . Here is their detailed roundup. 19. Philadelphia Eagles (12): The offense is going to appear virtually unrecognizable − probably necessary after last year’s showing. But can’t wait to see it, especially rookie WR Makai Lemon. If you’re going to put the Eagles at No. 19, don’t you at least have to give a good reason for such a head-scratching decision? The Vikings, led by Kyler Murray, are No. 17. The Commanders, still with virtually no offensive talent around Jayden Daniels, are No. 18. The Rams, Seahawks, Bears, 49ers, Cowboys, Lions, and Packers are all ahead of them. In short, this ranking postulates the Eagles are the 10th-best team in the 15-team NFC. There are undoubtedly many questions surrounding how the Eagles will do under Sean Mannion’s new offense. We all have them. They will miss not having elite A.J. Brown on the field anymore, although even if Brown was still an Eagle, the “elite” version of him last played in Super Bowl 59. It’s not a strong group of wide receivers, and it’s fair to question the health of the offensive line. But even if Jalen Hurts and Co. have some ups and downs, is there any world in which the Eagles are the 19th best team in the NFL? Vic Fangio’s defense along almost guarantees the Eagles will be a playoff team in 2026. They boast one of the deepest and most talented defensive lines in the NFL, a ridiculously talented linebacking corps, and a secondary that will frustrate the very best passing offenses in the NFL. There could be as many as 6-7 Pro Bowlers and 4-5 potential 1st or 2nd-team All Pros on that side of the football. Preseason rankings are supposed to be an objective look at the rosters of teams as teams enter training camp. Sure, one can project a disastrous season if every worst-case scenario happens, but how can an objective observer look at the roster of the Eagles, a team that has made the postseason five straight seasons with two Super Bowl appearances, and say the Vikings or Commanders are better right now? Maybe, by the time December rolls around, this ranking will be prescient. But there’s really no justifiable reason why the Eagles would rank this low, which is probably why the author did not present a justifiable reasons. At the end of the day, it’s just sports and it really doesn’t matter. What happens on the field will determine where the Eagles actually finish up. But in early August, this ranking just doesn’t make any logical sense.

title: Eagles News: “It’s fair at this point to doubt that [Makai Lemon] will start, at least early in the season”
summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Recalibrating the Eagles biggest positional needs after the start of training camp – PhillyVoiceThe Eagles did not select Makai Lemon to be a developmental player over time. He profiles more as an immediate contributor, and in my view the Eagles were hoping he would start […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JUNE 10: Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver Makai Lemon #9 is shown during the Philadelphia Eagles off season minicamp on June 10th, 2026 at the Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Recalibrating the Eagles biggest positional needs after the start of training camp – PhillyVoice The Eagles did not select Makai Lemon to be a developmental player over time. He profiles more as an immediate contributor, and in my view the Eagles were hoping he would start right away. Well, Lemon missed half the spring and so far half of training camp, and on the days he did practice he didn’t do a whole lot. It’s fair at this point to doubt that he will start, at least early in the season. Dontayvion Wicks and Darius Cooper have had good camps so far, but let’s be honest. If a month ago those guys were projected to be the WR2 and WR3 everyone would be saying that the Eagles need to trade for a receiver. In a weird way, I think the Eagles have a lot of playable receivers. Hell, they could even trade one away because they can’t all make the team. But Wicks has never really been better than his team’s WR4. Cooper has only played 212 career snaps and he has single-digit receptions. My concern would be at those WR2 and WR3 spots. Eagles training camp: 6 pressing questions after second week of practices – The Athletic I feel the same way you do about both DeVonta Smith and Lemon. With Lemon, he missed most of the spring with a hamstring injury. He’s already missed a week this summer. If this extends much deeper into August, he might be behind as a Week 1 contributor. You’ll hear the narrative that Cooper DeJean missed his spring and most of the summer (as you noted). That’s fair. But DeJean didn’t become a meaningful contributor on defense until Week 6. I’m not suggesting that Lemon’s rookie season will be washed away; I’m simply saying it could affect how much he’s used in the first month. That’s why the wide receiver depth is so important to monitor. Eagles 53-man roster prediction: Training camp updates – BGN WIDE RECEIVER: DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Darius Cooper, Makai Lemon, Hollywood Brown, Johnny Wilson (6) [12]. Smitty has missed most of training camp with a hamstring injury but he looked good as ever prior to getting hurt. Zero concerns with him. Smith’s absence has opened up more opportunities for Wicks, who has fully taken advantage of them by making a lot of catches. It’s clear that Hurts trusts Wicks, which is huge. Cooper makes plays every day. He’s already done enough to make the roster. The question is: will he actually get playing time? He deserves it. Lemon’s had a disappointing offseason; the 2026 first-round pick missed at least four of the Eagles’ eight spring practices and he’s missed five of their eight training camp practices so far. Even prior to getting hurt, Lemon wasn’t doing much to impress. It’s just hard to know what to expect from him at the moment. Brown has been outshined by others … but the Eagles gave him $5 million guaranteed, which impacted their compensatory pick formula. So, it’s not ea sy to see them cutting him. Maybe they can move off Hollywood in a trade? Wilson has had a good camp as a pass-catcher and he obviously brings value to the table as a big blocking receiver. Elijah Moore was a really tough cut here; he deserves to make the team and he’s been getting first-team reps. But he also doesn’t have special teams experience (19 career snaps there) and he’s not subject to waivers. Maybe the Eagles can get him to agree to be on the practice squad early in the season before eventually adding him to the roster once a spot frees up. Britain Covey saw a lot of targets early in camp but he’s been dealing with a hamstring injury and the team can probably keep him on the practice squad if they want him to be in the punt returner mix. Quez Watkins is also in practice squad contention. Go Birds! Radio, Part 1: Reacting To The Lane Johnson News (Feat. BLG) – Go Birds! Podcast James Seltzer, Eliot Shorr-Parks and Brandon Lee Gowton react to Lane Johnson’s announcement that he will probably retire at the end of 2026. Go Birds! Radio, Part 2: Two Unexpected Training Camp Standouts (Feat. BLG) – Go Birds! Podcast James Seltzer, Eliot Shorr-Parks and Brandon Lee Gowton continue their discussion on Eagles Training Camp and give two names for most surprising standout so far. In Roob’s Eagles Observations: How Andy Reid influenced Howie’s trade philosophy – NBCSP I’LL KEEP RAVING ABOUT DARIUS COOPER: This kid does something every day to jump out at you and I’m at the point where I’ll just be really surprised if he doesn’t make the 53-man roster. Cooper showed enough flashes last year that he made the team as an undrafted rookie and even caught nine passes, most by an undrafted Eagles rookie WR since Hank Baskett caught 22 in 2006. He looks better this year with a year under his belt. Cooper has made the routine catches, but he’s made three of the most spectacular catches of the summer as well. It’s fair to assume Cooper and Johnny Wilson are competing for one spot, since they are the two big, tough, physical blocking WRs in camp. But Cooper has caught the ball better than Wilson, and if you’re only going to keep one, it’s going to be Cooper. Helmet cams and VR sets: Eagles quarterbacks use different tools as they learn a new offense – Inquirer So Payton, a dual-threat quarterback out of North Dakota State, often is on the field late, after practice ends, working with quarterbacks coach Parks Frazier and sometimes Mannion on his footwork and technique. Payton called those post-practice sessions “huge,” but the on-field portion of camp is only part of the on-the-job training Payton is going through as he navigates his first NFL training camp. The Eagles were off Sunday, but Payton said he has spent some off days strapping a virtual reality headset on to get “mental visualization reps.” The tool, Payton said, was introduced to him by Frazier, who last year was the pass game coordinator and this year moved to quarterbacks coach. The Eagles, Payton said, had the sets last year, too. Payton can turn on the VR, select any stadium, go through his play calls, break the huddle, and simulate a real play. “It’s not live footage, it’s animated, but it’s a really good tool to visualize and see things,” Payton said Saturday. 2026 Philadelphia Eagles training camp: Latest intel, updates – ESPN Eagles running back Saquon Barkley made his presence felt. He got animated after a short touchdown run, chirping at Cooper DeJean before giving Quinyon Mitchell a playful shove. The offense switched from goal line to backed up work a short time later. Barkley used a nifty jump cut to speed to daylight on one play and followed that up by shaking defensive tackle Jordan Davis on his next carry. Barkley believes this new system can open up some things for him that he hasn’t been able to fully showcase to this point in his career. “That’s the plan,” said offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. “Saquon, he’s a tremendous player, and I think everything we do offensively ultimately is about how do we put all of our players in the best position to succeed and obviously Saquon is a focal point of our offense, that goes without saying.” Bowen: Lane Johnson’s journey to Eagles franchise icon was not the smoothest – PHLY This started the Lane Johnson Watch. You’re an Eagles fan, you paid to read this, so you know what I mean – the latest tally shows the Eagles are 120-62-1 when he is in the lineup, 19-29 when he is not. Last season, Johnson missed the final seven games with a foot injury, and then missed the excruciating playoff loss to San Francisco. Overall in 2025, it was 8-2 with Johnson, 3-5 without him. I’m going to break off my memory lane journey for a second to point out something: Hey, if…

full_text: Aug 03, 2026; Latrobe, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers running back Rico Dowdle (13) runs during a practice session at Training camp at Saint Vincent College. Mandatory Credit: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect LATROBE – About 50 minutes into practice, a booming voice came over the loudspeaker at Saint Vincent College to announce that, due to weather, there would be an immediate evacuation of the campus for the public. This unfortunately prevented us from seeing some of the Pittsburgh Steelers’ young receivers get opportunities as the top options in their passing attack. Let’s take a look at some of the biggest storylines from an abbreviated practice. Germie Bernard and Roman Wilson were thrust into important roles Both DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. did not practice today. Nothing seemed to be wrong with Metcalf, I would suspect more of a veteran’s day off for him, as we have seen others do throughout camp. Pittman missing practice is certainly notable after he hurt his left leg during Pittsburgh’s Saturday Night Lights practice. With that, it was set to be a big practice for both training camp star Roman Wilson and rookie Germie Bernard. As fans were exiting practice, there was a big rise from the crowd as Aaron Rodgers uncorked a downfield shot for Wilson, who caught the ball in stride. The ball was thrown at least 45 yards down the field and would have gone for much more in a game situation. It was a quiet start to practice for Bernard, who jumped offsides in 11-on-11 drills, resulting in him being replaced by Ben Skrownek for the play. It would have been nice to see Bernard in more situations with the first team firsthand had the weather held up. Dowdle and Nichols shine in running drills During Saturday’s practice, I took note of how fast Dowdle seemed to be bursting through the line. Today was no exception. Dowdle seems to have the best skillset for the runs in between the tackles, while Warren will still get carries, but might shine more as a receiver. It will be interesting to see how the workload is split up between the two toip backs in the Steelers offense. Lew Nichols has shined throughout camp, as the team’s RB3 job is seemingly wide open. Although the team isn’t tackling, Nichols broke free for what likley would have been a 20 yard touchdown scamper during the biginning of practice. Nichols stood out in the preseason for the Steelers last year, and will certainly be in line for a big workload on Thursday. Other notes: Rookie tackle Max Iheanachor was technically back at practice today. He could be seen with his pads and helmet on and participated in individual drills, but sat off to the side during live drills. It seems like the team is being extra cautious with their first round rookie. Joey Porter Jr., Jalen Ramsey, and Donte Kent, who are all on the physically unable to perform list, were seen running on the second practice field in Latrobe. A welcome sign that maybe a few of them are inching closer to being able to participate. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: Analyst’s offensive line grades reflect the promise of Steelers’ young core
summary: We’re still three days away from seeing the Steelers suit up for their first game action of the 2026 season. Even if most of Pittsburgh’s fans remain skeptical of the team’s ceiling this year — a sentiment I share, for what it’s worth — it’s important to remember that seasons can still be enjoyable and […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - DECEMBER 15: Zach Frazier #54 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Pennsylvania on December 15, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re still three days away from seeing the Steelers suit up for their first game action of the 2026 season. Even if most of Pittsburgh’s fans remain skeptical of the team’s ceiling this year — a sentiment I share, for what it’s worth — it’s important to remember that seasons can still be enjoyable and progress can be tracked even in the seasons that don’t end with hoisting the Lombardi trophy. While much is new with the team this year, the Black and Gold are running it back with Aaron Rodgers under center. Whether you think that’s good or bad is entirely up to you, but for me, it means that once again I will be grading this upcoming season through the lens of player development. Last summer, I wrote that the young offensive line’s progression would be the story of the 2025 season , and that remains true for this campaign. The Steelers have invested heavily in the offensive line since Omar Khan took over as general manager, and last year was a crucial moment for this unit. At this time last year: We were fairly certain that center Zach Frazier had “The Goods,” but we still wanted to know if he could be more durable after some injury concerns, and if he could build on an impressive but imperfect rookie season. It was a similar story with 2024 fourth-round guard Mason McCormick. Pressed to play sooner than expected because of an injury to James Daniels, McCormick showed he could hang as at least a replacement-level starter as a rookie. But 2025 would be key to showing if he was a player that could continue to improve or if he’d already tapped out his potential. 2024 first-round tackle Troy Fautanu was still largely a question mark after missing all but one game of his rookie season due to a knee injury. 2023 first-round tackle Broderick Jones had flashed moments through two seasons, but had also largely looked like a player still trying to figure out how to maximize all of his athletic potential. He entered the season needing to show major improvement if he hoped to have the Steelers pick up his fifth-year option following the year. ( They ultimately did not .) It was all but certain that Isaac Seumalo was playing his final year in Pittsburgh, which did come to fruition this offseason with the veteran guard’s departure for Arizona. While the results were mixed for these players during the 2025 season, the Steelers had to feel pretty good about how things were trending heading into the 2026 offseason. Frazier, Fautanu, and McCormick all performed like players the team should include in their long-term plans. The team also got the added bonus of seeing players like guard Spencer Anderson and tackle Dylan Cook prove that they could be capable starters, at least in the short term, meaning the team had more flexibility with how they would approach cementing the final two starting spots for both 2026 and again with how they approach the 2027 offseason. But you don’t have to just take my word for it. Bleacher Report’s Brandon Thorn is one of the most respected — if not THE most respected — analysts in the media when it comes to offensive line play. I know from reading some of the comments our readers leave that many of you are wary of “(Insert name analyst) ranks Steelers player” articles, but I find Thorn’s work to be well researched and informative. His interviews with players and coaches in the offensive line world are often insightful and teach me more about the game. Thorn recently graded 175 offensive linemen as part of Bleacher Report’s NFL 1000 series . Players were broken down and ranked by position based on a five-trait grading system. Those traits were: pass protection (25), run blocking (20), play strength/anchor (20), movement skills (20), and hand usage (15). Thorn included five Steelers in his grades: Frazier, Fautanu, Jones, McCormick, and Cook. It should come as little surprise to Steelers fans that Zach Frazier received the highest grade and praise among Pittsburgh linemen. Thorn graded Frazier out as the second-best center in the NFL — trailing only Kansas City’s Creed Humphrey — as well as the 12th-best lineman in the NFL overall. 12th overall Zach Frazier. Not sure people realize how good he is. On the podium for being the strongest C in football while having an unusual amount of refinement this early. A true 'leverage monster' who understands who he is and rarely ever lets defenders compromise that. pic.twitter.com/CozP3wubMI — Brandon Thorn (@BrandonThornNFL) August 4, 2026 Fautanu also received a favorable grade. Despite playing on the right side last season, Thorn included Fautanu with the left tackle group, ranking him as the 10th-best at the position and the 25th-best lineman in the NFL. Fautanu received his best grades as a pass protector (20 out of 25) and for his movement skills (17 out of 20). Thorn quote : “Fautanu is an explosive, aggressive blocker with good length, high-end movement skills and one of the league’s best snatch-trap techniques, allowing him to steal leverage and knock rushers off their feet when they lean into him or are lazy with their hands.” McCormick was dinged some for his athletic limitations, but was about league average as Thorn’s 17th-ranked left guard and 90th overall lineman. His running blocking (14 out of 20) and play strength (14 out of 20) were the traits Thorn highlighted most positively. Thorn quote : “He is not an overwhelming physical talent, but his active hands, quick refits and excellent strain allow him to stay attached, die slowly when initially beaten and prevent clean sheds. McCormick displays enough play-strength and movement ability to function across concepts, while his leverage, toughness and hand activity make him more difficult to discard than his raw traits suggest… McCormick is a classic greater-than-the-sum-of-his-parts starter whose technique, effort and consistency make him a net positive despite a capped ceiling.” Despite playing in just five career games, all coming late in the 2025 season, Thorn had Dylan Cook graded higher than Broderick Jones. This isn’t totally surprising; I think most Steelers fans would agree with that assessment even with such a small sample size. Thorn ranked Cook as the 28th-best left tackle and 135 overall. He graded Cook’s top skills as pass protection (15 out of 25) and his movement skills (13 out of 20). Thorn quote : “Cook showed better pass-protection feel than expected, especially with his positional leverage, strike-timing and ability to use a snatch-trap technique for clean wins. He is sturdily built with solid movement skills and enough pop to create jolt when his hands land on time. Limitations show up more in the run game, where he can lean into contact, lose balance when the picture changes post-snap, and get shed before sustaining.” Jones, meanwhile, was graded as the 34th-best left tackle and 153rd out of 175 linemen graded. Jones scored best in movement and play strength (both 13 out of 20), but was graded as subpar in pass protection (12 out of 25) and run blocking (12 out of 20), and he received a dismal grade for hand usage (7 out of 15). Having watched a ton of Steelers offensive line All-22 tape the past three seasons myself, I can assure you the hands usage grade is fair and accurate. Thorn quote : “Jones remains a solid mover with pop in his hands, but his technique remains too erratic. He will duck his head, throw his hands into contact and open quick access across his face, while his run-game sustain is inconsistent once defenders survive initial contact… his current profile is an inconsistent, guardrail-dependent tackle with major health and reliability concerns.” Overall, Thorn estimates the Steelers’ offensive line has two…

title: Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald addresses Terrion Arnold tryout
summary: The Seattle Seahawks brought in former Detroit Lions first-round pick Terrion Arnold for what is listed in the NFL transaction wire as an official tryout. Arnold is in legal limbo after his recent arrest on multiple felony robbery and kidnapping charges, with an arraignment hearing scheduled for later this week. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 30: Zach Charbonnet #26 of the Seattle Seahawks attempts to stiff arms Terrion Arnold #0 of the Detroit Lions during the second quarter at Ford Field on September 30, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks brought in former Detroit Lions first-round pick Terrion Arnold for what is listed in the NFL transaction wire as an official tryout. Arnold is in legal limbo after his recent arrest on multiple felony robbery and kidnapping charges, with an arraignment hearing scheduled for later this week. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald addressed the visit during Monday’s training camp media availability. “It’s enough right now that we had him in for a great visit, a great tryout,” Macdonald said of the team’s interest in Arnold. “It’s a situation where there’s some other things that are surrounding it as well—we’re aware of that. But we’re working through the situation right now. It was a great visit, I really enjoyed meeting him and I think he enjoyed being here, so we’ll see where it goes.” Arnold, a former standout cornerback at Alabama, figured to be a key piece of Detroit’s defense before his arrest and subsequent release. Now that he’s currently out on bail but can travel domestically for work, which means he can potentially sign with another NFL team, Seahawks obviously included. “We’re going to do our due diligence,” Macdonald added when asked about protecting the team culture. “There’s a lot of people in Terrion’s corner that we respect in terms of the type of guy he is, so we’re going to work through all that. I trust our people to make the best decision for us. We also think this is a great place to come work, too, and that people can be the best version of themselves if given the opportunity. It kind of works both ways.” One person on the coaching staff with at least some familiarity is defensive backs coach Karl Scott, who helped recruit Arnold to Alabama but left for the NFL prior to Arnold’s freshman season. “Karl recruited him to my knowledge but didn’t coach him, so it’s not as big of a relationship as you might expect, but he’s definitely a person that we would talk to,” Macdonald said. “You know, anybody that has a relationship with anybody that we’re going to bring in we’re going to seek that counsel so this is an example of that.” The Seahawks let Riq Woolen walk to the Philadelphia Eagles and followed that up by drafting three cornerbacks (Julian Neal, Andre Fuller, and Michael Dansby) and signing Noah Igbinoghene in free agency. With nothing set in stone at corner outside of Josh Jobe and Devon Witherspoon, the interest in Arnold given his ongoing case could be seen as an eyebrow raiser concerning the current group. “I have a ton of confidence in our defensive backfield room,” Macdonald said. “This is a situation of we’re kind of in everything all the time. We’re always trying to make our team the best we can possibly make it. Whether or not Terrion ends up here or not or it works out or it doesn’t, we’ll keep on rolling the way we know how.” Arnold is slated to meet with the New Orleans Saints, having met with the Houston Texans prior to his Seahawks tryout.

title: All-22 film shows why Nick Emmanwori is so important to the Seahawks defense
summary: One of the more fascinating aspects of the Seattle Seahawks’ defensive resurgence under Mike Macdonald is that it wasn’t built around a single superstar. While the roster certainly features standout talent, the defense’s success came from how well every piece fit within the larger structure. Players consistently embraced unselfish roles, allowing teammates to make plays […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Devon Witherspoon #21, Nick Emmanwori #3 and DeMarcus Lawrence #0 of the Seattle Seahawks react to a play during the first quarter of Super Bowl LX against the New England Patriots at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the more fascinating aspects of the Seattle Seahawks’ defensive resurgence under Mike Macdonald is that it wasn’t built around a single superstar. While the roster certainly features standout talent, the defense’s success came from how well every piece fit within the larger structure. Players consistently embraced unselfish roles, allowing teammates to make plays without sacrificing the integrity of the scheme. Few rookies embodied that philosophy better than Nick Emmanwori. Seattle’s second-round selection entered the NFL with enormous physical tools and equally high expectations. Many viewed him as one of the most intriguing defensive prospects in the 2025 draft, although there were legitimate questions about how quickly he would adapt to an NFL role that differed significantly from what he had played at South Carolina. While the Gamecocks have long valued versatility in the secondary, Emmanwori was never a full-time nickel defender in college. His responsibilities often changed from week to week, but consistently living inside as a nickel defender was not part of his collegiate résumé. That transition made his rookie season even more impressive. Learning a basically new position while adjusting to the speed and complexity of NFL offenses is a difficult assignment for any rookie. Emmanwori not only handled the challenge but quickly became an integral piece of Mike Macdonald’s defense, validating the coaching staff’s vision for how his unique skill set could elevate the entire unit. Whether or not he received the national recognition his season deserved is a debate for another day. The tape tells a much clearer story: Seattle didn’t find another defensive back; they found a player whose versatility expanded what the defense could do on a snap-to-snap basis. What stood out on Nick Emmanwori’s tape A nickel who played like a linebacker against the run Emmanwori's size lets him play the run like a linebacker. He takes on blockers and keeps Seattle in nickel without sacrificing physicality against the run. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-10T01:38:01.389Z Seattle’s success against the run was built on collective execution rather than individual dominance. The defensive line consistently sacrificed statistics by occupying double teams, controlling interior gaps and allowing the second level to flow freely to the football. It was a coordinated effort, not one player carrying the defense. Emmanwori became one of the key reasons that structure worked. Playing nickel normally forces a defense to sacrifice some physicality in the run game in exchange for better coverage personnel. Seattle largely avoided that tradeoff because Emmanwori consistently played the position with the mentality of a linebacker. On tape, he repeatedly attacked pulling blockers, took on offensive linemen without hesitation, stacked tight ends at the point of attack and willingly met fullbacks in the hole. Rather than trying to avoid contact, he embraced it, using his size, leverage and play strength to keep runs from reaching the second level. That versatility allowed Macdonald to keep nickel personnel on the field without becoming vulnerable against heavier offensive formations. In many ways, Emmanwori effectively gave Seattle an extra linebacker while preserving the coverage advantages of a defensive back. Perhaps more importantly, it allowed Seattle to stay in its preferred personnel far more often. Offensive coordinators couldn’t force the Seahawks into heavier packages by threatening the run because their nickel defender already functioned as a legitimate run defender. A valuable piece in Seattle’s pressure package Emmanwori became a key piece of Macdonald's pressure packages. His timing and acceleration made him a legitimate blitz threat, giving Seattle more ways to create pressure without tipping its intentions pre-snap. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-10T01:38:52.754Z Macdonald’s pressure packages rely heavily on disguise rather than sheer volume of blitzers, making versatile defensive backs especially valuable. Emmanwori quickly became one of the defense’s preferred pressure players. Whether aligned in simulated pressures, overload blitzes or late rotations, he consistently timed his rushes well and forced offenses to account for him before the snap. His acceleration allowed him to stress protections and frequently influenced quarterbacks, even when he didn’t finish with a sack. His value extended beyond production. Simply having a defensive back capable of threatening as a legitimate blitzer expanded the number of pressure looks Seattle could present without revealing its intentions before the snap. That kind of versatility is exactly what Macdonald looks for when designing pressure packages that rely as much on uncertainty as they do on numbers. Better in coverage than expected Before his rookie season start, one of the biggest questions surrounding Emmanwori centered on his ability to mirror quicker slot receivers. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-10T01:39:21.002Z Before his rookie season start, one of the biggest questions surrounding Emmanwori centered on his ability to mirror quicker slot receivers. Given his collegiate background as a safety, many expected him to excel against tight ends while struggling against smaller, more agile receivers working underneath. The tape often suggested the opposite. Emmanwori's coverage was more disciplined than expected. His footwork, patience and ability to stay in phase stood out, while his length and recovery speed limited separation. He became a dependable coverage defender rather than a matchup offenses could target — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-10T01:40:00.860Z Although he wasn’t asked to live in true man coverage every snap, Emmanwori displayed surprisingly disciplined footwork, remained patient at the top of routes and consistently stayed in phase against slot receivers. His combination of length, recovery speed and physicality prevented many receivers from creating clean separation. Rather than becoming a matchup offenses actively targeted, he proved to be a dependable coverage defender who comfortably handled responsibilities many questioned before the season. That development significantly raised his ceiling within Seattle’s defense. Instead of being a situational player whose usage had to be carefully managed, he demonstrated enough competence in coverage to stay on the field regardless of offensive personnel. In my view, this was Nick Emmanwori's best play of the season. He reads the QB's eyes in zone, identifies the route, transitions smoothly and uses anticipation to break up the pass. Outstanding rep — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-10T01:40:41.037Z In my view, this was Nick’s best play of the season. He’s playing zone coverage, reads the quarterback’s eyes, quickly recognizes the receiver’s route, transitions smoothly and uses his anticipation to break up the pass. Amazing. Areas for improvement Trusting his eyes before trusting his athleticism There’s no questioning Emmanwori’s athletic profile. His size, explosiveness and closing speed are exactly what made him such an intriguing prospect entering the league. Emmanwori's aggression was a weapon as a rookie, helping him trigger downhill, disrupt runs, attack screens and blitz. But he occasionally committed too quickly to the initial action, opening space that better patience could have prevented — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-10T02:10:51.808Z At times during his rookie season, Emmanwori’s aggressiveness worked in Seattle’s favor. His willingness to trigger downhill…

title: A 53-man Seattle Seahawks roster projection entering preseason
summary: Regular season 53-man roster projections usually start heating up towards the end of training camp and preseason. However, it is always fun to be wrong early in the game too. With that, here is a projection before any Seattle Seahawks preseason games have even started. Quarterback (3) Keep: Sam Darnold, Drew Lock, Jalen Milroe Cut: […]
full_text: Regular season 53-man roster projections usually start heating up towards the end of training camp and preseason. However, it is always fun to be wrong early in the game too. With that, here is a projection before any Seattle Seahawks preseason games have even started. Quarterback (3) Keep: Sam Darnold, Drew Lock, Jalen Milroe Cut: N/A Just like last season, it looks like Seattle will keep all three quarterbacks on roster. Seeing how Milroe does in the preseason games will be the biggest thing to keep an eye on. Could he perhaps play well enough to become a trade target for other teams? However, if he plays that well, the Seahawks may just want to keep him. Running back (3) Keep: Jadarian Price, George Holani, Emanuel Wilson PUP: Zach Charbonnet Cut: Velus Jones, Jacardia Wright, TJ Harden, Justin Jones Although there has been positive injury news for Charbonnet , it makes little sense to rush him back and take up a roster spot on an already difficult roster to cut down. Price, Holani, and Wilson seem to be locks to make this roster. Jones is an intriguing name to watch considering his flexibility to play wide receiver and in the return game. He and Wright should hopefully be able to survive the waiver wire and make it back to the practice squad. Fullback (2) Keep: Robbie Ouzts, Brady Russell Cut: Brocke Lampe Ouzts’ injury is a tough one. If he is out for much longer, he may enter the roster bubble territory – if he isn’t already there. Until there’s more clarity on his injury, he is a keep for now considering offensive coordinator Brian Fleury’s use of the position. Tight End (4) Keep: AJ Barner, Elijah Arroyo, Eric Saubert, Nick Kallerup Cut: Nick Vannett Speaking of Brian Fleury, he also loves the tight end position. The issue is, he isn’t alone in his love of the position. This era of the NFL is all about heavy personnel sets. This is why this projection has Seattle keeping four tight ends in addition to the two fullbacks. It seems too risky for the Seahawks to let go of a Saubert or Kallerup – two solid blocking tight ends. Wide Receiver (6) Keep: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Cooper Kupp, Rashid Shaheed, Tory Horton, Jake Bobo, Emmanuel Henderson Cut: Montorie Foster Jr., Ricky White III, Irv Charles, Cody White, Rashad Rochelle JSN, Kupp, Shaheed, Horton, Bobo are virtual locks. The question then becomes whether Seattle keeps any more receivers on top of those five. With Seattle going heavy at the FB/TE position, it could mean that they go light at WR. However, word out of camp is that the likes of Montorie Foster Jr. and Ricky White III are making that a difficult decision. There are legitimate arguments to keep most of the receivers on this roster. The question really becomes special teams’ ability and likelihood of losing these receivers on waivers. With those two considerations, I am keeping 6 th round pick, Emmanuel Henderson Jr. His speed and return ability make it a risky proposition to cut him. If Irv Charles shows his gunner ability in the preseason, he could also make a push for this last spot as well. Overall, receiver is one of the tougher positions to project. Offensive Line (9) Keep: Charles Cross, Grey Zabel, Jalen Sundell, Anthony Bradford, Abe Lucas, Josh Jones, Mason Richman, Beau Stephens, Logan Brown Cut: Amari Kight, Bryce Cabeldue, Olu Oluwatimi (Trade Candidate), Federico Maranges, Christian Haynes (Trade Candidate), Bobby Hart The Seahawks have some legitimate depth on this offensive line. That makes it even harder to project who makes the roster and who doesn’t. Oluwatimi and Haynes could be trade targets (similar to Mike Jarrell last season). The decision to keep Richman over Oluwatimi as backup center here is not necessarily because Richman is better, but rather due to club control. Oluwatimi is entering the last season on his rookie deal while Richman still has three years left on his deal. Cabeldue was a tough cut as well, one who hopefully survives waivers. Keeping Logan Brown gives Seattle a young tackle option – it will be interesting to see the battle between him and Amari Kight to see if either can make the 53-man roster. However, if Oluwatimi doesn’t end up being traded, they may not keep Kight or Brown. In that case, Oluwatimi and Richman would both make the roster, knowing that Richman can play tackle in a pinch. Defensive Line (5 ) Keep: Leonard Williams, Byron Murphy II, Jarran Reed, Rylie Mills, Brandon Pili Cut: Mike Morris, Deven Eastern, JR Singleton, Uso Seumalo, Bubba Thomas The conversation here is whether some of the back of the roster players like Morris and Eastern can do enough to justify keeping them on the 53-man roster. The other question is whether Seattle thinks they can survive waivers. Similar to Oluwatimi, Morris is entering his final year of his rookie deal which is what makes it more palatable to waive him. I project to keep Pili here as well despite the thought process that a veteran like him can sneak past waivers. The risk of losing Pili is too great to take since he is one of the only true nose tackles that Seattle has on their roster. If Eastern can push him for a roster spot, then Pili could be on the outs as well. Outside Linebacker (4) Keep: Demarcus Lawrence, Derick Hall, Uchenna Nwosu, Dante Fowler Jr. Cut: Connor O’Toole, Jared Ivey, Jamie Sherriff, Jalen Gaines, Aidan Hubbard, Marvin Jones Jr. Cutting O’Toole and Ivey is a tough decision here. Seattle would surely pray they can make it past waivers. The same argument can be had for Sherriff, although he likely has a better shot considering he has done so in the past. As will be discussed below, the larger number of defensive backs kept make it difficult to keep a fifth edge. The potential for Nick Emmanwori (and potentially Tyrice Knight) to play the edge also allows the Seahawks some more flexibility. Inside Linebacker (3) Keep: Ernest Jones IV, Drake Thomas, Tyrice Knight Cut: Chaz Surratt, Patrick O’Connell, Chris Paul Like outside linebacker, staying heavy at defensive back makes other positions thinner. O’Connell has survived waivers before; Seattle likely hopes that remains the case in 2026. Paul was a waiver claim by Seattle after the Los Angeles Rams cut him last offseason. That makes letting go of him a potential risk. Surratt is an interesting bottom of the roster discussion as well considering his impact on special teams. Defensive Backs (11 ) Keep: CB (6): Devon Witherspoon, Josh Jobe, Nehemiah Pritchett, Julian Neal, Noah Igbinoghene, Michael Dansby Nickel (2): Nick Emmanwori, D’Anthony Bell Safety: (3) Julian Love, Ty Okada, Bud Clark Cut: Rodney Thomas II, Andre Fuller, AJ Finley, Maxen Hook, Shemar Jean-Charles, Jordan Washington I decided to place all the defensive backs in one group because of how positionless this group can play. The real question in this group are whether certain veterans like D’Anthony Bell, Rodney Thomas II, and Noah Igbinoghene could survive waivers. Considering Emmanwori’s current injury and the fact that Bell has been his replacement as nickel, Bell makes the roster in this projection. Waiving Thomas is a risk, however Seattle will still have five players who can play safety (Love, Okada, Clark, Emmanwori, and Bell). At cornerback, both 7 th round rookies (Fuller and Dansby) have impressed. This makes this position very tough to project. Witherspoon, Jobe, and Neal are certain locks. The way Pritchett has looked in camp likely makes him a lock as well. The question really becomes whether the rookies have impressed enough for Seattle to feel comfortable putting a veteran like Igbinoghene on waivers. In this projection I don’t have that happening just yet. Dansby makes it over Fuller due to his freakish athleticism. Entering the draft process Dansby was unable to workout at all causing him to be a big question mark. However, that question mark seems to be going away with the way he has looked in camp (including his ability to cause turnovers). This makes me worry that he would be lost on…
