title: Forget the top 100, how many Seahawks make the NFL’s top 1000 players?
summary: The 2026 NFL Season is nearly here. Until then, it still remains rankings season. A fun one that recently came out is from Bleacher Report (B/R), who ranked the top 1,000 players in the league. This is an interesting ranking since most rankings only go up to 100. With a significantly larger number, there naturally […]
full_text: The 2026 NFL Season is nearly here. Until then, it still remains rankings season. A fun one that recently came out is from Bleacher Report (B/R), who ranked the top 1,000 players in the league . This is an interesting ranking since most rankings only go up to 100. With a significantly larger number, there naturally will be more Seahawks on the list to react to. With that being said, let’s see which Seattle players made the list (as well as which categories BR put them in). Backup, developmental #946: cornerback, Noah Igbinoghene (CB111) #937: fullback, Brady Russell (FB7) #890: running back, Emanuel Wilson (RB64) Some players on the bottom of the list were eye opening. It is interesting that Igbinoghene made the list over another Seattle corner, Nehemiah Pritchett. Could he potentially be getting a former first round pick bump? Russell getting ranked is also fascinating, especially since BR’s reasoning had nothing to do with his special teams’ ability. Could the recent Robbie Ouzts injury open an opportunity for Russell to play more offensive snaps? Wilson being ranked is another fun one. It will be fun to see how he plays into the running back snap count this season. Replacement Level #864: kicker, Jason Myers (K10) #835: wide receiver, Tory Horton (WR116) #786: running back, Zach Charbonnet (RB50) #770: tight end, Elijah Arroyo (TE63) #752: right guard, Anthony Bradford (RG22) The biggest gripe with this group is the fact that Jason Myers is considered “replacement level.” The fact that he is ranked the 10 th best kicker in the league is asinine. That being said, it is nice to see Horton getting some love despite an injury plagued second half of 2025. However, after watching his rookie campaign, it feels like he should be ranked higher than Arroyo. It will be interesting to see how much Charbonnet contributes after he returns from injury. I personally believe if he was given the opportunity to be a sole starting RB (rather than in a committee), he would be ranked much higher on many lists. Arroyo being this high is also eye opening considering his low stats from 2025. Although, word out of training camp is that he is in for an impressive 2026 campaign . Of the five starting offensive lineman for Seattle, Bradford is ranked the lowest. That isn’t too surprising. Being the 22 nd ranked right guard in the league feels about right as well. Functional Performer #600: center, Jalen Sundell (C17) #556: defensive lineman, Jarran Reed (DL52) #526: edge, Dante Fowler Jr. (Edge56) #514: safety, Ty Okada (S55) #494: punter, Michael Dickson (P1) #488: edge, Uchenna Nwosu (Edge50) If you were to list the five Seahawks starting lineman, putting Sundell at fourth seems right. Although it could be argued he should be ranked higher than the 17 th best center, it is nice to see an outside source giving him some love. Reed and Fowler on this list next to each other is fascinating, as well. Between the two, many Seahawk fans would likely prefer Reed. However, it wouldn’t be surprising to see Fowler have another breakout season under Mike Macdonald. Okada nearly making the top 500 is fun to see, although there could be gripes that he deserves to be ranked higher than the 55 th best safety. Speaking of top 500, Dickson is the highest ranked punter and one of only three specialists inside the top 500. Nwosu gets some love as well after a healthy 2025 season. Reliable Contributor #481: fullback, Robbie Ouzts (FB4) #457: cornerback, Josh Jobe (CB67) #423: linebacker, Drake Thomas (LB41) #398: edge, Derick Hall (Edge39) #320: wide receiver, Cooper Kupp (WR43) #306: right tackle, Abraham Lucas (RT10) #296: edge, Demarcus Lawrence (Edge26) Seattle’s other fullback makes an appearance in the top 500. Hopefully Ouzts can get healthy so he can get himself higher on the list next season. Jobe makes an appearance, although it feels too early, especially considering that BR ranks Riq Woolen at 198 and as the 28 th best cornerback. Thomas coming in as the 41 st best linebacker also seems too low. 2026 should have him vaulting up this list. The newly paid Hall makes an appearance as edge 39, while Lawrence comes in as edge 26. The fact that Mike Macdonald deploys a defense where no one edge defender accumulates a significant amount of sacks is perhaps hurting Seattle’s edges in this ranking. Kupp coming in as the 43 rd best receiver would place him as a WR3 on a team. However, the word out of training camp is that he is in for a potentially big 2026 . Lucas coming in at RT10 and as the third best lineman for the Seahawks is fascinating. Although Zabel had an impressive rookie campaign, there could be an argument that he has not surpassed Lucas just yet. Critical Roster Piece #271: wide receiver, Rashid Shaheed (WR36) #263: left guard, Grey Zabel (LG8) #233: left tackle, Charles Cross (LT11) #231: tight end, AJ Barner (TE19) #217: linebacker, Ernest Jones IV (LB13) Shaheed is a tough one to rank considering his 2025 campaign was full of splashy plays mostly on special teams. That being said, he should be in for a better offensive campaign in 2026 now that he has a full offseason with Sam Darnold. As mentioned above, Zabel had an impressive rookie campaign. It will be fun to see how high his ceiling really is. Cross coming in as LT11 is right in line with how the league has viewed him so far; a “critical roster piece” but one just outside the Pro-Bowl level (whatever that means now). The Seahawks being regularly underrated in rankings comes up a lot. However, it stands out especially here with Barner being the 19 th best tight end and Jones being the 13 th best linebacker. Both are criminally under ranked here. High-quality starter #140: cornerback, Nick Emmanwori (CB18) #120: defensive lineman, Byron Murphy II (DL10) #111: quarterback, Sam Darnold (QB15) #94: safety, Julian Love (S11) #85: defensive lineman, Leonard Williams (DL7) Jalen Carter (78), Cameron Heyward (73), Dexter Lawrence (59), Jeffery Simmons (56), Vita Vea (51), Quinnen Williams (48) This is where we enter the “big dogs” of the league. Emmanwori being ranked as a corner is fun to see, especially considering how much he lined up as the big nickel. B/R ranked cornerbacks in an overall sense but also ranked them as boundaries or nickels. For Emmanwori they ranked him as the 6 th best nickelback in the league, which seems too low for my liking. Murphy will surely catapult up this list as he seems to be on the precipice of a breakout 2026 campaign. Ranking quarterbacks is always a dangerous task to do. There have been offseason rankings showing Darnold all over the place. Placing him as the 15 th best quarterback seems like a safe way out for B/R. Despite an injury ridden 2025, Love is still feeling the “Love.” It will be interesting to see how he fares with a (hopefully) healthy 2026 season. Speaking of criminally underrated, here comes Leonard Williams. The players listed underneath him were all ranked ahead of “Big Cat.” Not sure I would take any of those guys before Williams. Pro Bowl Caliber #43: cornerback, Devon Witherspoon (CB6) Denzel Ward (41), Christian Gonzalez (37), Derek Stingley (30), Derwin James (18), Patrick Surtain (10) Despite being ranked as the sixth best cornerback, Witherspoon will very likely be resetting the cornerback market once he is paid. Witherspoon’s game doesn’t have the big stats that lots of lay-viewers look for. But anyone who watched Seattle’s defense can easily tell you how much of an impact he has – physically, mentally, and emotionally. He is a force multiplier whose absence is quickly felt (just look at the loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last season). All-Pro Ability #17: wide receiver, Jaxon Smith-Njigba (WR3) Justin Jefferson (11), Ja’Marr Chase (3) To nobody’s surprise, JSN comes in as the highest ranked Seahawk on BR’s list. JSN’s 2025 campaign not only won him the offensive player of the year award, but it also set some franchise records . After putting up 1,793 yards and…

full_text: SEATTLE - SEPTEMBER 04: Richard Sherman #25 of the Seattle Seahawks lines up on defense against the Green Bay Packers at CenturyLink Field on September 4, 2014 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jonathan Ferrey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ummm, yeah. I mean, duh. Let me be more specific: if this was the Baseball Hall of Fame, Richard Sherman would be a first ballot HOF’er, no question. As most any Seattle Seahawks fan will tell you, Sherman (with the help of Pete Carroll, et al) revolutionized the CB position. His command of the field, the position, and the opposition itself are literally concrete and formidable reasons to enshrine this fella and give him all the flowers, and the seeds. But, be wary. Even Coach Mike Holmgren, a legend before Sherman’s time, has yet to be enshrined, which is functionally absurd. title: 49ers News: Camp highlights are cool… Now do it against TEN
summary: 49ers guard Dominick Puni wondered if he’d peaked. Then he found a fix (paywall)“A coach tells you, ‘Man, if you keep doing that, you’re probably not going to get away with it much longer,’” Puni said. “But if it’s working, in my head, you’re just going to keep doing it. It’s hard to listen when […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - MARCH 21: Robert Saleh and head coach of the Wildcats FFC, Kyle Shanahan look on during the Fanatics Flag Football Classic at BMO Stadium on March 21, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images for for OBB Media - FANATICS STUDIOS) | Getty Images for for OBB Media - 49ers guard Dominick Puni wondered if he’d peaked. Then he found a fix (paywall) “A coach tells you, ‘Man, if you keep doing that, you’re probably not going to get away with it much longer,’” Puni said. “But if it’s working, in my head, you’re just going to keep doing it. It’s hard to listen when something’s working.” Once defensive tackles began beating him, the message landed. Puni embraced Foerster’s coaching and reversed his slide. “I found something later in the season, attacked it in the offseason and worked with coach Foerster,” Puni said. “We’ve been getting better at it ever since. I feel a lot more comfortable knowing I have a technique I can go to.” 49ers-Titans joint practice sets up clashes with Cam Ward, Robert Saleh and an All-Pro DT (paywall) “Morris and his sticky corners soon face their first true test across from blue-chip wide receiver Carnell Tate, whom the Titans drafted No. 4 overall out of Ohio State. Tate, the first wideout taken in April, reportedly caught three touchdowns passes in a given practice over the weekend. The quarterback throwing to him, of course, was Cam Ward, the No. 1 overall pick last April. The 49ers have a competitive cohort of cornerbacks. They make plays and let you know about it. Tuesday will be a telling clash. “Every now and then, I’ll try and poke at them to see if I can poke the bear … it kind of gets them going,” defensive backs coach Ray Brown said.” Aloha, Mr. Hands: 49ers cornerbacks dissect De’Zhaun Stribling’s strong start (paywall) “I would say him just catching away from his body, just kind of trusting his hands,” Lenoir said of Stribling’s strength. “He’s got that catch radius where he’s gonna catch it away from his body. He’s got strong fingertips.” ….Lining up at the F or slot position has created regular matchups with Stout, who’s also having a strong camp. He and the other cornerbacks have more license to play aggressively this year, which suits their styles and has led to plenty of tipped passes and incompletions in the middle of the field. That close coverage has vexed receivers like Jacob Cowing and Jordan Watkins, with Watkins in particular having an issue with contested catches early in training camp. But Stribling has looked confident with a cornerback or safety draped over his back. “He’s going to be a dog,” Stout said. Rising coach on 49ers’ staff? Former Seahawk K.J. Wright “Saleh says linebacker coaches need to know the entirety of the defense, the importance of communication and how pass rush and coverage work together, which gives them a leg up on other defensive coaches aiming to become coordinators. He calls it a “global understanding” that can be hard to gain from other positions. When Saleh left the Niners the first time in 2021, Ryans was the easy choice to replace him. If Morris, who has been a head coach twice, gets San Francisco’s defense back to previous levels, it’s not out of the question he could get another opportunity in the coming years. For now, Wright says he is only thinking of his current job and not the future.” The Good and Not So Good from Day 10 of 49ers Camp: McCaffrey Out with Tightness “Every day, Dugger bats down a pass in this drill. He’s a work in progress, but he already shows so much potential in coverage, which makes sense, considering he’s huge and a former safety.….All things considered, that’s a good day for Purdy. He’s working with a bunch of backups he barely knows, and he’s still playing well.” Undrafted rookie wide receiver Will Pauling vying for role with uncertain 49ers “The 49ers demand that their receivers are willing and effective blockers, and Pauling has turned heads. “No matter if he’s going up against a D-end, a linebacker, or a DB, he’s been sustaining blocks,” Hankerson said. “And that shows up a lot.” Pauling had 155 receptions for 1,753 yards and 15 touchdowns in his 48-game college career that began at Cincinnati in 2021. At the very least, he appears to be a strong candidate to stick around on the 49ers practice squad. But that is only if he does not make the 49ers’ regular-season roster or another team does not claim him.” Offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak shares updates ahead of 49ers-Titans preseason game “San Francisco 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak spoke with reporters after Monday’s training camp practice as the team gears up for its preseason game against the Tennessee Titans. Here’s everything he had to say.” 49ers bubble watch: One rookie whose job is in jeopardy “On Monday morning, the Patriots released offensive tackle Caedan Wallace, a third-round pick from the 2024 NFL Draft. Wallace’s rookie year was derailed by an ankle injury that landed him on the Injured Reserve. He’s played sparingly through two seasons and will look for a fresh start. If you’re the 49ers, you see the fourth pick of the third round two years ago. He’s 6’5”, 314 pounds with hand size (90th percentile) and broad jump (96th percentile) that you covet. The 49ers’ depth is so depleted that they are using Austen Pleasants at guard and have a forever camp body in Brandon Parker at tackle. One man’s trash is another man’s treasure, and in this instance, a player like Wallace could be just what the team needs to upgrade. During August, there may not be draft “busts” like Wallace available, but there will be plenty of different talents who could make the Niners think twice about Cruz Jr. Or at the very least, bring that player in to give one of the backups, like Cruz Jr., a run for their money.”
author: Yinon Raviv

title: 49ers hold tryouts for 2 running backs; have a visit with another who ran a 4.39 40-yard dash
summary: The San Francisco 49ers held tryouts for running backs Nyheim Miller-Hines and Zamir White on Monday, per the NFL’s transaction wire. They also hosted running back Blake Watson on a visit. This comes after the Niners were without Christian McCaffrey on Monday, as he sat out of practice due to tightness. With a joint practice […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 09: Blake Watson #25 of the Denver Broncos fights off the tackle of Jakob Robinson #49 of the San Francisco 49ers in second half of an NFL Preseason 2025 game at Levi's Stadium on August 09, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers held tryouts for running backs Nyheim Miller-Hines and Zamir White on Monday, per the NFL’s transaction wire. They also hosted running back Blake Watson on a visit. This comes after the Niners were without Christian McCaffrey on Monday, as he sat out of practice due to tightness . With a joint practice and a preseason game this week, it’s unlikely we’ll see any of the 49ers’ top four backs in action. With that in mind, San Francisco will need capable bodies in the backfield. Miller-Hines is a name that everyone is aware of. He was a fourth-round pick in the 2018 NFL Draft. He spent his first five seasons with the Colts. His career was derailed by an offseason injury in July 2023 when Miller-Hines tore his ACL and LCL in a jet ski accident. He was with the Chargers and the Saints last season, but only managed three total touches. Miller-Hines turns 30 in November. White was a fourth-round pick of the Raiders in 2022. His most productive season was in 2023, when White ran for 451 yards and had 98 receiving yards. White, 26, only had 12 carries for Las Vegas last year. He’s 6’, 215 pounds. It wouldn’t be surprising to see the team announce the signing of Watson on Tuesday morning, given the fact that he was on an actual visit. Watson was an undrafted free agent out of the 2024 NFL Draft. His speed is something every team covets. During Memphis’s Pro Day in March 2024, Watson ran a 4.39 40-yard dash with a 41.5-inch vertical jump and an 11-foot-3-inch broad jump. Each of those numbers is in the 90th percentile. That plays. Watson would have quite the opportunity with a banged-up depth chart to sneak onto the roster, or at the very least, stick around on the practice squad, if he signs and can show anything in the preseason. Last preseason, Watson had a couple of chunk plays against the 49ers. He had a 16-yard reception after making Nick Martin miss. He also had an 18-yarder after breaking a tackle from Martin. So, he was likely on San Francisco’s radar. Earlier on Monday, offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said, “anytime guys are out, it lets guys step up and gives them opportunities.” McCaffrey, Jordan James, Kaelon Black, and Isaac Guerendo are currently out. So that leaves Patrick Taylor Jr., Sincere McCormick, and Khalil Herbert as the only healthy backs on the roster. The door is open for Watson, Miller-Hines, White, or any free agent back to make a name for themselves.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers training camp battles: Left guard is ‘definitely an open competition’
summary: San Francisco 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak was asked about the left guard spot after Monday’s practice. Connor Colby lined up with the first team during the first block of practices. Since then, it’s been Robert Jones. According to Kubiak, it’s “definitely still an open competition. Those guys are going to compete all camp.” Kubiak […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JUNE 03: Robert Jones #65 of the San Francisco 49ers looks on during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on June 3, 2026 in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images San Francisco 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak was asked about the left guard spot after Monday’s practice. Connor Colby lined up with the first team during the first block of practices. Since then, it’s been Robert Jones. According to Kubiak, it’s “definitely still an open competition. Those guys are going to compete all camp.” Kubiak acknowledged that both Colby and Jones are going to play in the preseason “a lot” and the competition will resolve itself. Kubiak also said just because Colby was up first didn’t mean it was his job to lose, saying, “it’s no slight on Connor” and “I don’t think we said, ‘whoever is in there the first day is going to take it all the way.’” Kubiak didn’t mention Carver Willis, who has also been rotating with the second-team at left guard. We’ll see if the rookie has a say in this competition, or if it’s between Jones and Colby. Marques Sigle beefs up Second-year safety Marques Sigle looks locked in as a starter at safety. There was a rotation, but with Malik Mustapha out, it’s been Sigle and Ji’Ayir Brown. At the podium on Monday, Sigle said all of the cliches about new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris. “He’s allowing us to be more aggressive, play to our skill set.” “It’s making us not think and allowing us to be playmakers. I feel like that’s better for us. We have the type of guys to go out and play and not react.” Sigle said the gap in between the middle of the season before returning for the Eagles game allowed him to learn what he needed to work on. He said what most of us saw: “I feel like I was in the right spot, but had to make the play. So that mindset in practice and in film study is to be one step ahead instead of one step behind.” Sigle put on 8 to 10 pounds since the end of last season: “I just felt it was better for my skill set, and being more of a true safety. Just for blocks, dealing with tight ends, being more physical. And be at a weight where I can still keep my speed.” Sigle said one of the main things he worked on this offseason was getting in and out of his breaks. He’s been stealing traits from each of his teammates in an effort to improve: “RG[Renardo Green], just how he plays man and how aggressive he is. D-Mo, just how smart he is with the break points. Ji’Ayir Brown, just how he gets out of his breaks in the post. Malik Mustapha, just how he’s in and out of his breaks. Throughout the whole offseason, I just took one piece from each guy.” We’ve heard nothing but positive remarks about the secondary early on in camp. But that’s also been without the majority of the top wideouts. We will learn more through the preseason, and of course, in Week 1 against one of the most prolific offenses in the NFL.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers’ Christian McCaffrey is sitting out of practice due to ‘tightness’; Deebo Samuel gets running back reps
summary: It’s Monday, and the San Francisco 49ers are returning to the practice field. It’s a big week, as it’s officially preseason. The team will hold a joint practice on Tuesday and then a glorified scrimmage for their first preseason game Thursday. One player we’re unlikely to see is running back Christian McCaffrey. And that was […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: Christian McCaffrey #23 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s Monday, and the San Francisco 49ers are returning to the practice field. It’s a big week, as it’s officially preseason. The team will hold a joint practice on Tuesday and then a glorified scrimmage for their first preseason game Thursday. One player we’re unlikely to see is running back Christian McCaffrey. And that was before he sat out of Monday’s practice due to “tightness.” That could mean several different things, so we won’t speculate until the team provides accurate information. McCaffrey was already on a rep count according to Chris Foerster. Kyle’s update, 12:20 p.m. PT: Offensive Coordinator Klay Kubiak was asked how different this camp is for McCaffrey compared to previous ones: “I wouldn’t say much. Christian has always had his rep count in any camp. You guys are aware of the adjustments we’ve made to our schedule to keep them from having too many off days. In terms of his rep load, we’re right on track for where we wanna be. He’s a veteran player. You have to monitor him and get him ready for the first week.“ As far as McCaffrey’s injury, Kubiak said, “Just managing. He’s doing fine. Just managing as we go.” That means the top four backs aren’t on the practice field with McCaffrey, Jordan James, Kaelon Black, and Isaac Guerendo sidelined. That leaves Sincere McCormick, Patrick Taylor Jr., and Khalil Herbert. You know Kyle Juszczyk is itching to line up at running back. Kubiak said the injuries to the running backs are twofold. On the one hand, “it sucks, because you want those young guys out there. You want to see them compete and get better. Those guys will get out there. They’re not far away. But it’s giving guys opportunities to get better, too. You talk about guys like Patrick Taylor, Sincere McCormick, Khalil [Herbert], who we brought in. Gives us a chance to give Deebo in there and get some touches. Anytime guys are out, it lets guys step up and get opportunities. We’re looking forward to having those guys back, too.” Nick Bosa also missed his fourth straight practice due to “soreness.” It seemed like Bosa was progressing toward returning. On Saturday, Kyle Shanahan said there’s no reason to be concerned about Bosa’s absence: “No. He was doing great, and then he got sore just going through some of the individual. You wish that didn’t happen, but no, there’s no concern to where something’s happened that is a big setback or anything. We’ll wait until the soreness goes away and evaluate why the soreness has happened, but I still feel pretty good about that.” Wide receivers Mike Evans and Christian Kirk remain out, while De’Zhaun Stribling returned. Rookie Carver Willis has cleared the concussion protocol and returned to practice. He’s lining up at left guard with the second-team, while Robert Jones continues to play with the starters. It looks like Connor Colby’s demotion isn’t temporary, as he’s been a second-team right guard the majority of the time. Klay Kubiak is scheduled to speak after practice, so it’s unlikely there will be any updates on the injury front.

title: 49ers bubble watch: One rookie whose job is in jeopardy
summary: You can watch all of the college film, ask their coaches, and dig into their background, but you’ll never know the kind of prospect you’re getting until they are in your building. In the case of San Francisco 49ers fifth-round pick Enrique Cruz Jr., he’ll need a strong preseason to make the roster. Is Enrique […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JUNE 03: Enrique Cruz Jr. #69 and Carver Willis #74 of the San Francisco 49ers run a drill during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on June 3, 2026 in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images You can watch all of the college film, ask their coaches, and dig into their background, but you’ll never know the kind of prospect you’re getting until they are in your building. In the case of San Francisco 49ers fifth-round pick Enrique Cruz Jr., he’ll need a strong preseason to make the roster. Is Enrique Cruz Jr. in jeopardy of being cut? The next positive information to come out of the 49ers camp about Cruz Jr. will be the first. The 49ers used a fifth-round pick on a player some teams were planning on bringing in as a priority free agent after the draft. Unsurprisingly, Cruz Jr. looked like an undrafted free agent in camp. Whether it’s a 1-on-1 or a team setting, reports about the 49ers rookie have been consistent. His hand placement is erratic, and he cannot stay in front of anybody. It’s one thing to lose a rep to Romello Height in a 1-on-1 setting. Height is a speedster, and those drills are built for him. Still, not getting a hand on Height should’ve been a cautionary tale. With that said, Cruz is losing to the likes of players the Niners just signed off the street, like Titus Leo, Ogbo Okoronwko, and Quinton Bell during practice. The 49ers’ offensive line has supposedly left a lot to be desired in camp. Cruz Jr. isn’t alone. So when you hear about defensive linemen shining, there’s an asterisk attached to that: They’re likely going against a backup or somebody playing out of position. Ego could save Cruz Jr. if he continues to look lost during the preseason. Then again, the Niners haven’t had an issue moving off draft picks they felt didn’t belong or weren’t their type. Giving up on Cruz Jr. would have to be more about his skill. It would involve work ethic, lack of progression, and what’s available on the market, which brings us to our next point. All eyes on the waiver wire On Monday morning, the Patriots released offensive tackle Caedan Wallace, a third-round pick from the 2024 NFL Draft. Wallace’s rookie year was derailed by an ankle injury that landed him on the Injured Reserve. He’s played sparingly through two seasons and will look for a fresh start. If you’re the 49ers, you see the fourth pick of the third round two years ago. He’s 6’5″, 314 pounds with hand size (90th percentile) and broad jump (96th percentile) that you covet. The 49ers’ depth is so depleted that they are using Austen Pleasants at guard and have a forever camp body in Brandon Parker at tackle. One man’s trash is another man’s treasure, and in this instance, a player like Wallace could be just what the team needs to upgrade. During August, there may not be draft “busts” like Wallace available, but there will be plenty of different talents who could make the Niners think twice about Cruz Jr. Or at the very least, bring that player in to give one of the backups, like Cruz Jr., a run for their money.

title: Kyle Shanahan reveals 49ers plan at WR without Ricky Pearsall
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have been quite banged up with injuries during training camp this offseason, but none were more significant than Ricky Pearsall’s nagging PCL injury that is now expected to cost him the rest of the 2026 season. Pearsall’s early career has unfortunately been marred by injuries to this point, and his loss […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have been quite banged up with injuries during training camp this offseason, but none were more significant than Ricky Pearsall’s nagging PCL injury that is now expected to cost him the rest of the 2026 season. Pearsall’s early career has unfortunately been marred by injuries to this point, and his loss is a huge blow for the 49ers, given what they wanted to do on offense this season. It makes sense why. Pearsall was the one difference in the 49ers receiving room. They had big-bodied threats that could either win at the catch point extremely well (Mike Evans) or work after the catch (De’Zhaun Stribling). Christian Kirk and Deebo Samuel both felt like options that could work better in the short to intermediate range of the field and have the ball in their hands as well. San Francisco’s 2024 first-round pick hasn’t been that type of player. Instead, Pearsall has been much more of a man-coverage beater, winning on outside routes when facing 1-on-1 coverage, which has been a huge asset for Kyle Shanahan’s offense when the wideout is on the field. Now, without him, the 49ers are going to have to change up their plans at receiver, which Kyle Shanahan acknowledged on Saturday when talking to the media for the first time since his July car accident. “Losing Ricky was a real big deal. We’ve had a number of injuries in camp, but that’s really the only one that’s actually been not just a camp injury,” Shanahan said. “Losing a player like Ricky is a huge deal. It ties to everybody. You hope for [De’Zhaun] Stribling, you hope for Mike [Evans], you hope for that whole group. A lot of people have to step up, but no one here is wired exactly how Ricky is. They’re all a little bit different. “So, you do lose a big part of what we were planning on. That’s where guys do have to step up. That’s what gets frustrating when guys like Stribling tweak a muscle and stuff, because, yeah, you want guys to step up, but you’ve got to train them to do it. They’ve got to work to do it. They’ve got to be out there to be able to do it at an NFL level, which is coming real fast.” Now, the early indications from camp before Stribling’s recent minor injury were positive, so it seems like he could be ready to contribute sooner rather than later. And Samuel obviously has a good grasp of the offense and should fit in well. But without Pearsall, the 49ers will have to find different ways to win against man coverage. And that might put even more expectations on Mike Evans, who dealt with an injury-riddled campaign in 2025, and is currently nursing a quad injury. “Yeah, [Evans’s expectations] depends if he stays healthy,” Shanahan said. “Mike, to me, is always, if you’re a starting receiver, you’re out there a ton, which everyone is. I forget what it was last year, maybe hamstring, where he missed time, and when that happens you miss games. “But Mike’s going to be a starting receiver here, and we don’t like any of our guys to go every play. We want our guys going full speed, and it’s hard to go full speed every play. So, we’re always going to spell guys. But hopefully, he’s got a little quad right now, which I know Mike probably believes he could be back right now. We’re being smart with him, but he’s going to be good to go.” The 49ers have consistently produced quality offenses, and they’ll hope that 2026 is the same. But losing Pearsall was certainly a big blow for their passing game.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: Kyle Shanahan on the 49ers’ high injury count: ‘It feels pretty normal’
summary: San Francisco 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak shared the benefits of the team changing up their practice schedule as training camp was underway a week and a half ago. Head coach Kyle Shanahan spoke to the media on Saturday and was asked about the injuries and the practice schedule. Chris Foerster said the team was […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - DECEMBER 22: San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan exits the field after an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on December 22, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images San Francisco 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak shared the benefits of the team changing up their practice schedule as training camp was underway a week and a half ago. Head coach Kyle Shanahan spoke to the media on Saturday and was asked about the injuries and the practice schedule. Chris Foerster said the team was healthy . The 49ers have been pretty banged up for the second straight year in training camp. When Shanahan was asked whether it felt like a lot or if the team was minding the camp injuries to make it through, he said: “It feels pretty normal, give or take three. I think it does happen a number of times in camp. We also have a number of guys coming into camp that didn’t go on PUP that we weren’t trying to throw back in there right away. And that stuff’s always frustrating. That’s why you sometimes want it a little bit longer, but the thing that frustrates you the most is when you lose a guy, and there’s one guy like that right now, which we’ve had to grieve for a little bit. Then you’ve got to figure out how to adjust and move on from it.” Shanahan is referring to Ricky Pearsall. He said, “Losing Ricky was a real big deal. We’ve had a number of injuries in camp, but that’s really the only one that’s actually been not just a camp injury. Losing a player like Ricky is a huge deal. It ties to everybody. A lot of people have to step up, but no one here is wired exactly how Ricky is. So you do lose a big part of what we were planning on.” Shanahan was talking about how Pearsall and Deebo Samuel are completely different skill-set-wise, and that’s not a 1-for-1 swap. It’s hard to imagine Deebo filling the same role as Ricky. Samuel was never the type to beat press coverage consistently or stretch the field vertically. As for the practice schedule, the 49ers have a jog-through to break up their practice blocks and avoid going three days in a row. In Shanahan’s mind, it makes sense “science-wise.” “We used to go three days on and take one full day off and then go three days on again. We look into everything, and we thought that it would be better for us this year to never go three full days in a row. But, if you only go two full days in a row and then take a day off, you don’t really build anything. So, we thought it’d be better to go two full days full speed, then have a kind of mental day where they’re not totally off their feet. We’re jogging through, no one’s competing, we’re not throwing a football, but they’re still moving their body, which kind of is a little bit of a recovery. And then the fourth day you get our hardest practice of that set and then you get a day off. So, it ends up being about the same, just trying a different way on how you juggle it. It makes sense science-wise and everything, but there’s a lot more that goes into it than just science.” Even last week, there still seemed to be an injury, at least per practice. While it’s football, the other 31 teams in the NFL aren’t getting hurt at the same rate.

title: Ranking the Titans’ starting five offensive linemen from best to worst
summary: The Tennessee Titans allowed 56 sacks last season. That was sixth-most in the league. Rookie quarterback Cam Ward was sacked on 55 occasions, tied for the most of any quarterback in 2025. The Titans need to do a significantly better job protecting Ward in 2026. Improving the protection is a big-time priority for offensive coordinator […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans offensive tackle Peter Skoronski (77) heads out for warmups before the game against the Indianapolis Colts at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, Tenn., Sunday, Sept. 21, 2025. | Andrew Nelles / The Tennessean / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans allowed 56 sacks last season. That was sixth-most in the league. Rookie quarterback Cam Ward was sacked on 55 occasions, tied for the most of any quarterback in 2025. The Titans need to do a significantly better job protecting Ward in 2026. Improving the protection is a big-time priority for offensive coordinator Brian Daboll and position coach Carmen Bricillo. Coach Bricillo has a history of helping improve offensive line play after doing so with the New York Giants and Las Vegas Raiders. The Titans made offseason changes at various positions. With that in mind, we’ve ranked the Titans’ five projected starting offensive linemen from best to worst. Peter Skoronski, LG Peter Skoronski is the Titans’ one true elite offensive lineman. The former first-round pick deserves to sign a multi-year contract extension this offseason that makes him one of the highest-paid guards in the NFL. Skoronski is the only offensive lineman on the Titans’ roster they have no concerns about. JC Latham, RT The Titans desperately need JC Latham to be healthy and effective throughout 2026. The top-10 selection possesses massive upside, but hasn’t quite met the full expectations of his potential yet. It’s a massive season for Latham, as the Titans must decide on his fifth-year contract option next offseason. Austin Schlottmann, C The Titans signed Austin Schlottmann in free agency due to his familiarity with Daboll and Bricillo. He’s been a veteran journeyman as a former undrafted free agent, but impressed in four starts for the Giants last season. Schlottmann’s familiarity with the scheme could help him make a smooth transition as the Titans’ starting center. Dan Moore, LT Dan Moore is a league-average left tackle who is consistently available and rarely kills drives. The Titans overpaid him in free agency last campaign, but he wasn’t as bad as some analysts make him out to be. Regardless, the Titans may strongly consider releasing him next offseason once the potential cap savings become available. Cordell Volson/Jackson Slater, RG The Titans are holding a competition at right guard between sophomore Jackson Slater and veteran free-agent signing Cordell Volson. Everyone hopes Slater rises to the occasion, but Volson is a reliable veteran with 48 career starts. Given the mystery factor here, it has to rank as the Titans’ biggest concern on the offensive line until we know more.

title: Commanders News: Offense still sharp in camp with Coleman at left tackle
summary: The Daily Slop – 11 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room […]
full_text: The Daily Slop – 11 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) What can the Commanders expect to get from Brandon Coleman? [I]t’s easy to forget that Coleman actually filled in for Tunsil a few times down the stretch last year and held up relatively well. In the run game, I think Coleman will be absolutely fine. He showed he was a strong run blocker when he started at left tackle in 2024 and even when he struggled at guard last year, he was still good in the run game. The Commanders are expected to become more of an outside zone run team this year and Coleman has the athleticism to play that scheme to a high level. A lot of lineman struggle to make blocks in space because linebackers and defensive backs are more agile than them and can avoid the block, but Coleman uses his momentum and runs over [defensive players], bulldozing [them] to the ground. It shows off incredibly range and athleticism in the run game, which should be a strength for Coleman even as the starting left tackle. But Coleman’s issues as a rookie left tackle weren’t in the run game. His pass protection was inconsistent, often flashing some nice moves but frequently mixed in some poor reps too. Let’s start with the positives first. In 2024, he took on a variety of good pass rushers and had some nice reps against all of them. He was particularly efficient with a hand flash technique that got the better of both Brian Burns and Trey Hendrickson, two of the better pass rushers in the NFL. With star LT Laremy Tunsil injured, the Commanders are likely to turn to Brandon Coleman as his replacement. But what can the Commanders expect to get out of Coleman and how can they help him? I took a closer look: https://t.co/e1cdYdjZnp pic.twitter.com/aoylwFF1TT — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 10, 2026 Commanders.com Commanders confident Coleman can move back to tackle after ‘excellent’ offseason Coleman was the Commanders’ original plan for the position. There was some ambiguity among scouts on his role as an NFL player, but general manager Adam Peters and Quinn felt like he could be a quality tackle because of his size (6-foot-4 ½, 313 pounds), nearly 35-inch arms and smooth footwork. Although he missed some time in training camp, he ended up winning the job and received the seventh-best offensive grade among his fellow rookie offensive tackles from Pro Football Focus. The additions of Tunsil at left tackle and Conerly at right during the 2025 offseason forced Coleman to move to guard, where the Commanders felt he could still contribute because of his physicality in the running game. Coleman…did start the last three games at left tackle and allowed just two pressures on 87 pass blocking snaps. The transition back to tackle, Coleman said, is “kinda like riding a bike.” he looked natural working at the position during Monday’s practice. “We know that he’s ready for it,” Quinn said. “He’s put in an excellent offseason.” The transition from tackle to guard and back has not been a difficult one for Coleman. He tried to stay prepared for any possibility, even taking reps at center, because “you never know what happens. “My feet are good,” Coleman said with a smile, “so being able to dance with those guys, I’m able to keep up. And now that I’m getting my hands under control in terms of knowing where to punch, knowing what I wanna do, that stuff just helps out my feet even more.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic (paywall) Tunsil’s mentoring helped prepare Brandon Coleman to take his place Coleman said moving back to tackle is “like riding a bike” and hasn’t been a difficult transition because of his experience at the position. The more impactful change has come from his work away from the field. He spent much of the offseason in Tuscaloosa, Ala., training alongside Tunsil, who has become a mentor to Coleman and Conerly and invited both down to take part in his offseason training regimen. For several weeks, the three were immersed in Tunsil’s preseason boot camp , which includes on-field work with Tunsil’s personal offensive line coach, Mike Wahle; strength and conditioning work with his longtime strength coach, Dominic Studzinski; nutritional expertise from dietician Jacob Mertens; and customized meals courtesy of Tunsil’s personal chef, Ronald Shaw. For Coleman, the work was about both prepping for the season and learning what it takes to be a top offensive lineman. The Commanders replaced him at left guard last season in part because of nagging injuries that, Coleman believes, could have been prevented with better habits. “There’s priorities that I didn’t do the first couple years that I just had to reflect on and kind of be accountable on,” he said. “I changed that last year, but then even more this year. That’s why I went with Laremy for that month, and dragged my wife out there to Alabama, the middle of nowhere. But she understood. It’s just really seeing how one of the greatest tackles to ever do it does it. Like, how do I need to live to give myself a chance to be like that guy?” Coleman said he’s already incorporated some of Tunsil’s regimen into his own. He now uses Mertens regularly for nutritional guidance. He also hired a local chef to prepare meals, has used the coaching points and techniques Wahle taught him over the summer and started using some of the recovery modalities that helped him in Alabama. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated The Good and Not So Good From Commanders’ Ninth Training Camp Practice Brandon Coleman responded well in his first day replacing Laremy Tunsil, while Jayden Daniels stayed sharp and Washington’s kicking competition took a major step backward It is important to remember that while he is not Tunsil, Washington drafted Coleman to play tackle, and he started there for 12 games during his rookie season before eventually moving inside last year. Coleman’s day was highlighted by holding his own on one rush against Odafe Oweh , carrying him out of the play rather than allowing him to turn the corner. No one is expecting Coleman to miraculously become Tunsil, but the team is desperate for him to be competent enough to secure the spot. Andrew Wylie also received work at left tackle, giving Washington another option behind Coleman, but it’s important to remember that Wylie has only played a handful of snaps at the position in live game action. One name that is not going away on defense is Joshua Josephs, who was able to get his hands on Marcus Mariota for a sack during Monday’s practice. Josephs has repeatedly shown up in padded practices and has me legitimately ready to watch him closely once preseason starts. The proverbial bottom fell out of the kicking competition Monday as Jake Moody went 2-for-6, missing four straight field goals from 44, 49, 51 and 55 yards, while Drew Stevens did not fare much better, going 3-for-6, missing from 39, 51 and 55. Moody has hit a really bad spot now with 11 misses over the last four practices, after starting camp matching Stevens, kick-for-kick . Moody was not alone in having a bad day, as Stevens also posted his worst day of camp, and it was a moment he was not able to capitalize on Moody’s collapse. Moving forward, Stevens still has the advantage based on the larger body of work, but his first truly bad day keeps this from becoming a settled competition before the joint practice and preseason opener. Washington’s offense has now committed six pre-snap penalties over the last two practices, with the latest coming on third down during Monday’s two-minute drill. The reason something like this matters? A third-down penalty during a two-minute situation is exactly the type of procedural mistake that can sabotage an…

title: Commanders training camp: David Blough on Jayden Daniels, Stefon Diggs
summary: New Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough is asking Jayden Daniels to do some different things this year. His new scheme requires Washington to huddle. Daniels will largely start under center, using a system predicated on a strong zone rushing attack and playaction concepts. There’s a ton of pre-snap motions and checks to work through before […]
full_text: New Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough is asking Jayden Daniels to do some different things this year. His new scheme requires Washington to huddle. Daniels will largely start under center, using a system predicated on a strong zone rushing attack and playaction concepts. There’s a ton of pre-snap motions and checks to work through before actually receiving the ball. There’s plenty for the third-year quarterback to handle as compared to Kliff Kingsbury’s system , a fast-paced orchestration that essentially lived in the shotgun. Mistakes are expected with so much new. While growing pains have been experienced, Blough said that Daniels’ transition has been smooth. The results tell him so. “He hasn’t missed a beat,” Blough said during a press conference after Monday’s training camp practice. “We track everything. We’ve tracked every throw he has made over the last three years. We have metrics to measure all of those statistics. He’s as accurate as he has ever been. He has completed as many passes as he ever has. It’s a testament to asking him to do something different and him wanting to grow and evolve. That’s what this is all about for our whole group.” Blough’s full of ideas and concepts he’d like to explore, with more of them than he has time to install. Adjusting to real-time changes might be his biggest challenge to this point, with head coach Dan Quinn keeping Blough and new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones on their toes with unscripted periods of practice that put play callers under pressure. What Blough does with the time allotted will be key to what the Commanders do this season. “I have a lot of ideas and things that I would love to do, but this time is about finding out who we are,” Blough said. “This is about finding out what we do well, what Jayden does well, what the skill guys do, what we can and can’t do up front. There are times where I’m like, ‘Man, I’d like to have a bunch of things in,’ but we’ve gotta pull back and work on the fundamentals and find out who this Commanders offense is. “That has been a process. And we’ve done a lot of call-it periods. There are times when you walk out of practice thinking you were going to get through everything on the sheet and you don’t. Do you go back to it or do you keep pushing ahead? Those are the things I’ve navigated over the last 10 or 11 practices. A lot of lessons, but it has been really good.” Blough also complimented Jones’ attacking defense for “making it as hard as possible,” forcing his players, including Daniels, to think, process and adjust on the fly. “With some of the practices unscripted, we’re seeing some of the creativity come through,” Quinn said in his Monday presser . “I think what you’ll find through his weekly visits is that this is a really good competitor. He’s sharp. He can think quickly. Those are things, as a play caller, that you want to see. If defenses attack a certain way, how are you going to counter punch?” Daniels is most important in those moments, and Blough sees the behind-the-scenes work from this offseason helping the quarterback put the offense in position to succeed. Daniels has the mental acumen to absorb and apply what Blough is teaching and to help the system grow from what it is today. “The version of what you see here won’t be the same offense you see next year,” Blough said. “Everywhere you go, we’ll continue to evolve. I’m proud of him and the work he has put into it to this point, and he hasn’t missed a beat.” David Blough on Stefon Diggs Blough was given another offensive weapon last week in receiver Stefon Diggs, a veteran receiver who instantly upgrades his position group and allows Blough to call some creative things with Diggs on the field. Here are his early impressions of Diggs: “Stefon has played a lot of meaningful football and produced a lot of yards. Through three practices you feel his leadership, too. You feel him bringing the guys together, challenging everybody to keep pushing forward. In just a couple days – he had four catches the other day, at least 2-3 today – the ball finds him because he finds space.” A quick reader poll

title: Commanders injury news: Laremy Tunsil will have surgery on torn triceps
summary: Commanders left tackle Laremy Tunsil tore his triceps. The injury will require surgery. Tunsil will miss significant time.   Head coach Dan Quinn made those facts official before Monday morning’s training camp practice, confirming reports about the worst-case scenario following a Saturday 1-on-1 rep with Odafe Oweh where Tunsil got hurt. While his exact recovery […]
full_text: Commanders left tackle Laremy Tunsil tore his triceps. The injury will require surgery. Tunsil will miss significant time. Head coach Dan Quinn made those facts official before Monday morning’s training camp practice, confirming reports about the worst-case scenario following a Saturday 1-on-1 rep with Odafe Oweh where Tunsil got hurt. While his exact recovery timetable won’t be known until after surgery – Tunsil is still seeking medical opinions, so a procedure date hasn’t been set – Tunsil is expected to miss a vast portion of the season at minimum. It’s all bad news for the Commanders . Quinn didn’t sugarcoat that in his first public comments on the matter. “It’s always tough to talk about a player missing time with a great player like LT,” Quinn said in his Monday press conference. “Not only is he a great player, he is a fantastic teammate. He will be missed and we can’t wait to get him back.” Quinn also confirmed that Washington will roll with Brandon Coleman at left tackle, a position the TCU product played during the 2024 season and again when Tunsil got hurt last year. Coleman has 18 left-tackle starts to his credit, but was competing with Chris Paul to be the starting left guard in 2026. Coleman’s a versatile player, and working inside offered his best shot at playing time with Tunsil as an elite, every-down left tackle. Coleman has played a lot outside, so the transition shouldn’t be too tough. Quinn also said that Coleman has improved as a player since his rookie trial by fire at left tackle. “When you’re a rookie thrown into it and you go through the ups and downs, I think he, after going through some adversity and you get to Year 2 and you want to fight back,” Quinn said. “That’s the type of offseason he had. That’s why I think he’s been off to a good start inside at left guard. We’ll make the move to switch him outside, but, when you come through the tough things, you come out the other side stronger, harder after learning the lessons. Brandon and a couple of other guys are in that same space.” The Commanders will go with Coleman at left tackle and have chosen to leave 2025 first-round NFL draft pick Josh Conerly Jr. at right tackle despite extensive experience playing on the left in college. “We like the progression of where Josh is,” Quinn said. “(Tunsil) is going to be back, and we thought we’d keep the development of where Josh is, and not the shuffle of lots of shuffling.” Quinn also said the Commanders haven’t, to this point, discussed bringing in a left tackle from the outside. A quick reader poll Coleman’s the first option and can cement his place with solid work in camp. No matter what happens at left tackle replacing all Tunsil provides is impossible. “He’s in fantastic shape. He’s really on the top of his game right now,” Quinn said. “In the run and pass, he’s an equally strong player. This is a big deal. When the game’s on, you run behind a player like that. In pass protection, you don’t have to give a lot of help. That’s a good thing. “…The on-field portion speaks for itself. This is a great player. The off-field portion is also significant, with his teammates and how he interacts with them. On and off the field, this is significant for us.”

full_text: The Washington Commanders training camp rolls on for Day 9 in Ashburn, VA. The team had Sunday off, and they’re dealing with an injury to one of their top players. The Commanders are back in pads Monday for Military Appreciation Day. Head coach Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the start of today’s practice. Offensive coordinator David Blough held a Q&A after practice, along with players getting interviewed on the field. Left tackle Laremy Tunsil will require surgery on the triceps injury suffered on Saturday in a 1-on-1 drill vs Odafe Oweh. Quinn said its a tough loss for the team, and he felt bad for Tunsil who’s a leader on and off the field. Brandon Coleman will move over to LT , the position he started 18 games at over the last two seasons with Washington. The team didn’t want to move Josh Conerly Jr. from right tackle to the left side where he played in college. Quinn said they want to continue developing him at the position he played as a rookie. Quinn also said they weren’t planning on bringing in another tackle right away after Tunsil’s injury. The Commanders signed three OL before Tunsil was injured, and they will work with the players currently on the roster. Trey Amos also left practice early on Saturday, and Quinn said he landed awkwardly on his ankle while covering a deep pass to Terry McLaurin. He won’t be at practice Monday, and the team will have a better idea when he’ll return in the next few days. Amos had just returned from the broken fibula that ended his rookie season, and he was also dealing with some soft-tissue soreness that kept him out of all offseason activities. The second-year CB is important to the Commanders short- and long-term plans on defense, but injuries have restricted his ability to develop with the team. Commanders links Hit the road with us for Week 2 ✈️ @SeatGeek | #RaiseHail — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 9, 2026 Articles The Athletic (paywall) Commanders moving Brandon Coleman back to LT after Laremy Tunsil injury Only 72 hours after celebrating the signing of veteran receiver Stefon Diggs, the Washington Commanders lost five-time Pro Bowl left tackle Laremy Tunsil to a torn triceps , an injury that will keep him out for a good portion of the season, if not its entirety. Replacing a player of that caliber is a tall task, especially this late in the offseason. Washington may add to its offensive line — for depth, if not more — but for now, the plan is to turn to Brandon Coleman at left tackle, according to a team source who spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. Coleman, a former third-round pick out of TCU, is capable of playing all five spots on the line and started at left tackle for most of the 2024 season, when Washington reached the NFC Championship Game after going 12-5 in the regular season. Coleman spent much of this offseason training with Tunsil at University of Alabama, where he was immersed in Tunsil’s intense pre-camp regimen and worked with Tunsil’s personal strength and conditioning coach, nutritionist, chef and offensive line specialist. Moving Coleman back to left tackle allows Washington to keep Paul at left guard and Josh Conerly Jr. at right tackle, where he started last season as a rookie after playing on the left side at University of Oregon. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE From Last Man Standig: Nobody expects Coleman to perform at Tunsil’s high-end level, but there are reasons to think he can be effective on the outside. Having a replacement with Coleman’s upside is a relative luxury in an era where every team desperately searches for quality starting linemen. Having Coleman and Paul start would thin out the offensive line depth. Swing tackle Andrew Wylie is the likely primary backup at both tackle spots, though his playing experience is largely on the right side. For more from Ben Standig, click here From Sports Illustrated: The ripples of Laremy Tunsil’s injury will be felt until he returns, but the team is at least positioned to reshuffle what they already have. Now, we all will be waiting to see Coleman take the first-team left tackle reps when Washington returns to practice and what the corresponding first-team alignment looks like at left guard. Coleman has made 20 starts across the regular season and playoffs, with 18 of them coming at left tackle. According to Pro Football Focus, he played 390 total snaps in 2025, allowed 11 pressures and only one QB hit, gave up zero sacks, and earned a 64.6 overall grade . He basically revamped my whole approach to how I treat camp and the season. There’s a lot of stuff that I took from him, from his nutritionist to his strength guy, working with a chef, just taking care of my body a lot better. My prep for practice is a lot different. Seeing how a guy like that prepares, how he treats his body, what he does in his off time and how he recovers — that’s the type of stuff that you can’t get anywhere. There’s only one Laremy Tunsil, in my opinion. The best tackle in the league. Brandon Coleman on Laremy Tunsil To read more of this Sports Illustrated article, CLICK HERE JP Finlay Diggs in, Tunsil out; how do expectations change? Losing Tunsil is undoubtedly a downgrade. There’s no way to gloss this over. But football is a team game and the Eagles won’t care who lines up at left tackle come September 13th. Keep this in mind too: David Blough ’s offense will look much different than Kliff Kingsbury ’s scheme did. Daniels will not line up in the shotgun on nearly every snap. There will be more misdirection, there will be more play action, and there will likely be a better run game. All of those things will help the offensive line, with or without Tunsil. And don’t forget the Commanders did just sign Stef Diggs. It’s not good news. Losing Tunsil is bad news. But the season ain’t over yet either. It hasn’t even begun. Brandon Coleman trained with Laremy Tunsil in Alabama this offseason. Coleman told me earlier this week that experience "basically revamped my whole approach to how I treat camp and the season." I remain bullish on the upside long-term. pic.twitter.com/CJB3Q81yje — Brandon Thorn (@BrandonThornNFL) August 4, 2026 One thing to keep in mind with Decker: they are quite familiar with him. He’s also dealt with multiple health issues last few years: shoulder, toe, knee. They would know the toll those have taken on his game. Again: the 1st option is Coleman. — John Keim (@john_keim) August 9, 2026 Last season, Brandon Coleman made three starts at left tackle. Those starts were in the last three weeks of the season. He also made two starts at left guard last year. 390 total snaps. How much does Diggs move the needle for the WAS receiving corps? A ton. Compared to the 20 teams to have played in the last 10 Super Bowls, and before the signing of Diggs, you could make a credible case for the top 3 WAS receivers to be a SB-caliber group only if you included Chig Okonkwo as #2 and Rachaad White as #3. You could not argue that the WR group alone was SB-caliber. Terry is a solid #1, but anyone else would have to had a breakthrough year for the WR corp to have been credible – something tough to count on. Now, there is no question that the wide receivers and the receivers overall are SB caliber. You can count on both McLaurin and Diggs to get 80 catches and over 1000 yards receiving. McLaurin had 82 catches for 1096 yards in 2024, his last healthy year. His career averages (mostly with bad QBs) are 79 for 1106 yards. Diggs had 85 catches for 1013 yards last year, despite returning from ACL surgery midway through the prior year. His career averages are 99 catches for 1215 yards. I’d say 80 catches for 1000 yards from both of them is so safe a bet that it might be illegal. Chig is about average for a receiver #3 at any position. That means that without having a breakthrough year, but rather just repeating what they’ve already accomplished, Washington’s receiving corp is already Super Bowl caliber. Indeed, the weapons in WAS put the team near the best of the 20 teams to have played in the past 10 Super Bowls. Imagine that. title: 2026 Arizona Cardinals training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Cardinals training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Arizona Cardinals ' camp is at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona, and Cardinals reporter Josh Weinfuss has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Cardinals camp. We will update this file often. How will Arizona's quarterback situation shake out with  Jacoby Brissett  back on a reworked contract? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive into all the updates and check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Thursday.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest on the Cardinals 
 
 Tyler Allgeier 'building' relationship with rookie RB Jeremiyah Love 
 Source: Cardinals' Brissett guaranteed $15.5M in reworked deal 
 Cardinals TE Trey McBride walks back dig at Arizona fanbase 
 Sweat (knee) among four Cards added to PUP list 
 With deal done, Brissett can focus on Cardinals' playbook 
 
 

 Aug. 10 
 Despite expressing his desire to keep Michael Wilson in Arizona long-term, Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort didn't seem too sure that he'd be able to get an extension done with the receiver.

 When asked Monday if he expects to get a long-term deal done with Wilson, who had his first 1,000-yard season in 2025, Ossenfort wouldn't commit to the idea.

 "He's a guy that we want around here a long time," Ossenfort said. "There's no question about it. So, I mean, expect, that's a tough word.

 "I mean, I think our interest is in keeping him here and Michael's been a good player for us. He's going to continue to be a good player for us. So, I know coach [Mike] LaFleur feels the same way and we want Michael here for a long time."

 The two sides have already been negotiating, however, a deal has yet to be agreed upon.

 

 More observations: 

 
 Ossenfort didn't want to get into talks about an extension with left tackle  Paris Johnson Jr ., whose fifth-year option the team picked up for next season. "Honestly, just going to keep extension talks between us. Never really talked about that and don't really want to plan on getting into that." 
 Ossenfort said he always thought he'd get a new deal done with quarterback Jacoby Brissett and said that sometimes negotiations take a while. "This one was no different. And so I think that involves communication back and forth. And we had a lot of conversations over the course of those, the spring, throughout the summer up into training camp. So no, there's never a doubt in my mind that it was going to get done." 
 

 

 Aug. 9 

 Cardinals starting quarterback Jacoby Brissett struggled with the deep ball throughout practice Sunday, missing approximately seven deep balls. Some were long. Some were wide. Four were to Marvin Harrison Jr .

 It was an atypical performance from Brissett, who, until Sunday, had been consistent with his deep balls throughout training camp, typically putting them in a place where only his receivers can catch them.

 After practice, Brissett set out to rectify his misses.

 He and Harrison spent about 15 minutes working on deep balls from approximately 30 yards. It looked as though Brissett was working on his deep touch to get his passes where Harrison can make a play.

 
 Rookie quarterback Carson Beck had a strong finish to Sunday's practice. He hit rookie wide receiver  Reggie Virgil  for a touchdown in the back of the end zone and had a quiet celebration to himself afterward. That came after Beck hit wide receiver Bryson Green on a deep ball but then threw an interception. 
 The Cardinals tried a variety of defensive lineups Sunday. At one point, third-year cornerback Elijah Jones , who has played defense in just one game in his career, took first-team snaps. Second-year defensive back Kitan Crawford , who played 12 games on defense last season, also got some first-team reps. 
 Wide receiver Ihmir Smith-Marsette continued his impressive camp with another touchdown Sunday. He continues to make big catches and has been consistently making plays throughout camp. 
 

 

 Aug. 4 
 Thursday night's Hall of Fame game will not just be a run-through for the players, it will also be the first time the Cardinals' coaching staff will have a chance to be together during a game.

 "I think that's another great thing for us to have this game, to just get a little quick dry run-through on how game day operations go, just from time management, all that stuff," offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett said. "I think it's going to be great for all of us and there'll be some ups and downs and you work through those and grow every day."

 Hackett said he'll be in the booth watching the action unfold from above but with new coach Mike LaFleur calling the plays and quarterback coach Matt Schaub handling Carson Beck , Hackett will be able to help whoever needs help. But that'll also be part of this staff's first time together: Figuring out his role in all of it.

 More observations: 

 
 Even though Josh Sweat hasn't practiced this camp and there isn't a set timeline for his return, defensive coordinator Nick Rallis said Tuesday that Sweat is "locked in" with meetings and post-practice tape. 
 

 
 Aug. 3 
 Deep balls were the theme of the day for the Cardinals as Jacoby Brissett ,  Gardner Minshew II  and Carson Beck put on an aerial display.

 Brissett unleashed a bomb to Marvin Harrison Jr ., who, after letting a deep ball earlier in practice go off his fingertips, came down with a diving grab that would have gained more than 50 yards.

 Beck showed off his deep ball, hitting fellow rookie Reggie Virgil on a beautiful pass. On another deep shot, Beck froze two defenders in the second level before finding a receiver who made the catch a step in front of a defender.

 More observations from the day:  

 
 Tight end Trey McBride was banged up briefly after he was hit in the middle of the field. He went down and was slow to get up but later returned to the offensive drills. 
 The tip drill paid off for the defense on two different plays Monday. On one, defensive lineman  Zachary Carter  tipped a pass by Minshew and L.J. Collier came down with it. On another play, defensive lineman  Roy Lopez  batted down a Beck pass. 
 The catch of the day came from Virgil, who made an impressive one-handed catch in mid-air as he was falling to the ground on a pass from Beck along the sideline. 
 

 

 Aug. 2 
 Jacoby Brissett continues to get more and more comfortable with the offense, as was evident Sunday.
 He had seven drives with the first-team offense, totaling 29 snaps, and finished 13-for-16 passing with two interceptions.

 The first was by defensive back Sean Murphy-Bunting , who jumped the route in front of Michael Wilson for the pick. The second was by second-year linebacker Cody Simon . Brissett's other incompletion was an overthrow.

 Overall, though, Brissett looked to be better in command of what's being asked of him. He didn't have a completion to Marvin Harrison Jr ., who was the intended target on Simon's interception, but Brissett did find a favorite receiver in tight end Trey McBride , who caught all six of the targets thrown his way.

 Back-up quarterback  Gardner Minshew II  was 9-for-13 passing and Carson Beck was 9-for-12 passing. While Beck wasn't consistent with his deep passes, he completed a couple of passes while he was off-balance, showcasing poise in the pocket.

 

 More observations from the day: 

 
 Second-year defensive lineman Walter Nolen III said the discomfort with his left knee during Friday's practice -- the same knee that ended his rookie season in 2025 -- was just a little hiccup. He said he wasn't concerned when it happened. He told…
